questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presents with complaints of sudden, involuntary, and uncontrollable dance-like movements. He also complains of facing difficulty with his memory. His wife says he has gotten very emotional recently. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Huntington's chorea

The clinical presentation of sudden, involuntary, and uncontrollable dance-like movements, along with cognitive and emotional symptoms, is characteristic of Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea.

Huntington's disease (HD) is a degenerative disease of the caudate and putamen (“striate neurons”) caused by an autosomal dominant inheritance of a trinucleotide repeat (CAG) in the Huntington gene (chromosome 4), which results in motor, behavioral, oculomotor, and cognitive dysfunction. HD is characterized by rapid, nonpatterned, semi-purposeful, involuntary choreiform movements of limb, face, or trunk. A phenomenon referred to as anticipation is seen particularly in males, with subsequent generations having larger numbers of repeats and earlier ages of disease onset.

Tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine are inhibitors of VMAT2 and cause presynaptic depletion of catecholamines. Deutetrabenazine is a newer form of tetrabenazine approved for the treatment of chorea associated with Huntington's disease. Deutetrabenazine takes advantage of the stronger bonds that deuterium forms with carbon (deuterated tetrabenazine). They have a longer half-life than the corresponding products of tetrabenazine metabolism.

Tetrabenazine is extensively metabolized by CYP2D6. It may cause hypotension and depression with suicidal tendencies. It can also cause Parkinsonism. Deutetrabenazine has adverse effects similar to those of tetrabenazine.

Other Options:

* Parkinson's disease is characterized by tremors, bradykinesia (slow movement), and rigidity. It does not typically cause the dance-like choreiform movements seen in HD.

* Friedreich ataxia is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the nervous system, causing progressive ataxia (loss of coordination). It does not typically present with choreiform movements.

* Alzheimer's disease primarily affects memory and cognitive function, but it does not cause dance-like choreiform movements.
questions.learning: Huntington's chorea — The clinical presentation of sudden, involuntary, and uncontrollable dance-like movements, along with cognitive and emotional symptoms, is characteristic of Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 24-year old male patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. His heart rate was 100/min, respiratory rate was 24/min, and his chest X-ray is given below. Which of the following is contraindicated in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chest tube insertion

The given radiograph shows elevation of the left hemidiaphragmatic line along with the bowel loops and stomach seen in the pleural cavity. The probable cause would be a diaphragmatic hernia following blunt injury due to a road traffic accident. Chest tube insertion is contraindicated in diaphragmatic hernia due to risk of injury to bowel.

Chest tube insertion/thoracostomy is indicated cases of pneumothorax, hemothorax, chylothorax, pleural effusion, and pleural empyema. Contraindications include pulmonary adhesions, pulmonary trauma, coagulopathy, and diaphragmatic hernia.

Chest radiography performed after the placement of a nasogastric tube can be helpful in identifying any herniation of the stomach into the chest. Log roll and epidural anesthesia are not contraindicated in diaphragmatic hernia.

Blunt trauma to the diaphragm results in a linear diaphragmatic rupture, which is typically large and accompanied by the herniation of abdominal contents into the chest. Acute diaphragmatic injuries require repair through the abdominal approach to address associated visceral injuries. The diaphragmatic edges are approximated using Allis clamps, and the defect is closed with a running 1-0 polypropylene suture.
questions.learning: Chest tube insertion — The given radiograph shows elevation of the left hemidiaphragmatic line along with the bowel loops and stomach seen in the pleural cavity.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young adult presents with a fracture of the neck of the femur. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: In young adults, the primary goal of managing a femoral neck fracture is to preserve the patient's native hip joint. Unlike elderly patients, young adults have a robust blood supply and better bone healing potential, making anatomical reduction and internal fixation (e.g., using screws or a plate) the treatment of choice. External fixation (Option A) is typically reserved for temporary stabilization in severe polytrauma and is not a definitive treatment for this fracture. Hemiarthroplasty (Option C) replaces only the femoral head and is reserved for elderly, low-demand patients. Total hip replacement (Option D) is the gold standard for arthritic hips or active elderly patients with displaced fractures but is avoided in young adults due to the limited lifespan of prosthetic implants. Therefore, internal fixation is the most appropriate strategy to ensure long-term joint function in a young patient

• Age: 6 months – 3 years

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A kindergarten teacher believes that all her students are failing because of her. She also reports hearing voices commenting on her actions. What is the best treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Antidepressant + Antipsychotic

The patient has features of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) with psychotic features (psychotic depression).

• Delusion of guilt (“All my students are failing because of me.”)
• Auditory hallucinations (voices commenting on her actions)

These are mood-congruent psychotic symptoms, which occur in severe depression.

The treatment of psychotic depression is:

• An antidepressant + an antipsychotic
• Alternatively, Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) is considered first-line in severe cases, especially with suicidality, catatonia, refusal to eat, or the need for rapid improvement.

Why not the other options?

• A. Psychotherapy alone: Inadequate for psychotic depression.
• B. Antidepressant alone: Does not adequately treat psychotic symptoms.
• D. Mood stabilizer: Used for bipolar disorder, not unipolar psychotic depression.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the investigation shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mammography

The image shown above is of mammography.

The mammogram is an X-ray picture of the breast. The anode in the X-ray tube is made up of molybdenum. The X-ray film used is a single-sided coated film.

The views used are two types: Craniocaudal and Mediolateral oblique

Uses of the mammogram:

* Routine screening for (ductal carcinoma in situ) DCIS.

* The most important sign of malignancy in a mammogram is clustered microcalcification (more than 5 particles in 1 cm², 3 particles of less than 0.5 mm size)

Radiological findings in other diseases of the breast:

* Popcorn calcification is seen in fibroadenoma.

* Broken-needle type of calcification is seen in duct ectasia.

* Tea-cup calcification is seen in fibrocystic disease.

Differences between mammography and conventional radiography:

* Mammography involves the use of low-energy and high-amperage waves.

* The target anode is made of a tungsten disc in conventional X-ray tubes and molybdenum in mammography X-ray tubes.

* Most mammography tubes use beryllium exit windows between the evacuated tube and the atmosphere.

* The conventional X-ray tube has an aluminum filter, but in mammography, a molybdenum filter is used.

Some indications for mammography:

* Evaluation of breast signs and symptoms like masses, skin changes, deformities, nipple retraction, discharge, and eczema

* Breast cancer screening

* Follow-up for patients treated for breast cancer

* Localization of lesions not visible on ultrasound

Pearl PF1991: Breast Cancer Screening

Breast Cancer Screening*

Individuals are encouraged to conduct a risk assessment by 25 years of age. This helps classify them into average risk or increased risk groups.

Recommendations:

* Average-risk (no known genetic or family history of breast cancer)

* 25-39 years of age: clinical breast examination every 1-3 years;

* ≥ 40 years of age: clinical breast examination and mammogram annually

* Increased risk (positive family or genetic history of breast cancer)

* Consult a healthcare professional every 6-12 months after 21 years of age

* Annual mammogram or MRI from 25 years of age or 10 years prior to the age at which the youngest family member was diagnosed with breast cancer (whichever is earliest)

* Asymptomatic women with previously treated breast cancer

* Consult a healthcare professional every 6-12 months

* Annual mammogram

* Annual MRI to be considered

* Mammogram and USG are not contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women

High-risk patients for breast cancer:

* Women (or a first-degree relative) with a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation or TP53 or PTEN genes

* Two first-degree relatives with breast cancers with or without gene mutations

* Women with a history of chest irradiation between the ages of 10 and 30

* Women with previously biopsy-proven breast cancer

* Women with ≥ 20% lifetime risk for breast cancer based on breast cancer risk models

*According to NCCN 2022 guidelines

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the options below best defines LD50?
options: 50% animal mortality in an experiment after exposure to the drug
50% reduction of infection in the given population of experimental animals
Dose of the drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population
Range of concentration at which the likelihood of efficacy is high and the probability of adverse effects is low
questions.explanation: 50% animal mortality is an experiment after exposure to the drug In toxicology and pharmacology, Median Lethal Dose (LD50) is a standardized measure used to evaluate the acute toxicity of a substance. It is specifically defined as the dose required to cause death in exactly 50% of the tested population of experimental animals within a specified time frame. Option B is incorrect as it describes the curative dose (ED50) or infection control. Option C refers to the Median Toxic Dose (TD50), which measures adverse side effects rather than lethality. Option D describes the Therapeutic Window or Index, which is a safety margin between effective and toxic concentrations. Determining the LD50 is a fundamental step in safety assessment, helping researchers understand the relative danger of chemicals and drugs. A lower LD50 value indicates higher toxicity, as a smaller dose is needed to reach the 50% mortality threshold in the study subjects.
questions.learning: 50% animal mortality is an experiment after exposure to the drug In toxicology and pharmacology, Median Lethal Dose (LD50) is a standardized measure used to evaluate the acute toxicity of a substance.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A female patient presents with ambiguous genitalia and rapid virilization. She also complains of excessive facial hair growth, voice deepening, and an enlarged clitoris over the past few months. CT scan is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

The presented clinical scenario, along with the CT scan findings of bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with nodules in the adrenal cortex, suggests a likely diagnosis of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH).

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a disorder of cortisol synthesis. It has an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Cortisol deficiency increases the secretion of the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), causing adrenal hyperplasia with the overproduction of intermediate metabolites. This child has clitoromegaly due to increased androgen synthesis. The enzyme 21-hydroxylase helps in the downstream synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone. A deficiency of aldosterone causes salt wasting that presents as low blood pressure.

The presentation depends on the enzyme that is deficient, which could result in mineralocorticoid deficiency or excess, incomplete virilization or precocious puberty in affected males, and virilization or sexual infantilism in affected females.

Given below is the pathway and enzymes involved in adrenal steroid synthesis:

Other options:

Option B: Adrenocortical carcinoma might appear as a large, irregular mass within the adrenal gland. The mass could have areas of necrosis or hemorrhage, contributing to its irregular appearance.

Option C: A pheochromocytoma typically presents as a well-defined, solid mass within the adrenal gland. It might be associated with areas of hemorrhage, leading to a heterogeneous appearance.

Option D: The adrenal glands may appear normal in size or slightly enlarged on a CT scan in case of primary hyperaldosteronism. There might not be distinct masses or nodules in the adrenal glands.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are local complications of acute pancreatitis? 1. Pseudocyst 2. Pleural effusion 3. Ileus 4. Acute fluid collection Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Complications of acute pancreatitis are classified into local and systemic complications according to the Revised Atlanta Classification (2012). Local complications arise from inflammation or necrosis within and around the pancreas, whereas systemic complications involve distant organ dysfunction.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Pseudocyst ✅

• A pancreatic pseudocyst is a late local complication that usually develops ≥4 weeks after interstitial edematous pancreatitis and contains enzyme-rich fluid enclosed by a fibrous wall.

• 2. Pleural effusion ✅

• Pleural effusion, especially left-sided, is a recognized local extrapancreatic complication due to the spread of pancreatic inflammation or pancreaticopleural fistula.

• 3. Ileus ❌

• Ileus is considered a systemic manifestation of acute pancreatitis resulting from severe inflammation and electrolyte disturbances, rather than a local pancreatic complication.

• 4. Acute fluid collection ✅

• Acute peripancreatic fluid collection (APFC) develops within the first 4 weeks of interstitial edematous pancreatitis and is one of the earliest local complications.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Complications of acute pancreatitis are classified into local and systemic complications according to the Revised Atlanta Classification (2012).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant presents with excessive watering of the right eye and mucopurulent discharge emerging from the right punctum. Based on this presentation, what is the most appropriate management or treatment option?
questions.explanation: This infant is presenting with Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (CNLDO), a common condition where the lacrimal duct fails to canalize, most often at the Valve of Hasner. This leads to chronic tearing and secondary infection, resulting in mucopurulent discharge. In infants under one year of age, the first-line treatment is "Crigler’s lacrimal sac massage" combined with topical antibiotics if infection is present. This conservative approach is successful in over 90% of cases as the duct often opens spontaneously. Option A (Syringing) and Option B (Probing) are invasive and are generally reserved for cases that fail to resolve after 12 months of age. Option D (DCR) is a major bypass surgery used for adults or older children who have failed probing. For a 3-month-old, starting with conservative massage is the most appropriate, least invasive, and highly effective initial management strategy
questions.learning: This infant is presenting with Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (CNLDO), a common condition where the lacrimal duct fails to canalize, most often at the Valve of Hasner.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Does Von Gierke's disease involve a deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Von Gierke's disease, also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (GSD I), is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose 6-phosphatase. This enzyme is essential for the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, as it converts glucose 6-phosphate into free glucose in the liver and kidneys. Without it, patients experience severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (due to glycogen accumulation), hyperuricemia, and lactic acidosis. Liver phosphorylase deficiency (Option A) causes GSD Type VI (Hers disease), which is generally milder. Lysosomal alpha-glucosidase deficiency (Option B) causes GSD Type II (Pompe disease), characterized by cardiomegaly and muscle weakness. Hepatic glycogen synthase deficiency (Option C) is known as GSD Type 0, which results in decreased glycogen stores rather than accumulation. Understanding these enzymatic defects is fundamental for metabolic biochemistry and pediatrics. Von Gierke's requires frequent feedings with uncooked cornstarch to maintain stable blood glucose levels and prevent life-threatening hypoglycemic episodes and metabolic derangements

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 28-year-old male patient presents with a history of progressive vision loss and night blindness. Upon examination, the patient displays characteristic retinal degeneration with peripheral bone spicule pigmentation. Which of the following syndromes is not likely associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marfan syndrome

The patient has retinitis pigmentosa (RP), characterized by:

• Progressive night blindness
• Peripheral visual field loss (“tunnel vision”)
• Bone spicule pigmentation on fundus examination
• Attenuated retinal vessels and waxy optic disc pallor

Pathophysiology: Progressive degeneration of rod photoreceptors followed by cones

Syndromic associations of RP:

• Usher syndrome → sensorineural hearing loss
• Refsum disease → phytanic acid accumulation, ataxia, neuropathy
• Kearns–Sayre syndrome → mitochondrial disorder with ophthalmoplegia and pigmentary retinopathy

Marfan syndrome is not classically associated with retinitis pigmentosa.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Causes of AUB are subdivided by the acronym PALM-COEIN. What are the characteristics of PALM causes? I. Structural lesions II. Diagnosed by ultrasound III. Confirmed by histopathology Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and III

The FIGO PALM-COEIN classification is the standard system used to classify the causes of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) in reproductive-aged women.

The PALM group includes structural causes that can usually be identified by imaging and confirmed by histopathological examination, whereas the COEIN group comprises non-structural causes. All the statements regarding PALM causes are correct:

• I. Structural lesions: PALM includes structural abnormalities of the uterus.
• II. Diagnosed by ultrasound: Most PALM lesions can be detected by transvaginal ultrasonography, saline infusion sonography, hysteroscopy, or MRI.
• III. Confirmed by histopathology: Tissue diagnosis confirms conditions such as endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, adenomyosis (after hysterectomy), and polyps.
questions.learning: I, II and III — The FIGO PALM-COEIN classification is the standard system used to classify the causes of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) in reproductive-aged women.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 54-year-old chronic alcoholic patient presents with altered sensorium and confusion. He also complains of weakness in both lower limbs and occasional tingling in his legs. His staple diet includes white polished rice. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Beri beri

The given clinical scenario of a 54-year-old chronic alcoholic, who consumes polished rice as a staple diet, and presents with altered sensorium and tingling sensation (neuritis), points to the diagnosis of Beri-beri.

The vitamin deficiency associated with this condition is thiamine (vitamin B1). It is commonly seen in people who consume polished rice-based monotonous diets. Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

The two principal deficiency diseases of thiamine are:

Dry beri-beri is associated with neurological deficits such as peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability. Wet beriberi (cardiac) is associated with tachycardia, cardiomegaly, cardiac failure, edema.

Thiamine deficiency can also be named based on the pattern of dietary deficiency seen. These include oriental beri-beri (diet predominantly including polished rice) and occidental Beri-beri (a diet rich in refined flours and food fads). The latter form is commonly seen in alcoholics. Complications include lactic acidosis and Wernicke's encephalopathy in adults.

High-risk groups for thiamine deficiency are:

* Lactating mothers

* Patients on regular haemodialysis

* Persistent vomiting

* Prolonged gastric aspiration

* People who go on long fasts

* High-risk groups should be treated with direct supplementation of thiamine.

Other options:

Option A: Phrynoderma is a form of asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic follicular hyperkeratosis, where follicular papules of various sizes with central keratotic plugs that block the follicle openings develop on the skin.

Option C: Pellagra will classically present with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia in a predominantly maize-consuming population, not with neuritis in an alcoholic patient consuming white polished rice.

Option D: Eczema is inflammation of the skin seen in a variety of skin conditions.Eczema. It is characterized by itching, dryness, erythema, fissuring, hyperkeratosis, lichenification, scaling, and vesiculation of the affected areas.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 80-year-old man develops pain and swelling in the right calf following immobilization for a right intertrochanteric fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient possesses several classic risk factors for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) (Option B): advanced age (80 years), a recent major lower limb fracture, and immobilization . The clinical signs of pain and swelling localized specifically to the calf muscle are the most common presentations of an acute clot in the lower extremity venous system. Chronic osteomyelitis (Option A) presents with long-term discharge and localized bone pain, not acute swelling. Compartment syndrome (Option C) is a surgical emergency characterized by "pain out of proportion" and loss of pulses, typically following acute crush injuries rather than prolonged immobilization. Arterial claudication (Option D) causes pain only during exercise that is relieved by rest. Therefore, because the patient fits the "Virchow's Triad" perfectly (stasis and vascular injury), DVT is the most probable and dangerous diagnosis. Clinicians must urgently confirm this with Doppler ultrasound to prevent a lethal pulmonary embolism
questions.learning: The patient possesses several classic risk factors for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) (Option B): advanced age (80 years), a recent major lower limb fracture, and immobilization .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a cause of secondary PPH? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Placenta previa

Secondary postpartum hemorrhage (secondary PPH) is excessive vaginal bleeding occurring:

• After 24 hours postpartum
• Up to 6 weeks after delivery

Common causes include:

• Retained placental tissue or retained cotyledon
• Endometritis
• Placental polyp
• Subinvolution of the placental site

Placenta previa is a cause of antepartum hemorrhage, not secondary postpartum hemorrhage.

Important concepts:

• Retained products prevent proper uterine contraction and involution
• Infection causes uterine inflammation and delayed healing
• Placental polyp refers to retained placental tissue forming a vascular mass

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old presented with flaccid bullae on her skin which are easy to rupture. The biopsy revealed a suprabasal split. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pemphigus vulgaris

The given clinical vignette of a bullous disorder with the histologic picture pointing towards a suprabasal blister suggests the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3. Rarely antibodies against desmoglein 1 can also be found. The antibodies are commonly IgG antibodies. Desmoglein 3 is mainly present in the basal and suprabasal layers of the skin and mucosa.

The patients, therefore, present with flaccid bullae over the skin and mucosal ulcerations. Oral mucosa is commonly affected. Other areas where ulceration can be seen are conjunctiva, nasopharynx, larynx, etc. Cutaneous lesions are more common over the scalp, face, neck, upper chest, and back.

Direct immunofluorescence will show the deposition of antibodies around the keratinocytes in the epidermis. It presents with a characteristic fish-net appearance in the immunofluorescence assay It is treated with steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, etc.

The images attached below depict the lesions, the suprabasal split, and the fish-net pattern respectively seen in a case of pemphigus vulgaris.

Option B: Pemphigus foliaceus is a benign form of pemphigus, an inflammatory blistering disorder. This is a form of a subcorneal blister, where the stratum corneum forms the roof of the bulla. It is caused by autoantibodies that result in the dissolution of intercellular attachments within the epidermis. Antibodies against desmoglein 1 are mainly seen in pemphigus foliaceous. There is no involvement of the mucosal epithelium in pemphigus foliaceus.

Lesions are most common on the scalp, face, chest, and back. Bullae are superficial and mainly present as areas of erythema and crusting. These represent superficial erosions at sites of blister rupture.

Option C: Pemphigus vegetans is a rare form of the bullous disorder that presents with large, moist, verrucous, vegetating plaques studded with pustules on the groin, axillae, and flexural surfaces. It is associated with eosinophilic microabscess. It has two types, a severe Neumann type, and a milder Hallopeau type.

Option D: Erythema multiforme is a self‐limiting cytotoxic dermatitis resulting from cell‐mediated hypersensitivity most commonly to infection or drugs. The common triggers are

• Herpes simplex infection
• Mycoplasma infection
• Bacterial infections
• Fungal infections
• Vaccinations
• Malignancy: carcinoma, lymphoma, leukemia
• Drug reactions: sulfonamides, cotrimoxazole, penicillins
• Miscellaneous: Lupus erythematosus (Rowell Syndrome), Sarcoidosis, Polyarteritis Nodosa

It presents clinically with macular, papular, or urticarial lesions, along with the classic acral iris or target lesions. The lesions are distributed on the distal extremities, palms or trunk, and oral and genital mucous membranes.

Target lesions are less than 3 cm in diameter, rounded, and have three zones:

• The central area of dusky erythema or purpura
• Middle paler zone of edema
• The outer ring of erythema with a well‐defined edge

Atypical lesions will have only 2 zones. They fade in 1-2 weeks leaving dusky discoloration.
questions.learning: Pemphigus vulgaris — The given clinical vignette of a bullous disorder with the histologic picture pointing towards a suprabasal blister suggests the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which cellular process does Bedaquiline primarily target to exert its therapeutic effect?
questions.explanation: Bedaquiline is a novel, breakthrough diarylquinoline antibiotic used specifically for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Its unique mechanism of action involves the inhibition of ATP synthesis within the Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacterium. It specifically binds to the C-subunit of the mycobacterial ATP synthase enzyme, which is the rotary engine that generates ATP through the proton gradient. By cutting off the energy supply, bedaquiline effectively kills both active and dormant bacilli, as even non-replicating bacteria require ATP for survival. Mycolic acid synthesis inhibition (Option B) is the mechanism of isoniazid and ethionamide. Protein synthesis inhibition (Option C) is how aminoglycosides or linezolid work. Inhibiting reverse transcriptase (Option D) is the mechanism for antiretroviral drugs used in HIV. Clinically, bedaquiline is reserved for complex cases due to its risk of QT interval prolongation, but its targeted action on bioenergetics makes it a cornerstone of modern MDR-TB regimens

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following do not cause polyhydramnios?
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid) results from either an overproduction of fluid or a failure of the fetus to swallow and process it. Renal agenesis (the absence of kidneys) causes Oligohydramnios (too little fluid) because fetal urine is the primary source of amniotic fluid in the second and third trimesters. This is the hallmark of Potter's sequence. Neural tube defects (Option A) cause polyhydramnios due to increased transudation of fluid from the exposed neural tissue and impaired swallowing. Twin gestation (Option B), especially with twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, can lead to polyhydramnios in the recipient twin. Esophageal atresia (Option C) prevents the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid, leading to its accumulation in the sac. Other causes include maternal diabetes and fetal hydrops. Differentiating between causes of fluid imbalance is critical for prenatal diagnosis and management. Polyhydramnios is associated with an increased risk of preterm labor and placental abruption due to uterine overdistension
questions.learning: Polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid) results from either an overproduction of fluid or a failure of the fetus to swallow and process it. Renal agenesis (the absence of kidneys) causes Oligohydramnios (too little fluid) because fetal urine is the primary…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For a newborn born to an HIV-positive mother who did not receive antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy, what is the recommended initial post-exposure prophylaxis regimen to reduce the risk of mother-to-child HIV transmission?
questions.explanation: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) is critical for HIV management. When a newborn is delivered by a high-risk woman (e.g., one who was not on treatment or has a high viral load), dual post-exposure prophylaxis is required. The current recommendation is a combination of Nevirapine and Zidovudine for 6 weeks. This intensified regimen is more effective than monotherapy in preventing vertical transmission in high-risk scenarios. Nevirapine monotherapy for 6 weeks (Option D) is the standard for low-risk infants whose mothers were stable on ART. Options A (6 months) and B (Zidovudine only) are not the standard protocols for this specific situation. Alongside prophylaxis, these infants require early infant diagnosis via HIV-DNA PCR testing at 6 weeks. Breastfeeding recommendations vary; in India, exclusive breast feeding is encouraged for 6 months if the mother is on ART. Early identification of maternal status and rapid neonatal intervention significantly reduce the rate of pediatric HIV
questions.learning: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) is critical for HIV management. When a newborn is delivered by a high-risk woman (e.g., one who was not on treatment or has a high viral load), dual post-exposure prophylaxis is required.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An overweight man (90 kg) presented with complaints of not being able to squat and rest pain of left hip for 6 months duration. He had a past history of steroid and creatine use. His X-ray revealed destruction of the articular surface of femoral head with the presence of subchondral cysts and positive crescent sign. His MRI is suggestive of marrow edema. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Osteonecrosis of femoral head

The complaints of hip pain in an overweight man with a history of long-term steroid use along with the radiological findings of subchondral cysts and positive crescent sign in the femoral head are characteristic of osteonecrosis of the femoral head.

Avascular necrosis or osteonecrosis is a painful bone condition that results from diminished blood supply mainly due to trauma or non-traumatic etiologies. Alcohol, corticosteroids, immunosuppressives, and cytotoxic drugs, either singly or in combination, are the most common causes of non-traumatic osteonecrosis. The typical features are pain with movements in or near the joint, click in the joint, joint stiffness, limping gait, and deformity. Restriction of movements is also a feature of this condition.

An x-ray shows reactive new bone formation, increased radiolucency in the subchondral bone, and a distorted articular surface. The crescent sign is a subchondral fracture overlying the necrotic segment of the femoral head seen on radiography. MRI is the investigation of choice in early disease. It allows the identification of AVN of the femoral head and also determines the exact stage and extent of the pathologic process.

Management is based on Ficat and Arlet Classification:

Stage
Findings
Management
Method

1
X-ray normal, MRI +ve
Conservative
Bisphosphonates

2a
X-ray: sclerosis, cysts, no collapse
Conservative
Bisphosphonates

2b
X-ray: crescent sign, no collapse
Surgical decompression
Core decompression

3
Collapse+loss of sphericity
Surgical
Osteotomy

4
Advanced arthritis
Reconstructive
Total hip replacement

Other options:

Option A: Tuberculosis of the hip is characterized by painful and restricted movements of the hip, especially at night. The radiographic findings are not appreciable in the early stages. Later stages show periarticular osteoporosis, hazy and irregular joint margins with a reduction in the joint space, and wandering acetabulum.

Option B: Fracture neck of femur is common in elderly people after a trivial fall due to osteoporosis. Examination reveals tenderness in the groin along with shortening and external rotation of the leg. Xrays show a break in Shenton’s line and trabecular stream, overriding of greater trochanter so that it lies at the level of the head of the femur, and external rotation of the femur is evident by prominent lesser trochanter.

Option C: Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors commonly present in adolescents. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. They are usually painless. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

While testing the deleterious health hazards on a group of people after giving a new drug and a placebo, the following results were obtained as tabulated. Based on these results, which of the following is true?

Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 10% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.9
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 10
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 10% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 9
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1

In the given scenario, absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1.

Let us reconstruct the design table in the following way:

Health hazard (+)
Health hazard (-)
Total

New drug

Relative risk (RR) is given as a/(a+b) ÷ c/(c+d).

RR = 1603/15225 ÷ 1804/15225 = 0.106/0.118 = 0.89 ≈ 0.90.

Relative risk reduction (RRR) = 1 – Relative risk. In this scenario, RRR = 1 – 0.9 = 0.1 or 10%.

Absolute risk rate of the group using new drug = a/(a+b) = 1603/15225 = 0.106 or 10.6% ≈ 11%.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient, who is a known case of HIV with a CD4 count of 200 cells/cu.mm, presents with a 5-day history of cough and high-grade fever without chills and rigors. There is no history of diarrhea, vomiting, or nuchal rigidity. Chest X-ray is normal. Which of the following will be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Co-trimoxazole only

The clinical scenario of an HIV-infected patient with a CD4 count of 200/mm3 with fever, cough, and a normal chest X-ray is indicative of underlying Pneumocystis pneumonia. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients. It is treated with co-trimoxazole.

Patients usually present with fever and nonproductive cough. It can also affect other organs like lymph nodes, spleen, and liver.

The classic radiographic appearance is likely normal or could consist of faint bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Perihilar infiltrates are less common in patients with AIDS. CT will show diffuse ground-glass opacities.

Histopathology of the tissue will show foamy alveolar infiltrate and mononuclear interstitial infiltrates, which is pathognomonic of PCP. Specific stains like methenamine silver, toluidine blue O, or Giemsa can show the cysts. Other tests that are used for the diagnosis of PCP are polymerase chain reaction, (1→3)-β-d-glucan, etc.

The treatment of PCP is with cotrimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).

For patients with a PaO2 <70 mmHg or with an arterial-alveolar (a–A) gradient >35 mmHg, adjunct glucocorticoid therapy should be used in addition to cotrimoxazole. As the clinical stem does not indicate poor oxygenation, steroid therapy does not have to be initiated. (Option B)

Atovaquone, pentamidine, and primaquine + clindamycin are alternative agents for the treatment of PCP.

Other options:

Option A: Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid + azithromycin is used for the empirical management of bacterial pneumonia on an outpatient basis. Bacterial pneumonia, however, tends to present with consolidation on chest X-rays, which is not seen in this patient.

Below is an image of bacterial pneumonia showing consolidation on X-ray:

Option D: Antitubercular therapy would be indicated if tuberculosis was suspected in the patient. Tuberculosis in HIV-infected patients can be seen in relatively higher CD4 counts and typically presents with fever, cough, weight loss, night sweats, and an abnormal chest X-ray revealing upper lobe cavitary disease.

Pearl PF1966: Opportunistic Infections/HIV related conditions and ART initiation

Clinical scenario
Action

Any undiagnosed active infection with fever
Diagnose and treat first; start Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) when stable

Tuberculosis (TB)
Start TB treatment first; start ART as soon as possible after 2 weeks and before 2 months. For those with CD4 less than 50/cmm, start ART within 2 weeks Caution is needed for PLHIV with TB meningitis, since immediate ART is associated with more severe adverse events than initiating ART 2 months after the start of TB treatment

Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)

Treat PCP first; start ART when PCP treatment is completed

Invasive fungal diseases: Oesophageal candidiasis, penicilliosis, histoplasmosis
Start treatment for oesophageal candidiasis first; start ART as soon as the patient can swallow comfortably. Treat penicilliosis, and histoplasmosis first; start ART when the patient is stabilized or opportunistic infection treatment is completed.

Cryptococcal meningitis
Treat cryptococcal meningitis. ART initiation should be deferred until there is evidence of sustained clinical response to anti-fungal therapy and after 4 weeks of induction and consolidation treatment with amphotericin B containing regimen.

Bacterial pneumonia
Treat pneumonia first; start ART when treatment is completed

Malaria
Treat malaria first; start ART when treatment is completed

Acute diarrhoea which may reduce absorption of ART
Diagnose the cause and treat diarrhoea first; start ART when diarrhoea is stabilized or controlled

Non-severe anaemia (Hb< 9 g/dl)
Start ART if no other causes for anaemia are found (HIV is often the cause of anaemia)

Skin conditions such as PPE and seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, HIV-related exfoliative dermatitis
Start ART (ART may resolve these problems)

Suspected Mycobacterium Avium Complex (MAC), Cryptosporidiosis and Microsporidiosis
Start ART (ART may resolve these problems)

Cytomegalovirus retinitis
Start treatment for CMV urgently and start ART after 2 weeks of CMV treatment

Toxoplasmosis
Treat toxoplasmosis; start ART after 6 weeks of treatment and when the patient is stabilized
questions.learning: Co-trimoxazole only — The clinical scenario of an HIV-infected patient with a CD4 count of 200/mm3 with fever, cough, and a normal chest X-ray is indicative of underlying Pneumocystis pneumonia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer from the sub-Himalayan belt had a thorn prick injury a year back and developed a warty, verrucous growth at the site of prick. A skin biopsy sample was taken and sent for histopathological examination. The characteristic microscopic body as shown in the image was seen. Which of the following could be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromoblastomycosis

The history of a slowly spreading warty, verrucous lesion following a thorn prick injury and the histopathological image showing medlar bodies is suggestive of chromoblastomycosis.

Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation. Over months to years, the primary lesion becomes verrucous and wart-like with extension along the draining lymphatics.

Histologically, the lesions are granulomatous and the dark sclerotic bodies may be seen within leukocytes or giant cells called medlar/copper penny bodies.

• Sporothrix schenckii

• Cladophialophora carrionii

• Phialophora richardsiae

• Wangiella dermatitidis

• Madurella mycetomatis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 35-year-old female, a known case of sickle disease came with complaints of unprovoked pain in the extremities and torso. A thromboembolic episode was suspected. What is the first drug to be started for prophylaxis of thromboembolic events in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Heparin

The clinical scenario is suggestive of a sickle cell crisis. This patient with unprovoked pain in the extremities and torso most likely has a thromboembolic episode. The first drug to be started for prophylaxis of thromboembolic events is heparin.

The mainstay of prophylaxis of thromboembolic events lies in anticoagulant medication. The initial parenteral therapy with heparin, LMWH, or fondaparinux shifted to a novel oral anticoagulant like dabigatran with warfarin acting as a bridge drug, followed by a long oral monotherapy with rivaroxaban or apixaban for a few weeks.

Pearl PF1167: Prophylaxis for DVT

Mechanical prophylaxis

Early ambulation

Acts by activating the calf pump mechanism

Pneumatic compression stocking

Prevents stasis by periodically compressing the calves

Pharmacological prophylaxis

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) - Enoxaparin

Fondaparinux

Prevent thrombus formation by inhibiting factor Xa

Apixaban

Rivaroxaban

Oral factor Xa inhibitors

Unfractionated heparin (UFH)

Prevents action of factors VIII - XII and production of thrombin/fibrin.

Used in renal insufficiency

Warfarin

Inhibits hepatic production of factors II, VII, IX and X
questions.learning: Heparin — The clinical scenario is suggestive of a sickle cell crisis. This patient with unprovoked pain in the extremities and torso most likely has a thromboembolic episode.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man develops headache, nausea, and breathlessness while trekking at high altitude. To relieve his symptoms, the physician prescribes a medication. This drug primarily acts on which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from acute mountain sickness (AMS) due to high-altitude hypoxia. The standard pharmacological intervention is acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that primarily acts on the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron. By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the PCT, the drug prevents bicarbonate reabsorption, leading to mild metabolic acidosis. This acidosis stimulates the central respiratory centers, prompting compensatory hyperventilation which increases blood oxygenation and alleviates AMS symptoms. Regarding the distractors, loop diuretics (Option B), thiazides (Option C), and potassium-sparing diuretics (Option D) act on different segments of the nephron and do not address the physiological causes of altitude sickness. Therefore, the PCT is the specific site where acetazolamide exerts its therapeutic effect for mountain climbers
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from acute mountain sickness (AMS) due to high-altitude hypoxia. The standard pharmacological intervention is acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that primarily acts on the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which article of the Indian Constitution confers Right to Life to the citizens of India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Article 21

The Right to Life is given in Article 21 of the Indian Constitution.

Option A: Article 11 defines the right of the parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.

Option C: Article 23 defines the prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labor.

Option D: Article 25 defines the freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with progressive difficulty in swallowing for both solids and liquids for 8 months. Barium swallow done is shown below. Upper GI endoscopy and manometry are performed in this patient. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?
options: Loss of lower esophageal sphincter pressure causing reflux
incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter
It is is a primary motility disorder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of lower esophageal sphincter pressure causing reflux

The given clinical scenario and the barium swallow showing bird beak appearance is suggestive of Achalasia cardia.  The diagnostic criteria for achalasia with manometry are impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis with elevated LES pressure.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) in response to swallowing. There is incomplete(<75%) relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

Manometry is considered the most sensitive investigation to diagnose achalasia as it identifies early disease before esophageal dilatation and food retention.

Endoscopy is useful for ruling out pseudoachalasia.

Note: 24 hours pH monitoring is ideal and most accurate in patients with the features of gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Pearl PF0313: Achalasia Cardia

Achalasia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis.

Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus.

Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility.

Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease

Clinical features:

* dysphagia (solid and liquid food)

* regurgitation

* chest pain

* weight loss

* bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration

Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, Chagas’ disease, and pseudoachalasia

On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance

Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive)

Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation and Heller myotomy

Pearl PF1482: Barium swallow

Diffuse esophageal spasm: Corkscrew appearance

Feline esophagus: Transient transverse bands seen in the mid and lower esophagus on a double-contrast barium swallow. It is seen in active gastroesophageal reflux, hiatus hernia, and eosinophilic esophagitis.

Achalasia: Dilated esophagus with a retained column of barium and bird beak sign.

Zenker's diverticulum: Posterior outpouching of the hypopharynx through a weakness in the muscle layer called Killian dehiscence.

Esophageal carcinoma: Irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction, and shouldered margins.

Schatzki's ring: Thin submucosal circumferential ring in the lower esophagus at the squamocolumnar junction.

Esophageal web in a patient with Plummer Vinson syndrome. Esophageal webs are thin membranes of normal esophageal tissue consisting of mucosa and submucosa. Translucent part denotes esophageal web.
questions.learning: Loss of lower esophageal sphincter pressure causing reflux The given clinical scenario and the barium swallow showing bird beak appearance is suggestive of Achalasia cardia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 84-year-old man with a history of stroke 2 years ago, who is on prolonged bed rest, develops a pressure ulcer with partial thickness skin loss and a clean base. What is the grade of his pressure sore?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Grade 2

The pressure sore is of grade 2 in this case.

Grade 2 of bedsore corresponds to partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis.

Pressure sores, also known as bedsores, pressure ulcers, or decubitus ulcers, are defined as tissue necrosis with ulceration due to prolonged pressure. When the external pressure exceeds the capillary occlusive pressure, blood flow ceases leading to tissue anoxia, necrosis, and ulceration. An external pressure of >30 mmHg leads to the formation of pressure sores.

The common sites of pressure sores in decreasing frequency are the ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleolus (lateral followed by medial), and occiput.

Given below are images showing the stages of pressure sore.

Prevention is the best treatment for pressure sores. They can be prevented with good skincare, the use of air-fluidized beds, special pressure-dispersion cushions, or foams. Fecal or urinary diversion can be considered in special cases.

The position of the bedridden patients should be changed once every 2 hours and wheel-chair bound patients should be taught to get off their chairs for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.

Surgical management of pressure sores follows the same principles involved in acute wound treatment. Prior to the operation, the pressure sores should be adequately debrided, and vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) can be used to promote the growth of granulation tissue required for surgical closure. Large skin flaps that have muscle with sensory innervation are best for reconstruction.

VAC is done by applying intermittent negative pressure of approximately -125 mmHg to hasten debridement and promote granulation tissue formation. Negative pressure decreases edema, removes interstitial fluid, and increases blood flow. This decreases bacterial growth and increases cell proliferation.
questions.learning: Grade 2 — The pressure sore is of grade 2 in this case. Grade 2 of bedsore corresponds to partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy from a rural area is brought to the orthopedic clinic by his parents. He has a history of a congenital foot deformity that was never treated during infancy. On physical examination, he has a fixed, rigid equinovarus deformity of his right foot. He walks on the lateral border of his foot and has significant pain with ambulation. Radiographs demonstrate severe structural adaptation of the tarsal bones with degenerative changes in the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints. Because the patient has passed the window for soft tissue correction, surgical management is planned to provide a stable, painless, plantigrade foot. Which of the following surgical procedures is the definitive treatment of choice for this patient?
options: Ponseti casting and percutaneous Achilles tenotomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triple arthrodesis

Triple arthrodesis is the treatment of choice for neglected, rigid congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) in older children and adolescents who have completed the window for soft tissue correction.

It involves fusion of three joints:

• Subtalar joint (talocalcaneal)
• Talonavicular joint
• Calcaneocuboid joint

Indications:

• Age >10–12 years with skeletal maturity approaching
• Rigid, fixed deformity
• Painful gait
• Degenerative changes in the tarsal joints
• Failure or absence of early treatment

Why not the other options?

• A. Ponseti casting + percutaneous Achilles tenotomy: First-line treatment for newborns and infants with flexible clubfoot.
• B. Turco posteromedial soft tissue release: Used in young children (typically <2–4 years) with resistant deformity; ineffective in long-standing rigid deformities.
• D. Ilizarov external fixator alone: Can gradually correct severe neglected deformities but is generally an adjunct; definitive treatment for rigid, arthritic clubfoot is triple arthrodesis.
questions.learning: Triple arthrodesis Triple arthrodesis is the treatment of choice for neglected, rigid congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) in older children and adolescents who have completed the window for soft tissue correction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about GFR? GFR- Glomerular filtration rate RPF- Renal Plasma Flow
options: Increase in sympathetic function increases GFR
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in RPF increases GFR

The true statement about GFR is that the increase in RPF increases GFR.

With a constant glomerular hydrostatic pressure, an increase in blood flow into the glomerulus tends to increase the GFR and a lower rate of blood flow into the glomerulus tends to decrease the GFR.

GFR decreases with sympathetic stimulation as there is afferent arteriolar constriction. Strong activation of the renal sympathetic nerves can constrict the renal arterioles and decrease renal blood flow and GFR.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presents with complaints of sudden, intense urges to carry out certain actions that arise abruptly and without prior planning. These urges are experienced as uncontrollable and are not triggered by any external stimulus. This clinical presentation is most consistent with which psychiatric symptom?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a sudden, overwhelming, and uncontrollable urge to perform an action without premeditation or clear rational motivation is the definition of an Impulse. Impulses are characteristically experienced as "ego-dystonic" urges that the individual feels compelled to act upon, often followed by a sense of relief or gratification. Hallucinations (Option A) are sensory perceptions in the absence of an external stimulus. Pseudohallucinations (Option B) are similar to hallucinations but are perceived in internal subjective space and recognized as "unreal" by the patient. Delusions (Option C) are fixed, false beliefs that are not amenable to reason or contrary evidence. Impulses are central to disorders such as kleptomania, pyromania, and borderline personality disorder. Understanding the spontaneous and uncontrollable nature of impulses is vital for psychiatric diagnosis and risk assessment. Management typically involves cognitive-behavioral therapy and sometimes pharmacological intervention to improve impulse control and reduce the associated distress or harmful behaviors
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a sudden, overwhelming, and uncontrollable urge to perform an action without premeditation or clear rational motivation is the definition of an Impulse.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When is dilatation and curettage contraindicated? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic inflammatory disease

Dilatation and curettage (D&C) is a gynecologic procedure used for:

• Endometrial sampling
• Management of abnormal uterine bleeding
• Incomplete abortion
• Removal of retained products of conception

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is a contraindication because instrumentation of an infected genital tract may:

• Spread infection
• Worsen pelvic sepsis
• Increase risk of infertility and tubo-ovarian abscess

Why other options are incorrect:

• Ectopic pregnancy may require uterine curettage for diagnostic purposes
• Menstrual irregularities are a common indication for D&C
• Endometriosis is not a contraindication
questions.learning: Pelvic inflammatory disease Dilatation and curettage (D&C) is a gynecologic procedure used for: • Endometrial sampling • Management of abnormal uterine bleeding • Incomplete abortion • Removal of retained products of conception Pelvic inflammatory disease…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old girl is provided a few cubes and asked to create the structure in the image provided. If she can create the Structure A, but cannot make the Structure B, her developmental quotient (DQ) in the fine motor domain is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 62.5

Structure A is gate (5 years); B is steps (6 years)

The child is 8 years old (chronological age). The ability to construct Structure A but not Structure B corresponds to a developmental age of 5 years in the fine-motor domain.

Developmental Quotient (DQ):

• Chronological age = 8 years
• Developmental age = 5 years

DQ = Developmental age / Chronological age × 100

DQ = 5/8 × 100 = 62.5

• DQ 90–110 → Normal
• DQ <70 → Significant developmental delay
• DQ 75 → Mild/borderline delay
questions.learning: 62.5 Structure A is gate (5 years); B is steps (6 years) The child is 8 years old (chronological age). The ability to construct Structure A but not Structure B corresponds to a developmental age of 5 years in the fine-motor domain.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In ORS, sodium is given along with glucose to facilitate___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Co-transport

In ORS, sodium is given along with glucose to facilitate co-transport.

Glucose co transported with sodium is an example of Secondary Active transport.

The glucose-dependent sodium and water absorption is the principle behind replacing glucose and sodium in a 1:1 molar ratio in the WHO oral rehydration solution (ORS). The low osmolarity of the ORS in the lumen as compared to the blood facilitate absorption of fluid and hence the electrolytes due to the solvent drag.

The low-osmolality World Health Organization (WHO) oral rehydration solution (ORS) is now the global standard of care in the management of acute gastroenteritis.

Note:

Types of transport:

* Active transport:

* Primary

* Energy is derived from the transporter itself. Eg Na+ K+ ATPase pump.

* Secondary:

* Energy is derived indirectly. Eg. SGLT – Sodium linked glucose transport

* Passive transport

* Simple:

* No energy is required.

* No carrier molecule is involved.

* Eg. O2 exchange in alveoli.

* Facilitated:

* No energy is required.

* Carrier molecule involved.

* Eg. Glucose transport by GLUT transporters.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Carbon monoxide and cyanide cause death primarily due to their interference with which of the following cellular processes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cytochrome oxidase

Carbon monoxide and cyanide cause cellular hypoxia by inhibiting the final step of the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

• Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) in mitochondria.
• This blocks the transfer of electrons to oxygen, preventing formation of water.
• As a result, oxidative phosphorylation stops, ATP production ceases, and cells develop histotoxic hypoxia (oxygen is present but cannot be utilized).

Carbon monoxide (CO) contributes to hypoxia by two mechanisms:

1. High affinity binding to hemoglobin → formation of carboxyhemoglobin → reduced oxygen delivery.

2. Binding to mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase → inhibition of cellular respiration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Please determine the size of the thyroid gland based on the provided image.
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland extends from C5 to T1 vertebral levels, which corresponds to: 1. A = C5 (upper limit) 2. D = T1 (lower limit) 3. So, the correct range is A to D. The thyroid gland is located in the anterior neck, just below the larynx, and lies opposite the C5 to T1 vertebrae. It consists of two lateral lobes connected by an isthmus that lies anterior to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. The superior poles of the thyroid reach up to the level of the thyroid cartilage (around C5), while the inferior poles extend downward to approximately the C7–T1 level. Radiologically, especially in lateral neck X-rays, these vertebral landmarks are used to estimate the size and extent of the thyroid gland. Since the gland spans from C5 (A) to T1 (D), the correct option is A to D. Other options are incorrect because: 1. B to D misses the upper limit (C5) 2. A to C misses the lower extension (T1) 3. C to D includes only the lower portion of the gland
questions.learning: The thyroid gland extends from C5 to T1 vertebral levels, which corresponds to: 1. The thyroid gland is located in the anterior neck, just below the larynx, and lies opposite the C5 to T1 vertebrae.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is wrongly matched with their associated enzymes?
options: Vitamin B9 (Folic acid) : FIGLU excretion/Histidine load test
Vitamin C : Serum methyl malonate level
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin C : Serum methyl malonate level

Option D is wrongly matched as Vitamin B12 is associated with serum methyl malonyl levels and not Vitamin C.

There are two vitamin B12-dependent enzymes:

* Methionine synthase (Homocysteine methyltransferase): Catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to methionine

* Methylmalonyl CoA mutase: Methylmalonyl CoA, formed as an intermediate in the catabolism of valine, isoleucine, and propionyl CoA is converted to succinyl CoA

The below figure shows B12 serving as a cofactor of methionine synthase. Its deficiency may cause  folate trap.

Other options:

Option A: Thiamine pyrophosphate (Vit B1) is the cofactor of transketolase. Transketolase and transaldolase are involved in the nonoxidative phase of the HMP pathway.

Option B: Riboflavin deficiency is assessed by measurement of the activation of erythrocyte glutathione reductase by FAD added in vitro. Riboflavin provides the reactive moieties of the coenzymes flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).

Option C: FIGLU is converted to L-Glutamate by the enzyme glutamate formimino transferase. This enzyme uses folate (vitamin B9). In Vitamin B9 deficiency, FIGLU accumulates in the body and is excreted in the urine. The FIGLU excretion test is used to detect folic acid deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with renal calculus of > 4 cm of the staghorn type. What is the best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy

The best management for staghorn renal calculus of >4 cm is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).

The initial management of renal stones depends on the stone size and includes conservative management, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL), and PCNL. PCNL is preferred for stones > 2cm in size and for staghorn calculi, while ESWL is used to treat renal stones of size 0.6 to 1.5 cm. PCNL is indicated in

• Renal stones >2 cm
• Staghorn calculus
• Failed shockwave lithotripsy (SWL) or retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) for renal calculi
• Lower pole renal stones with anatomy that is unfavorable for ESWL

Other options:

Option C: Ureteroscopic removal is attempted for failed SWLs or PCNLs, and is not the first choice in the surgical management of renal stones.

Option D: RIRS is a minimally invasive procedure similar to ureteroscopic removal, where the kidney is accessed using a slim and flexible ureteroscope in a retrograde manner via the ureteric orifice. It is indicated for lower pole renal stones < 2 cm.
