questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: On neurologic examination, a patient is not able to identify an object but is able to recognize the object from its texture, colour and pattern. Which of the following is likely to have been affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inferior temporal lobe

The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvement would be the inferior temporal lobe.

• Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia. According to De Jong, visual agnosia is further classified into:

• Apperceptive visual agnosia - the visual image appears distorted to the patient and hence they are unable to recognise it. This occurs due lesions in the parieto-occipital region
• Associative visual agnosia - inability to visually identify objects in the absence of visual impairment, with ability to identify the object using other sensory modalities (as suggested in the scenario). This occurs due to lesions of occipito-temporal junction, which is present in the inferior temporal lobe. Prosopagnosia is a type of associatetive visual agnosia which refers to the inability to visually identify faces.

The occipital lobe acts as the primary visual area and a lesion in this region would result in cortical blindness and achromatopsia, which is the inability to visualise colour. In the given scenario, as the patient is also able to identify colour, it indicates that the occipital lobe (Option A) is unaffected and (hence inferior temporal lobe is the better answer).

Stereognosis is the ability to identify an object by a perception of the form and nature of an object without looking at it. In the given scenario, the patient is able to recognize the object from its texture and pattern which indicates that stereognosis is intact. Loss of this ability is known as astereognosis which occurs in lesions of the superior parietal lobule (Options B and C) and dorsal column pathways.
questions.learning: Inferior temporal lobe — The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvement would be the inferior temporal lobe. • Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following congenital heart disease has equal saturation in all the chambers of the heart?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation

In total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC), there is equal saturation in all chambers of the heart.

In TAPVC, the oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins reaches the right atrium (having deoxygenated blood) instead of the left atrium. It occurs due to the draining of the pulmonary veins to the superior vena cava or to the inferior vena cava or to both. This is a total mixing lesion. The blood from this right atrium (RA) passes to the right ventricle and pulmonary artery. This blood also reaches the left atrium through the atrial septal defect or the patent foramen ovale, and subsequently, to the left ventricle The left atrium is not receiving any blood because all of the pulmonary veins are draining to the right atrium. Therefore, this shunt will be the only source of blood to it. Since blood from right atrium reaches all the other chambers, the oxygen saturation of the blood in all four chambers is the same.

In (TAPVC), there are three main types: supra-cardiac, cardiac, and infra-cardiac. In supra-cardiac TAPVC, the pulmonary veins merge to form a single vein that drains into either the superior vena cava or the left innominate vein. In cardiac TAPVC, the pulmonary veins directly drain into the right atrium or coronary sinus. The most dangerous type is infra-cardiac TAPVC, which is always obstructive. In this type, the pulmonary veins drain into either the portal vein or the inferior vena cava.

Diagnosis of TAPVC is the demonstration of any vein with doppler flow away from the heart because the normal venous flow is usually toward the heart.

Surgical correction of TAPVR is done in infancy. Pulmonary venous confluence is anastomosed directly to the left atrium, the ASD is closed, and any connection to the systemic venous circuit is interrupted.

Other options

Option A - Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) comprises right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, ventricular septal defect (VSD), overriding of the aorta over the ventricular septum, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction increases the pressure in the right ventricle. This causes right to left shunt through the ventricular septal defect. The deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle mixes with the oxygenated blood in the left ventricle. Therefore, in this condition, the left atrium has a higher oxygen saturation compared to the left ventricle due to mixing. The right atria and ventricles have the least oxygen saturation.

Option C - Tricuspid atresia is the congenital absence of the tricuspid valve. Therefore, the blood in the right atrium is shunted to the left atrium through the patent foramen ovale or the atrial septal defect. In the left atrium, the blood from the right atrium mixes with the oxygenated blood and the oxygen saturation decreases. However, the oxygen saturation in the left atrium and left ventricle is still greater compared to that of the hypoplastic right ventricle.

Option D -  Transposition of great arteries (TGA) is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. Because of this, the pulmonary and systemic circulations remain separate. The right side of the heart has deoxygenated blood and the left side of the heart has oxygenated blood. The pulmonary artery saturation is always higher than the aortic saturation.
questions.learning: Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation — In total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC), there is equal saturation in all chambers of the heart.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiology resident is revising heterophile antibody-based agglutination tests used in infectious diseases. Which of the following tests is NOT based on the detection of heterophile antibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rose–Waaler test

Heterophile agglutination tests detect cross-reacting antibodies produced against one antigen that agglutinate unrelated antigens because of shared epitopes.

The Rose–Waaler test is not a heterophile test. It is an autoantibody test used for the detection of Rheumatoid Factor (RF).

In this test:

• Sheep RBCs are coated with rabbit anti-sheep erythrocyte antibodies.
• Rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc portion of IgG) causes agglutination.

Thus, it detects an autoantibody, not a heterophile antibody.

Why the other options are heterophile tests?

• A. Paul–Bunnell test ✅: Detects heterophile antibodies produced in infectious mononucleosis (EBV) that agglutinate sheep or horse erythrocytes.
• B. Weil–Felix test ✅: Detects antibodies in rickettsial infections that cross-react with Proteus OX strains (OX2, OX19, OXK).
• D. Cold agglutination test ✅: Detects cold-reacting IgM antibodies produced in Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection that agglutinate human red blood cells at low temperatures.
questions.learning: Rose–Waaler test Heterophile agglutination tests detect cross-reacting antibodies produced against one antigen that agglutinate unrelated antigens because of shared epitopes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Healthcare workers should be vaccinated against ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatitis B

Healthcare workers should be vaccinated against Hepatitis B.

These are most likely to be transmitted by the handling of biomedical waste.

Yearly health check-ups should be done, and a booster dose should be given if needed.

Post-exposure prophylaxis for HBV:

When the Hepatitis B status of the source patient is unknown: HCW is managed as if the source patient were HBsAg-positive.

When the source patient is HBV-positive:

* HCW whose response is unknown after one round of HBV vaccination - HBIG (hepatitis B hyperimmune globulin) 0.06 ml/kg as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours and should simultaneously reinitiate the course of HBV immunization with three doses of hepatitis B vaccine.

* HCW is a non-responder after two rounds of HBV vaccination - HBIG (hepatitis B hyperimmune globulin) 0.06 ml/kg as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours and a second dose of HBIG, 1 month after the first dose.

* Healthcare worker (HCW) is immunized and a responder (anti-HBs antibodies >10 mIU/ml) - They are protected. No need for hepatitis B immunoglobulin after a potential or confirmed exposure to hepatitis B.

* HCW is incompletely vaccinated/unvaccinated - HBIG (hepatitis B hyperimmune globulin) 0.06 ml/kg as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours and should simultaneously start/reinitiate the course of HBV immunization with three doses of hepatitis B vaccine.

Follow-up: After the three-dose vaccination series is completed, antibodies to the surface antigen is checked 1–2 months later. If the titres are <10 mIU/ml a second three-dose vaccine series is started or the HCW is checked for HBsAg positivity.

Some other vaccines that are given to healthcare workers include:

* Tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis (Tdap) vaccine

* Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine

* Influenza vaccine

* Varicella (chickenpox) vaccine

* Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine
questions.learning: Hepatitis B Healthcare workers should be vaccinated against Hepatitis B. These are most likely to be transmitted by the handling of biomedical waste.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 100 mg elemental iron and 500 μg folic acid. ✅

• 2. Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 60 mg elemental iron and 0.5 mg folic acid. ❌

• 60 mg elemental iron is recommended for pregnant women under ANC programs, not under WIFS.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the role of caffeine in wakefulness?
options: Blocks adenosine action and causes wakefulness
Activates locus coeruleus and cause wakefulness
No role in maintaining wakefulness if taken 1hr before sleep
Activates histamine release and prevents sleep
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blocks adenosine action and causes wakefulness

Caffeine = adenosine receptor antagonist → removes “sleep pressure” → promotes wakefulness

Caffeine promotes wakefulness by blocking adenosine receptors, particularly A₁ and A₂A, in the brain. Adenosine normally accumulates during wakefulness and induces sleepiness; its blockade reduces sleep drive.

Thus, caffeine causes increased alertness and delayed sleep onset.

| Time awake | Adenosine level | Effect

| ---------- | --------------- | ------

| Morning | Low | Alert

| Afternoon | Moderate | Slight fatigue

| Night | High | Sleep drive ↑

Caffeine does NOT reduce adenosine, it just blocks its effect

| Neurotransmitter | Source | Role

| ---------------- | ------ | ----

| Adenosine | ATP metabolism | Promotes sleep

| Norepinephrine | Locus coeruleus | Arousal

| Histamine | Tuberomammillary nucleus | Wakefulness

| Dopamine | VTA | Alertness

| Orexin | Hypothalamus | Stabilizes wakefulness
questions.learning: Blocks adenosine action and causes wakefulness Caffeine = adenosine receptor antagonist → removes “sleep pressure” → promotes wakefulness Caffeine promotes wakefulness by blocking adenosine receptors, particularly A₁ and A₂A, in the brain.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A conscious 35-year-old male patient was brought to casualty with a history of a road traffic accident and a head injury. When the doctor asked questions about the incident, his answers were irrelevant to the questions, but his speech was clear. What could be the potential site of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior temporal gyrus

Fluent aphasia is seen in the lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus due to the involvement of the Wernicke's area. The speech is full of jargon and neologisms that make little sense.

Aphasia is a language disorder that develops after brain damage. Wernicke's aphasia is marked by the ability to speak fluently but with difficulty understanding language. The patient cannot understand words or recognise symbols, whether they are auditory, tactile or visual. People with this condition often don't recognise that their speech is unclear, and they may experience significant agitation or paranoia as a result.

Lesions in the categorical hemisphere lead to

* Broca's aphasia is caused by an injury in the inferior frontal gyrus. It causes nonfluent aphasia. Affected individuals have slow speech and difficulty in generating verbal or written words. For example, a patient with Broca's aphasia may say "walk dog" instead of "I want to take the dog for a walk". Speech therapy in Broca's aphasia is more successful than in Wernicke’s aphasia.

* Wernicke's aphasia is caused by a lesion in the posterior end of the superior temporal gyrus. It produces a type of fluent aphasia in which speech itself is normal, but it is full of jargon and neologisms that make little sense. The patient also fails to comprehend the meaning of spoken or written words, so other aspects of the use of language are compromised.

* Anomic aphasia – When a lesion damages the angular gyrus in the categorical hemisphere without affecting Wernicke's or Broca's areas, there is no difficulty with speech or the understanding of auditory information. But there is trouble understanding written language or pictures because visual information is not processed and transmitted to the Wernicke area.

* Global aphasia—In this, both understanding and speaking are impaired. It is also non-fluent aphasia.

* Acalculia—impairment of mathematical ability. Occurs due to an impairment to the parietal lobe, particularly the angular gyrus.

Conduction aphasia is seen in lesions of the arcuate fasciculus, the bundle of nerve fibres connecting the Wernicke and Broca's areas. Repetition of words is impaired and paraphasias are observed, though not as much as in Wernicke aphasia.

Dysarthria, in contrast to aphasia, is a motor dysfunction due to disruption in innervation to the face, tongue or soft palate that results in slurred speech but intact fluency and comprehension.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The radiograph shown below is done for better assessment of the frontal sinus. What is the common name of this view?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Caldwell view

The frontal sinus is best seen in Caldwell's view (occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position).

The structures seen in Caldwell's view include:

• Frontal sinuses (seen best)
• Ethmoid sinuses
• Maxillary sinuses
• Frontal process of the zygoma and the zygomatic process of the frontal bone
• Superior margin of the orbit and lamina papyracea
• Superior orbital fissure
• Foramen rotundum (inferolateral to superior orbital fissure)

The nose and forehead are touching the X-ray film and the X-ray beam is projected 15 degrees caudally in Caldwell's view.

Other options:

Option A: Water's view (occipitomental view or nose-chin position) is a radiographic view where an X-ray beam is angled at 45 degrees to the orbitomeatal line. Structures seen are the maxillary sinus (best seen), sphenoid sinus (if the film is taken with an open mouth), frontal sinus, zygoma, zygomatic arch, nasal bone, and infratemporal fossa.

Option C: Pierre's view is the occipitomental with an open mouth. It helps in visualizing the sphenoid sinus as well, in addition to the sinuses that can be seen in water's view.

Option D: Towne's view is an angled anteroposterior radiograph of the skull. Structures seen are the petrous part of the pyramids, arcuate eminence, superior semicircular canal, mastoid antrum, internal auditory canal, tympanic cavity, cochlea, and external auditory canal. This view is taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 48-year-old smoker presents to the OPD with complaints of cramping pain in both the calves on walking to about 100–150 metres. The pain is relieved on taking rest for about 2–3 minutes and the patient is able to walk for some more distance again before the pain appears. This presentation is suggestive of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intermittent claudication

Intermittent claudication is the classical symptom of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the lower limbs. It is characterized by exercise-induced ischemic muscle pain that is reproducible, relieved by rest, and recurs after walking a predictable distance. The patient has cramping calf pain after walking 100–150 meters, which is relieved within a few minutes of rest and recurs with exertion—this is the classic presentation of peripheral arterial disease (PAD).

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Muscular fatigue: Causes generalized tiredness rather than reproducible ischemic calf pain related to walking distance.
• B. Osteoarthritis of the knee: Pain is localized to the joint, worsens with movement, and is not consistently relieved within minutes of rest.
• D. Neurogenic claudication: Seen in lumbar spinal canal stenosis. Pain is relieved by sitting or spinal flexion (shopping cart sign) rather than simply stopping walking. Walking uphill is often easier than downhill.
questions.learning: Intermittent claudication Intermittent claudication is the classical symptom of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the lower limbs.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During intercostal drain insertion, which anatomical location is considered the most appropriate for placing the chest tube?
options: Upper border of the lower rib
Lower border of the lower rib
Lower border of the upper rib
questions.explanation: The most critical anatomical consideration during the insertion of an intercostal tube drain is the location of the neurovascular bundle (intercostal vein, artery, and nerve). This bundle runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib. Therefore, to avoid catastrophic hemorrhage or nerve injury, the tube must be inserted by sliding over the upper border of the lower rib in the chosen intercostal space. Placing the tube near the lower border of the upper rib (Option C) would directly risk damaging these structures. The middle of the space (Option D) and the lower border of the lower rib (Option B) are less anatomically precise and do not offer the same safety margin. The standard insertion site is within the "safe triangle" bounded by the pectoralis major, the latissimus dorsi, and the 5th intercostal space. Adhering to this "upper border" rule is a fundamental surgical safety principle to minimize procedural morbidity
questions.learning: The most critical anatomical consideration during the insertion of an intercostal tube drain is the location of the neurovascular bundle (intercostal vein, artery, and nerve).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old lactating female with an 18-month-old child comes with a history of irregular, heavy bleeding seeking contraceptive advice. Which is the contraceptive of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mala N

Mala N is a combined oral contraceptive (COC) commonly used in national family planning programs.

| Factor | Explanation

| ------ | -----------

| Child age 18 months | Lactation no longer contraindicates COCs

| Heavy bleeding | COCs reduce menstrual bleeding

| Irregular cycles | COCs regulate menstruation

Mechanism:

Estrogen + Progesterone

↓

Suppress FSH and LH

↓

Inhibit ovulation

↓

Endometrial stabilization

↓

Reduced menstrual bleeding

Progestasert (progesterone IUD) / Copper T/ progesterone implant are not ideal in someone already having bleeding problems. Mala N (combined oral contraceptive) is not recommended in a lactating female as estrogen affects the milk output.  Some sources say an 18-month period of lactation justifies COCPs since the child would be on complementary feeds. The best answer hence remains controversial.

A) Progestasert

• Rarely used now
• Less effective than modern options.

B) Copper-T 380A

• Highly effective contraception
• May increase menstrual bleeding, which would worsen symptoms.

D) Norethisterone enanthate depot

• Can cause irregular bleeding
• Not ideal when patient already has heavy irregular bleeding.

Contraception in Lactating Women

| Time after delivery | Recommended contraception

| ------------------- | -------------------------

| <6 weeks | Progestin-only methods

| 6 weeks–6 months | POPs, IUCD

| >6 months | Combined OCPs allowed

Since the child is 18 months old, COCs are safe.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During development, thymic cells recognizing self-antigens are removed to prevent autoimmunity. Which gene among the following is involved in the process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. AIRE

The above process is called central tolerance and the AIRE (AutoImmune REgulator) protein is necessary for this process.

Immature self-reactive T and B lymphocyte clones recognize self-antigens during their maturation in the central lymphoid organs (thymus for T cells, bone marrow for B cells). They are killed or rendered harmless.

The removal of self reacting T lymphocytes in the thymus is called negative selection/ deletion. For this process, AIRE protein is needed. Mutations in the AIRE gene results in autoimmune disorders (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy).

B cells undergo a process called receptor editing. When developing B cells encounter an antigen, it formulates a change in the receptor that makes the antigen unrecognizable. Self-reacting B cells can also undergo apoptosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The Anemia Mukt Bharat program aims to reduce anemia across India through targeted interventions. Which statement correctly describes how Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation is administered under this program?
options: IFA is provided during the 2nd trimester of pregnancy and continues during lactation for up to 6 months
IFA supplementation is administered solely during pregnancy
A 100-day course of IFA supplementation is sufficient
Administering IFA during the 1st trimester is adequate.
questions.explanation: The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy follows a comprehensive "6x6x6" framework to reduce anemia prevalence across the life cycle. For pregnant women, the protocol mandates the administration of one Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) tablet daily, containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid. This starts in the second trimester (after the first 12 weeks of pregnancy) and continues for 180 days throughout the remainder of the pregnancy. Crucially, the supplementation must continue postpartum during lactation for an additional 180 days (6 months). Solely administering it during pregnancy (Option B) is insufficient to replenish maternal iron stores depleted during childbirth. A 100-day course (Option C) was the older standard, now replaced by the 180-day regimen to ensure better clinical outcomes. First-trimester administration (Option D) is generally avoided to prevent aggravating nausea and because the physiological demand for iron increases most rapidly during the second and third trimesters

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient reports the belief that his thoughts and feelings are being controlled or influenced by an external agency. What is this psychopathological phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: The belief that one's feelings, thoughts, or movements are being controlled or influenced by an external agency is known as a Passivity phenomenon (or delusion of control). This is one of Schneider’s First-Rank Symptoms of schizophrenia. Delusion of nihilism (Option A, Cotard’s syndrome) involves the belief that one is dead or that the world doesn't exist. Delusion of reference (Option B) is the belief that neutral events (like news broadcasts) have a special, personal meaning meant only for the patient. Othello syndrome (Option C) is a delusion of morbid jealousy, where the patient is convinced of a partner's infidelity without cause. Passivity phenomena are highly diagnostic for psychotic disorders. The patient may feel like a "puppet," with their will being overridden by outside forces. Identifying these core psychotic features is essential for differentiating schizophrenia from other mental health conditions and starting appropriate antipsychotic management
questions.learning: The belief that one's feelings, thoughts, or movements are being controlled or influenced by an external agency is known as a Passivity phenomenon (or delusion of control).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding innervation of the uterus?
options: Sensory level is from T10 to L1
Uterine contractility is mediated by innervations from level T7 - T8
In the 1st stage of labor, pain is due to the fibres at level of T10 - L1
In early labor, pain is usually because of the uterine contraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Uterine contractility is mediated by innervations from level T7 - T8

The incorrect regarding innervation of the uterus is statement B. Uterine contractility is mainly mediated by hormonal mechanisms. Estrogen, prostaglandin, and oxytocin produce contraction, while progesterone causes relaxation.

Uterine sensory supply is by ascending afferent fibers which pass through the inferior hypogastric plexus and enter the spinal cord through T10-T12 and L1 roots.

Labor pain is due to stimulation of nociceptors in the genital tract caused by ischemia.

• First stage labor: Pain is mediated by T10 to L1 spinal segments. It is caused by distension of the cervix and low uterine segments along with isometric uterine contraction.
• Second stage labor: Pain is carried by T12 to L1 and S2 to S4 spinal segments. It is caused by tissue damage in the pelvis and perineum

Analgesia in labor is achieved by intramuscular injection of pethidine 50 mg. Metoclopramide is added to prevent vomiting. Pethidine is avoided within 2 hours of delivery as it is a known respiratory depressant to the fetus. When relief of pain is required throughout labor, regional analgesia is preferred through pudendal nerve block, epidural analgesia, spinal anesthesia or combined epidural-spinal anesthesia.
questions.learning: Uterine contractility is mediated by innervations from level T7 - T8 The incorrect regarding innervation of the uterus is statement B. Uterine contractility is mainly mediated by hormonal mechanisms.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the most effective circuit for anaesthesia under spontaneous breathing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mapleson A

The most effective circuit for anesthesia under spontaneous breathing is Mapleson A or Magill's circuit.

When the Mapleson A circuit is used for spontaneous ventilation, the fresh gas flow rate of the circuit is closest to the physiological minute ventilation of the patient. Hence it is preferred over other circuits.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient has a long arm span, hypermobile joints and hypermobile lens. What is the defective protein?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of a long arm span relative to height, joint hypermobility, and ectopia lentis (lens subluxation) are classic for Marfan syndrome. This connective tissue disorder is caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene, which leads to a defect in the protein Fibrillin-1. Fibrillin-1 is a crucial component of microfibrils that provide structural integrity to tissues and regulate TGF-β signaling. Collagen defects (Option B) are associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or osteogenesis imperfecta; while these may share joint laxity, they lack the specific Marfanoid skeletal and ocular phenotype. Elastin deficiency (Option C) is linked to Williams syndrome and supravalvular aortic stenosis. Keratin (Option D) is a structural protein of epithelial cells, and its mutations cause skin and hair disorders. Thus, the specific combination of skeletal, joint, and lens abnormalities identifies a Fibrillin-1 defect

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following is the most common complication following ligation of the first vessel during abdominoperineal resection for rectal carcinoma?

(APR - Abdominoperineal resection)
options: Parasympathetic - bladder dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation.
Sympathetic - retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction.
Sympathetic - Impotence and loss of cutaneous sensation in perineal region
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sympathetic - retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction.

The first vessel that is usually ligated during abdominoperineal resection (APR) is the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). A high inferior mesenteric artery ligation during abdominoperineal resection can injure the superior hypogastric nerve, resulting in sympathetic dysfunction and leading to retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction.

Abdominoperineal resection is the complete excision of the rectum, anal canal, and sphincter apparatus. This is done with the creation of a permanent colostomy. This is commonly preferred in elderly patients with distal rectal cancer with poor sphincter function. In these patients, the end colostomy offers a better quality of life.

Complications:

• Higher recurrence rates compared to low anterior resection.
• Anastomotic leaks or dehiscences
• Necrosis of the transposed colon
• Bleeding
• Strictures

The sympathetic innervation of the rectum is from L1, L2, and L3, which together form the superior hypogastric plexus. They divide into left and right hypogastric nerves at the level of the sacral promontory supplying the rectum and the genitourinary system. A high IMA ligation during surgery can result in sympathetic dysfunction causing retrograde ejaculation.

Injury to the pelvic plexus and nervi erigentes, during the division along the pelvic side wall, can cause erectile dysfunction, impotence, and atonic bladder. Injury to the periprostatic plexus can lead to sexual and bladder dysfunction.
questions.learning: Sympathetic - retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction. The first vessel that is usually ligated during abdominoperineal resection (APR) is the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is the investigation of choice for diagnosing the presence of stones in the gallbladder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transabdominal ultrasound

Transabdominal ultrasonography (USG) is the investigation of choice for diagnosing gallbladder stones (cholelithiasis). It is non-invasive, inexpensive, radiation-free, and has a sensitivity and specificity >95% for detecting gallstones larger than 2 mm.

Ultrasound can also identify:

• Gallbladder wall thickening
• Pericholecystic fluid
• Sonographic Murphy’s sign
• Biliary sludge
• Dilatation of the biliary tree

Why not the other options?

• B. Erect X-ray abdomen: Incorrect. Only 10–20% of gallstones are radiopaque (pigment stones). Most cholesterol stones are radiolucent and not visible on X-ray.
• C. Capsule endoscopy: Used to evaluate small bowel diseases, not gallbladder pathology.
• D. Computed Tomography (CT): Less sensitive than ultrasound for detecting gallstones, especially cholesterol stones. CT is mainly useful for detecting complications such as perforation, emphysematous cholecystitis, or malignancy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following medications may be used in a child diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder? I. Carbamazepine II. Methylphenidate III. Atomoxetine IV. Clonazepam Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II and III

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that interfere with functioning at home, school, or social settings. Treatment includes behavioral interventions and pharmacotherapy, with stimulants being the first-line medications.

Why is B correct?

• I. Carbamazepine ✘

• Carbamazepine is an antiepileptic drug used for epilepsy, trigeminal neuralgia, and bipolar disorder.
• It is not routinely used in ADHD.

• II. Methylphenidate ✔

• First-line drug for ADHD. ⭐
• It is a central nervous system stimulant that inhibits the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, improving attention and reducing hyperactivity and impulsivity.

• III. Atomoxetine ✔

• A selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI).
• Used in children who do not tolerate stimulants, have contraindications to stimulants, or have comorbid anxiety or tic disorders.

• IV. Clonazepam ✘

• A benzodiazepine used for seizures and anxiety disorders.
• It has no role in the routine treatment of ADHD.
questions.learning: II and III Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that interfere with functioning at home, school, or social settings.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a blast injury, which of the following organs is least vulnerable to the blast wave?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Liver

In a blast injury, the liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury.

Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion. Primary blast injuries result from the rapid overpressure or shock waves produced by an explosion. These injuries result from the dramatic changes in barometric pressure projecting outwards from the point of detonation. They predominantly cause damage to air-filled hollow organs of the body from rapid pressure change (barotrauma). This includes the middle ear, lungs, and GIT.

The most sensitive and most frequently injured hollow organs are the tympanic membranes > lungs. Blast damage to the lungs is the most common cause of life-threatening injury following an explosion.

Solid organs are the most resistant to blast injuries as the parenchymal disruption requires very high levels of overpressure.

Classification of blast injuries:

Classification
Explanation
Injury type
Examples

Primary blast
Due to air pressure from the blast
Shockwave (overpressure)
Tympanic membrane injury, blast lung, intestinal blast injury

Secondary blast
Fragments from the blast, following a detonation
Penetrating/fragmentation
All penetrating injuries

Tertiary blast
Gross movements of persons, objects, or infrastructure by the blast wind
Blunt trauma
Blunt and crush injuries. Traumatic amputation.

Quaternary blast
Miscellaneous causes
Exposure to explosive products or toxic substances
Burns, inhalation injury

Quinary blast
The intentional addition of biological or radioactive material to the explosive device
Environmental contaminants
Radiation sickness, infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old HIV patient presented with a painful lesion, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kaposi sarcoma

The above image showing a violaceous growth on the hard palate in an HIV patient is diagnostic of Kaposi sarcoma.

Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is very common in patients suffering from acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). KS is considered to be an AIDS-defining disease.

AIDS-associated KS is an AIDS-defining illness and is the most common malignancy associated with HIV infection. Involvement of the oral cavity is most common in AIDS-related KS, but it can be seen in other variants also. Oral KS (OKS) most often involves the hard and soft palate, gingiva, and dorsal tongue with plaques or tumors. The color of the lesions may range from non-pigmented to brownish-red or violaceous.

Other forms of KS include

• Classic Kaposi sarcoma: It has the following three clinical stages patches, plaques, and nodules.
• Endemic African KS
• Transplant-associated KS is more common after solid organ transplant patients receive immunosuppression as compared to the marrow or stem-cell transplant patients.

The given images show coalescent red-purple macules and plaques of the skin and the histologic appearance of Kaposi sarcoma, demonstrating sheets of proliferating spindle cells:

There is no definitive cure but KS is highly radiosensitive and achieves complete response in most cases. In AIDS‐associated KS, instituting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) often (but not always) results in regression of KS. In localized cutaneous KS, excision and cryotherapy can be used. Intra-lesional administration of vinblastine, interferon‐α2b, and imiquimod is also effective.

Other options:

Option A: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) most commonly tends to occur in sun-exposed areas of the face like the nose, eyelid, and other parts of the face. BCC can vary from red, flesh-colored, or white macules or papules, to nodules and ulcerated lesions. The nodular variant is the most common subtype characterized by raised, pearly pink papules with telangiectasias and occasionally a depressed tumor center with raised borders giving the classic “rodent ulcer” appearance.

The image below shows a case of basal cell carcinoma.

Option C: Malignant melanoma primarily arises from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction but may also originate from mucosal surfaces of the oropharynx, nasopharynx, eyes, proximal esophagus, anorectal, and female genitalia. Lentigo maligna, superficial spreading, acral lentiginous, and nodular are the variants of malignant melanoma. It includes pigmented lesion that has enlarged, ulcerated, or bled. Amelanotic lesions appear as raised pink, purple, or flesh-colored skin papules. The diagnostic clue for melanoma is the ABCDE criteria.

It comprises of

• Asymmetry
• Border irregularity
• Color variegation
• Diameter of more than 6 mm
• Evolution or change

The image below shows a case of malignant melanoma.

Option D: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the second most common skin cancer. UV radiation exposure is the primary risk factor for SCC. Classically, it appears as a scaly or ulcerated papule or plaque that can bleed with minimal trauma, but the pain is rare. It can exhibit in situ (confined to the epidermis) or invasive subtypes. Wide surgical excision including subcutaneous fat is the treatment of choice for SCC.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following marked structures does not form part of the laryngeal skeleton?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

The structure marked as 'A', is the hyoid bone, which is not a part of the laryngeal skeleton.

The structures marked in the image are:

1. Hyoid bone
2. Thyroid cartilage
3. Epiglottis
4. Cricoid cartilage

The laryngeal skeleton is formed by a series of cartilages that are connected by ligaments and fibrous membranes:

• The thyroid, cricoid, and the greater part of the arytenoid cartilages consist of hyaline cartilage.
• The corniculate, cuneiform, tritiate, and epiglottic cartilages and the apices of the arytenoid cartilage consist of elastic cartilage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following genetic mutations is most commonly associated with familial cases of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder that destroys motor neurons. Approximately 10% of cases are familial, and the most common genetic cause identified in these instances is a mutation in the SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) gene. This mutation leads to a toxic gain-of-function in the SOD1 protein, triggering motor neuron death through oxidative stress and protein aggregation. The CFTR mutation (Option A) is the cause of cystic fibrosis, affecting chloride transport in epithelial cells. The HTT mutation (Option C) involves a CAG repeat expansion causing Huntington's disease. The FMR1 mutation (Option D) results in Fragile X syndrome, the leading inherited cause of intellectual disability. Therefore, SOD1 remains the definitive genetic marker for familial ALS

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzyme that is not used in cholesterol synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HMG CoA lyase

Among the given options, the enzyme HMG CoA lyase is not used in cholesterol synthesis. It is a mitochondrial enzyme involved in the breakdown of proteins and fats.

Cholesterol is a 27-carbon compound consisting of four rings and a side chain. It is synthesized from acetyl-CoA.

The major sites of synthesis of cholesterol are the liver, adrenal cortex, testes, ovaries, and intestine. All nucleated cells can synthesize cholesterol, including arterial walls. The enzymes involved in the synthesis of cholesterol are partly located in the endoplasmic reticulum and partly in the cytoplasm.

Initially, two molecules of acetyl-CoA condense to form acetoacetyl-CoA catalyzed by cytosolic thiolase. This acetoacetyl- CoA enters the cholesterol synthesis pathway along with a molecule of acetyl-CoA.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a limbal scar, a deep anterior chamber, and absence of the lens on slit-lamp examination. He reports difficulty with both distance and near vision. His vision improves to 6/9 with a +11D lens. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aphakia

Aphakia is the absence of the crystalline lens, leading to marked hypermetropia.

• Deep anterior chamber
• Absence of lens on slit lamp
• Severe blurred vision (distance + near)
• Improved with high plus lens (+10 to +12 D)

Clinical clues in question:

• Limbal scar → previous surgery/trauma
• +11 D correction → classic for aphakia

Why not others:

• Pseudophakia → artificial IOL present
• Subluxation → lens still visible
• Presbyopia → only near vision affected

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For ectopic pregnancy, how often should hCG levels be repeated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 48 hours

In ectopic pregnancy, hCG levels should be repeated every 48 hours, as the normal doubling time of hCG in a viable intrauterine pregnancy is 48 hours.

Serum β hCG can be used to differentiate tubal ectopic pregnancy from missed abortion and early intrauterine pregnancy. If the level is ≥2000 IU/L, ectopic pregnancy is suspected. If the level is <1500 IU/L, a repeat serum β hCG is taken after 48 hours. If the levels are:

* Doubled - early intrauterine pregnancy

* Decreased - abortion

* Increased but less than doubled value - ectopic pregnancy

Investigations for ectopic pregnancy:

* Serum β hCG - lower levels compared to normal pregnancy, prolonged doubling time

* Transvaginal ultrasound - empty uterine cavity, fluid in pouch of Douglas, adnexal mass

* Colour Doppler - ring of fire pattern

* Diagnostic laparoscopy may be done when the diagnosis is still uncertain after serial β-hCG monitoring and repeat ultrasonography.

* Dilatation and curettage - decidua identified without villi

* Serum progesterone

* Culdocentesis

Pearl PF2195: Beta hCG in pregnancy

The pattern of beta hCG :

First detectable in plasma 7 to 9 days post-LH surge

⇓

Doubles every 2 days

⇓

Peaks at 8 to 10 weeks of gestation(~100 IU/mL)

⇓

Begins to decline at 10 to 12 weeks

⇓

Plateau at 16 weeks till term

* Higher maternal plasma hCG levels- Multifetal pregnancy, erythroblastosis fetalis, gestational trophoblastic disease, Down syndrome.

* Lower hCG plasma levels -early pregnancy wastage and ectopic pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic small bowel diarrhea. Duodenal biopsy reveals villous atrophy, and laboratory tests are positive for anti-endomysial antibodies and IgA tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical and laboratory triad of persistent small bowel diarrhea, villous atrophy on biopsy, and positive IgA tissue transglutaminase (TTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies is pathognomonic for Celiac sprue (Celiac disease) . This is an autoimmune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals. Short bowel syndrome (Option A) results from the physical loss of intestinal length, typically after surgery. Whipple's disease (Option B) involves infection with Tropheryma whipplei and shows PAS-positive macrophages on biopsy. Tropical sprue (Option C) also causes villous atrophy and malabsorption but is associated with travel to endemic regions and is not linked to these specific autoantibodies. Because the TTG and endomysial antibodies are highly specific for gluten-sensitive enteropathy, Celiac sprue is the definitive diagnosis. Management requires a lifelong, strict gluten-free diet to allow the intestinal villi to recover and prevent long-term complications like lymphoma or osteoporosis
questions.learning: The clinical and laboratory triad of persistent small bowel diarrhea, villous atrophy on biopsy, and positive IgA tissue transglutaminase (TTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies is pathognomonic for Celiac sprue (Celiac disease) .

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presented with paracetamol poisoning and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was administered as an antidote. How does NAC prevent toxicity?
options: It inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for formation of toxic metabolite
It neutralizes the free radicals produced by paracetamol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It replenishes glutathione levels

N-acetylcysteine is considered a definite antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning and it works by replenishing glutathione levels.

Acetaminophen toxicity is an important cause of acute liver failure. Ingestion of ≥25g can be fatal. Cytochrome P450 CYP2E1 metabolizes acetaminophen to a toxic metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine (NAPQI). NAPQI is normally neutralized through conjugation with a reduced form of glutathione(GSH), after which it is excreted in the urine. When glutathione reserves are depleted or large amounts of NAPQI are formed, it binds to hepatocyte macromolecules. This can then lead to hepatocyte necrosis.

N-acetylcysteine repletes GSH stores and also conjugates with NAPQI and prevents oxidative damage to the cell. It also protects against extrahepatic injury due to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

Early manifestations of acetaminophen toxicity(within 4-12 hours) include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Later, renal failure and myocardial injury may be seen. Low bilirubin levels along with raised aminotransferase levels are characteristic of the condition.

Initial management includes gastric lavage and oral charcoal or cholestyramine. It should be carried out within thirty minutes of ingestion. If they are used, gastric lavage must be done afterwards before using another agent. Acetaminophen blood levels can be estimated from a nomogram plot. In patients with high acetaminophen levels, intravenous N-acetylcysteine administration within 8 hours of ingestion is recommended. It helps in the replenishment of glutathione. It is partially effective even up to 36 hours. Liver transplantation is necessary if signs of hepatic failure continue despite therapy.
questions.learning: It replenishes glutathione levels N-acetylcysteine is considered a definite antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning and it works by replenishing glutathione levels.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An overweight 12-year old girl has the following blackish discolouration on her neck, as shown below. What is this condition and its' association?
options: Cafe au lait spots - McCune Albright syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthosis nigricans - Insulin resistance

The condition shown in the above image is likely acanthosis nigricans - that is strongly associated with insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia

Acanthosis nigricans is a darkening of the skin of the intertriginous areas. The hyperpigmentation is generally velvety with poorly defined borders and thickening of the skin.

It can be grossly classified into benign and malignant.

Benign acanthosis nigricans is associated with obesity or insulin resistance. Insulin resistance is the most accepted hypothesis used to explain the pathophysiology of the condition. Elevated circulating fatty acids are considered a major factor in developing insulin resistance.

Malignant acanthosis nigricans has a rapid onset and is characterized by symmetrical, hyperpigmented, rugose, velvety plaques. It affects the axillae and flexures, nape of the neck, and mucosal surfaces. If it occurs de novo and is associated with weight loss, malignancy should be suspected. Generalized pruritus and skin changes of tripe palms (acanthosis palmaris) are also associated with malignancy. Associated malignancies are generally GI or lung carcinomas. In malignancy, tumor cells are believed to produce transforming growth factor-alpha or cytokines that activate insulin-like growth factors.

Acanthosis nigricans can only be treated by treating the underlying disease. In addition, treatment specific to acanthosis nigricans is done for aesthetic reasons. Medications like keratolytics, topical vitamin D, and melatonin can be used. Procedures like laser, dermabrasion, and chemical peels are also available.

Other options:

Option B: Stria Albicans is a stretch mark that is white or pearly in color. It is most common in pregnant women and people who have gained or lost weight quickly. Stria Albicans is not associated with Cushing syndrome, which is a hormonal disorder caused by excess cortisol production and produces a strechy, purplish rash most commonly over the abdomen/flanks.

Option C: Xeroderma pigmentosum - malignancy is a rare genetic disorder that makes the skin extremely sensitive to ultraviolet radiation from the sun. People with xeroderma pigmentosum have a greatly increased risk of developing skin cancer.

Option D: Cafe au lait spots - McCune Albright syndrome is a genetic disorder that causes multiple light brown, oval-shaped birthmarks on the skin. It is also associated with other symptoms, such as precocious puberty and bone abnormalities - polyostotic fibrous dysplasias.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. On evaluation, a diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome is made. Which cranial nerves are compressed in this condition?
questions.explanation: Superior orbital fissure syndrome involves compression of the structures passing through the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone. These include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), and the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1). Compression leads to total ophthalmoplegia (inability to move the eye) and ptosis. The maxillary nerve (V2) (Option B) is not affected because it passes through the foramen rotundum. The optic nerve (CN II) (Options C and D) is also spared because it enters the orbit through the separate optic canal. Thus, any syndrome resulting in extraocular muscle paralysis along with sensory loss in the forehead (V1) but sparing vision (CN II) and the mid-face (V2) specifically localizes to the superior orbital fissure
questions.learning: Superior orbital fissure syndrome involves compression of the structures passing through the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 21-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 36 weeks’ gestation presents to the hospital after being found to have a blood pressure of 190/110 mm Hg in the office. Initial laboratory studies show elevated serum creatinine and transaminases. She is treated with nifedipine and magnesium sulfate, and labor is induced with oxytocin. Six hours later, her blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. She now complaints of nausea, headache, generalized muscle weakness, and respiratory distress. On examination, deep tendon reflexes are absent. What is the most likely cause of the findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal insufficiency

This patient with severe preeclampsia was treated with magnesium sulfate, which is used to prevent eclamptic seizures.

Magnesium sulfate is excreted by the kidneys, so renal impairment can lead to magnesium accumulation and toxicity.

Features of magnesium toxicity:

• Loss of deep tendon reflexes (early sign)
• Muscle weakness
• Nausea and headache
• Respiratory depression/distress
• Severe cases → cardiac arrest

In this patient, elevated serum creatinine indicates renal insufficiency, which reduces magnesium excretion, leading to magnesium toxicity.

Management of magnesium toxicity:

• Stop magnesium sulfate
• Administer IV calcium gluconate as an antidote
• Provide respiratory support if needed
questions.learning: Renal insufficiency — This patient with severe preeclampsia was treated with magnesium sulfate, which is used to prevent eclamptic seizures. Magnesium sulfate is excreted by the kidneys, so renal impairment can lead to magnesium accumulation and toxicity.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: True regarding Oral Cholera vaccine ‘Sanchol’ is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bivalent with 2 doses

Shanchol is an oral killed whole-cell cholera vaccine that is bivalent, providing protection against Vibrio cholerae O1 and O139.

It requires two doses, given at an interval of about 2 weeks, to achieve adequate immunity.

DUKORAL:

Type: Killed whole-cell Vibrio cholerae O1 + recombinant B subunit of cholera toxin (rCTB)

Age: Approved for ≥2 years

Key feature: Contains B subunit toxin → provides additional antitoxin immunity (reduces severity of diarrhea)

Administration: Given orally with bicarbonate buffer (protects antigen from gastric acid)

Schedule:

• ≥6 years: 2 doses (1–6 weeks apart)
• 2–5 years: 3 doses

Protection: Duration \~ 2 years (booster needed thereafter)

Extra benefit: Also offers partial protection against ETEC (traveler’s diarrhea) due to B subunit similarity

Shanchol® / mORCVAX®

• Killed whole-cell vaccine containing:

• V. cholerae O1 (El Tor + Classical biotypes)
• V. cholerae O139

• No B subunit

Age: Approved for ≥1 year

Administration: Oral, no buffer required (major operational advantage in mass campaigns)

Schedule: 2 doses (2 weeks apart)

Protection: Duration \~ 3–5 years (longer than Dukoral in field use)

Public health use:

• Preferred for mass vaccination programs (WHO-recommended in endemic areas)
• Cheaper, easier logistics
questions.learning: Bivalent with 2 doses Shanchol is an oral killed whole-cell cholera vaccine that is bivalent, providing protection against Vibrio cholerae O1 and O139.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension and diabetes, recently diagnosed with end-stage renal disease (stage 5) and on hemodialysis, seeks dietary advice. Which of the following characterizes the ideal feed for him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low volume, high calories

•

In patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis, the ideal diet is low volume and high calorie.

•

Fluid intake must be restricted to prevent volume overload, hypertension, and pulmonary edema, while adequate calories are required to prevent protein-energy malnutrition and maintain nutritional status.

•

Thus, feeds should be calorie-dense with restricted fluid volume and controlled sodium, potassium, and phosphorus intake.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormone crosses the plasma membrane for its action?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroxine

Thyroxine crosses the plasma membrane for its action.

Thyroid hormones enter the nucleus and bind to thyroid hormone receptors. The hormone-receptor complex in the nucleus binds to DNA via zinc fingers. This increases the expression of a variety of different genes that code for proteins regulating cell function.  Although thyroxine is an AA derivative, there are transporters to move it into the cell, hence they are intracellular receptors acting on the nucleus.

Epinephrine, glucagon, and insulin bind to cell surface receptors.
questions.learning: Thyroxine Thyroxine crosses the plasma membrane for its action. Thyroid hormones enter the nucleus and bind to thyroid hormone receptors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency room after consuming 8 digoxin tablets. On examination, he was found to be unstable, with a heart rate of 56 beats per minute. An ECG revealed a third-degree heart block. What is the next step in this patient's care?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Digoxin Immune Fab

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Digoxin ingestion | Possible overdose

| Bradycardia | Increased vagal tone

| Complete heart block | Classic toxicity complication

This patient has acute digoxin toxicity with life-threatening bradyarrhythmia (complete heart block) and hemodynamic instability.

The definitive treatment is Digoxin Immune Fab, which binds free digoxin and rapidly reverses toxicity. Treatment: Digoxin Immune Fab

The antidote for digoxin toxicity is: Digoxin Immune Fab (Digoxin-specific antibody fragments)

Mechanism:

• Antibody binds free digoxin
• Forms inactive complexes
• Complexes are excreted in urine

Result: Rapid reversal of toxicity.

DC cardioversion is contraindicated as it can precipitate malignant arrhythmias in digoxin toxicity.

Antiarrhythmics like lidocaine or phenytoin are adjuncts, not definitive therapy in unstable patients.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man reports a gradual decline in hearing over several years, with particular difficulty understanding conversations in noisy surroundings and perceiving high-frequency sounds. He denies vertigo, tinnitus, or a sensation of ear fullness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Presbycusis is the symmetric, bilateral, age-related sensorineural hearing loss that occurs due to the degeneration of hair cells at the cochlear base. It typically affects high frequencies first, making it difficult for patients to understand speech, particularly in noisy settings. Meniere's disease (Option A) is characterized by fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss accompanied by vertigo and tinnitus. Otosclerosis (Option B) is a conductive hearing loss that often starts in early adulthood and characterized by improved hearing in noisy environments (Paracusis Willisii). Acoustic neuroma (Option D) typically presents with unilateral progressive hearing loss and imbalance. The gradual, symmetric high-frequency loss without autonomic features described here is pathognomonic for presbycusis. Management focuses on hearing aids and auditory rehabilitation to prevent social withdrawal
questions.learning: Presbycusis is the symmetric, bilateral, age-related sensorineural hearing loss that occurs due to the degeneration of hair cells at the cochlear base.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The mother of a newborn in your unit is extremely sick and is unable to feed her baby. The relatives have arranged a breast milk donor and wish to feed the baby using the device shown in the image. This method of primary feeding can be recommended in newborns with a gestational age of _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 32-34 weeks

The given image shows paladai. It can be used as a primary feeding method during routine feeding in neonates born at gestational age 32-34 weeks only. Sick mothers or mothers with contraindications to breastfeeding can feed their child using paladai. The milk can either be expressed breastmilk or they can resort to using undiluted cow milk or formula feeds.

Newborns with a gestational age of <32 weeks will not have the coordination between swallowing and breathing. So, paladai can only be used occasionally.

Newborns with a gestational age >34 weeks will have a completely mature sucking pattern when breastfeeding becomes more preferred.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The term demographic bonus is denotes______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decline in dependency ratio

The term demographic bonus denotes the decline in dependency ratio due to declining fertility.

A decline in the dependency ratio especially young age dependency ratio has been identified to be a key factor underlying the rapid economic development.

Demographic burden refers to an increase in the total dependency ratio, mostly caused by increased old-age dependency ratio.

Dependency ratio:

* Adults ≥65 years and children from 0 – 14 years are considered dependents.

* The total dependency ratio is the ratio of the combined dependent population to those in the age group of 15 – 65 years.

* Total dependency ratio = (children 0-14 years age + population above 65 years age) x 100/Total population in the age group of 15 – 64 years).

* It is also called societal dependency ratio.

* The total dependency ratio can also be divided into young age dependency ratio and old age dependency ratio.

* As of 2016, the dependency ratio of India is 52%.

* The potential support ratio is the inverse of the old age dependency ratio. It is the number of persons aged 15 to 64 per one older person aged 65 or more.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 27-year-old man has an asymptomatic retraction pocket of the tympanic membrane without keratin debris. The TM is mobile on Valsalva. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wait and watch

• Mild retraction pockets without keratin accumulation are managed conservatively.
• Normal TM mobility indicates preserved Eustachian tube function.
• Observation with periodic otoscopic follow-up is recommended.
• Surgery is indicated if:

• Progressive retraction
• Keratin debris
• Cholesteatoma
• Hearing loss

• Ventilation tubes are reserved for persistent middle-ear effusion or dysfunction.
• Tympanoplasty is unnecessary in an asymptomatic mobile membrane.
• Retraction pockets can remain stable for years.
• Regular follow-up prevents delayed cholesteatoma.
• No keratin + mobile TM = Observe.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive woman in her third trimester presents to the hospital with a viral load of 1,200 copies/mL and is started on antiretroviral therapy. She delivers a healthy infant at 38 weeks via normal vaginal delivery. The baby is exclusively breastfed. Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylactic therapy for the newborn?
options: Nevirapine single dose and continue breast feeding
Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 6 weeks and continue breast feeding
Nevirapine for 12 weeks and stop breast feeding
Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding

In HIV-exposed infants, the choice and duration of prophylaxis depend on maternal viral load and transmission risk.

High-risk exposure (e.g., maternal viral load >1000 copies/mL, late ART initiation) → dual prophylaxis is required.

Recommended management:

• Zidovudine + Nevirapine for 12 weeks
• Continue exclusive breastfeeding (with maternal ART)

Why not others:

• Single-dose nevirapine → inadequate prophylaxis
• 6 weeks regimen → for low-risk infants only
• Stopping breastfeeding → not recommended in resource-limited settings (benefits outweigh risks with ART)
questions.learning: Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding In HIV-exposed infants, the choice and duration of prophylaxis depend on maternal viral load and transmission risk.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A neonate presented with mild intermittent upper abdominal pain.On examination, the infant has a scaphoid abdomen and breath sounds are decreased on both sides. X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bochdalek hernia

The given clinical picture of respiratory distress, intermittent abdominal pain, scaphoid abdomen, absent breath sounds in both sides of the chest, and an X-ray image showing bowel loops in the thoracic cavity is diagnostic of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), the most common variant being Bochdalek hernia.

If the defect is posterolateral it is called Bochdalek hernia and if it's anteromedial it is called Morgagni hernia.

Clinical features :

* Respiratory distress is a cardinal sign in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

* Early respiratory distress, within 6 hr after birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign.

* Children with CDH may also have a scaphoid abdomen and increased chest wall diameter.

* Bowel sounds may also be heard in the chest, with a bilateral decrease in breath sounds.

* The point of maximal cardiac impulse may be displaced away from the side of a hernia if a mediastinal shift has occurred.

* Retroperitoneal fat, left kidney, spleen or only the omentum commonly herniates through the defect. If the defect is large, most abdominal contents including the stomach may herniate.

Diagnosis:

* Chest radiography and passage of a nasal gastric tube confirm the diagnosis.

* CDH can be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasonography (between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation)

* High-speed fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can further define the lesion.

Differential diagnosis:

* Diaphragmatic eventration

* Cystic adenomatoid malformation

* Bronchogenic cyst

* Cystic teratoma

Treatment:

Variable period of time (24-72 hours) to allow for stabilization before surgical repair. Immediate respiratory support should be provided, including rapid endotracheal intubation and sedation.

Bag and Mask Ventilation is contraindicated in newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia because it causes distension of the stomach which in turn may limit the expansion of the already hypoplastic lung.

During surgery, the viscera are reduced into the abdominal cavity, and the posterolateral defect in the diaphragm is closed using interrupted, nonabsorbable sutures.

In most cases (80%-90%), a hernia sac is not present. If identified, it is excised at the time of repair.

Conventional mechanical ventilation, high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV), and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) are the 3 main strategies to support respiratory failure in the newborn with CDH.

Good relative indicators of stability are as follows:

* Requirement for conventional ventilation only

* Low peak inspiratory pressure

* Fi-O2 <50

If the defect is too large, a porous polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex) patch is used.

Other options:

Gastric volvulus: This is an uncommon condition and presents with the characteristic Borchardt triad which includes:

* Sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain

* Recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus

* Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube

It can be organoaxial or mesentroaxial. Chest X-ray may show intrathoracic upside-down stomach and retrosternal or mediastinal air-fluid level.

Image showing intrathoracic gastric volvulus with mediastinal gastric bubble-

Eventration of the diaphragm: It refers to the abnormal contour of the dome of the diaphragm without any disruption to the diaphragmatic continuity. It usually involves a segment of the hemidiaphragm. It can cause respiratory distress in newborns and is usually asymptomatic in adults.

Radiographic findings: The affected portion of the hemidiaphragm is elevated and is seen as a smooth hump, while the normal contour is seen in the remaining part. 'Double diaphragmatic contour' may be seen in frontal view and is confirmed with a lateral X-ray.

Image showing eventration of the right dome of the diaphragm-

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a displaced nasal bone fracture after a road traffic accident (RTA). Which instrument is used for nasal bone reduction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Walsham forceps

Walsham forceps are specifically designed for closed reduction of displaced nasal bone fractures.

They allow controlled elevation and repositioning of the nasal bones with minimal trauma.

Other options:

·     Asch forceps: used for reduction of nasal septal fractures

·     Luc forceps: used for removing tissue (e.g., polyps)

·     Thudiculum/ Killian forceps/speculum: used for nasal examination and septal procedures
questions.learning: Walsham forceps Walsham forceps are specifically designed for closed reduction of displaced nasal bone fractures. They allow controlled elevation and repositioning of the nasal bones with minimal trauma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Oral contraceptive pill prevents all except?
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) offer significant protective benefits against several malignancies but are associated with a slightly increased risk of cervical cancer, particularly with long-term use. This is likely due to hormonal influences on HPV persistence. Conversely, OCPs are well-documented to prevent epithelial ovarian cancer (Option B) by suppressing ovulation and endometrial cancer (Option C) by providing a progestin-dominant environment that counteracts estrogen's proliferative effects. Evidence also suggests a modest protective effect against colon cancer (Option D). Because the use of OCPs does not protect against cervical malignancy and may instead elevate the risk, Option A is the correct "except" choice in this profile. Regular screening remains essential for OCP users to monitor for cervical neoplasia
questions.learning: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) offer significant protective benefits against several malignancies but are associated with a slightly increased risk of cervical cancer, particularly with long-term use.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man has the following lesion over the face. He complains of bleeding while itching. Which of the following is seen in the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rolled out edge

The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is an epithelial tumor arising from basal cells. It is the most common type of skin cancer most commonly seen over the face, above the line joining corner of the mouth, and lobule of the ear. Risk factors for BCC include ultraviolet radiation (strongest risk factor), age 40-80 years with excessive sun exposure, light-skinned people, and exposure to arsenic compounds, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and infrared light. It is more common in males than females. It is also associated with syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum and Gorlin's syndrome.

Features of BCC include:

* Pearly nodule with rolled border

* Tortuous telangiectatic vessels

* Surface which can get ulcerated with raised and beaded edge, often with a central depression or umbilication

* Bleeding on minor trauma

BCC has various subtypes such as nodular (most common type), pigmented, nodulocystic, morphoeic, infiltrative, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus.

It is locally aggressive and can erode the bone or facial sinuses. It rarely metastasizes via lymph nodes.

The occasional presence of melanin in the nodular variant of BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

Diagnosis is confirmed by a wedge biopsy. X-ray or CT may be needed if there is a local invasion. Histology shows peripheral palisading of cells.

Treatment:

* Surgical: Wide excision (4-6 mm clearance) with a skin graft or flap or primary suturing

* Mohs' surgery for BCC close to the eyes, nose, or ear to preserve more tissue.

* Non-surgical: Radiotherapy, vismodegib and sonedegib.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with facial palsy, as depicted in the image. Which anatomical structure is most likely involved in this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows clear facial asymmetry, including drooping of the corner of the mouth and incomplete eye closure on the affected side, which is characteristic of a 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve) palsy, commonly known as Bell's palsy. This lower motor neuron lesion affects all muscles of facial expression on the same side. Regarding the distractors, a 3rd nerve palsy (Option B) would present with ptosis (eyelid drooping) and abnormal eye deviation, but would not cause a drooping mouth. Erb's palsy (Option C) is a brachial plexus injury affecting the arm's "waiter's tip" position, not the face. An isolated orbicularis oculi palsy (Option D) would only affect the ability to close the eye and would not explain the lower facial drooping seen here. Therefore, the global hemifacial weakness confirms 7th nerve involvement

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Among the following food items, which one generally contains the highest sodium content?
questions.explanation: Among the options provided, canned soup contains the highest concentration of sodium. Processing and preservation techniques in the food industry frequently utilize significant amounts of sodium chloride and other sodium-containing preservatives (like MSG) to enhance flavor and extend shelf life. A single serving of canned soup can often exceed 50% of the recommended daily sodium intake. In contrast, natural, unprocessed foods like sugar cane (Option A), barley (Option B), and fresh fruit juices (Option D) are naturally very low in sodium. High dietary sodium is a primary risk factor for hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Clinicians often advise patients, especially those with heart or kidney conditions, to avoid processed and "canned" items in favor of fresh alternatives to manage their sodium load. Therefore, canned soup is the definitive answer for the highest sodium content among the listed foods

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 10-year-old child with hereditary spherocytosis and hypersplenism presents to the hospital. A splenectomy is planned for this child. All the following vaccines are recommended before splenectomy, except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Typhoid vaccine

The typhoid vaccine is not part of recommendations for a patient undergoing splenectomy.

Splenic insufficiency following splenectomy leads to increased susceptibility to sepsis caused by encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococci, meningococci, and H.influenzae. Such patients must be vaccinated against these agents to reduce the risk of sepsis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the ulcer shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Venous ulcer

The image of a healing ulcer with a sloping edge in the Gaiter's area indicates a venous ulcer.

Venous ulcers due to chronic venous insufficiency are most commonly seen in the lower ⅓ of the leg and foot. They usually lie just proximal to the medial or lateral malleolus.

Ambulatory venous hypertension is the most acceptable theory in the pathophysiology. They have a sloping edge and the floor contains granulation tissue covered by slough and exudate. Marjolin’s ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma seen in chronic long-standing venous ulcers. These are accompanied by lipodermatosclerosis and hemosiderosis.

Management of venous ulcers:

1) Bisgaard's regimen (4Es)

* Education of the patient

* Elevation of the affected limb to reduce the edema

* Elastic compression stockings - The ideal interface pressure in venous ulceration is 35-40 mmHg.

* Evaluation

2) 4-layer bandaging system comprising of:

* Orthopaedic wool

* Cotton crepe

* Elastic bandage - first compressive layer

* Cohesive bandage - second compressive layer

3) Antibiotics are given only if the wound is infected.
4) Regular dressing.
5) Medical management by oral pentoxifylline is considered which helps in reducing the viscosity and improving circulation.
6) Surgical management by ulcer excision with pinch mesh grafting has a good outcome and helps in preventing recurrence.

Note: Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) is a negative pressure dressing. An occlusive dressing is placed over the sore and it is connected to VAC that generates -125mmHg of pressure. It is used in chronic non-healing ulcers, venous ulcers, diabetic ulcers, burn wounds, and bed sores.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic cough and weight loss for three months. Biopsy of a lung mass shows tumor cells expressing chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most likely to be associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of chromogranin and synaptophysin on lung biopsy indicates a neuroendocrine tumor, most likely small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). SCLC is highly notorious for producing ectopic hormones. The most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with SCLC is the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion (SIADH), caused by ectopic ADH production. Hypercalcemia (Option A) is more classically associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung due to PTHrP secretion. While SCLC can cause Cushing syndrome via ectopic ACTH, SIADH is more frequently encountered in clinical practice for this tumor type. Gynaecomastia (Option C) is associated with certain germ cell tumors or liver disease, not neuroendocrine lung cancers. Therefore, given the specific neuroendocrine markers identified in the biopsy, SIADH is the most likely paraneoplastic manifestation to observe in this patient

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Aschoff Nodules are a pathognomonic cardiac finding in which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatic carditis

Aschoff nodules (Aschoff bodies) are the characteristic histopathological lesions of acute rheumatic fever, particularly rheumatic carditis. They represent areas of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by inflammatory cells, including characteristic Anitschkow cells (“caterpillar cells”).

Why not the other options?

• B. Infective endocarditis: Shows vegetations containing microorganisms, fibrin, and inflammatory cells, not Aschoff bodies.
• C. Rheumatoid arthritis: May produce rheumatoid nodules, characterized by central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes.
• D. Takayasu arteritis: Causes granulomatous inflammation of large arteries with intimal thickening and fibrosis.
