questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which murmur is depicted in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ejection systolic

The image given above is of an ejection systolic murmur.

This murmur starts after S1, increases in intensity to reach the peak, and ends before A2.

Ejection systolic murmur(ESM) is most commonly heard in aortic stenosis and in pulmonary stenosis. They are differentiated based on the difference in symptoms, site of murmur, etc.

Auscultation of ESM in aortic stenosis.

* In the early stages, an early systolic ejection sound may be heard. It disappears when the valve becomes calcified and rigid.

* As the stenosis worsens, the LV systole gets prolonged and there is delayed closure of the aortic valve. This leads to the narrowing of S2 sound, and in severe cases, it might lead to the paradoxical splitting of S2.

* S4 and S3 sounds may be heard in severe cases when the diastolic and systolic functions of the left ventricle have been reduced.

* Murmur: The murmur in aortic stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur. The murmur radiates to the neck and base of the heart. It is augmented by squatting and reduced by the strain of the Valsalva maneuver.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in his left eye. Neuro-ophthalmic evaluation localizes the lesion to the structure labeled "A" on the visual pathway diagram, corresponding to the left optic nerve before the optic chiasm. Which of the following visual field defects is most likely?
options: Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky")
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ipsilateral monocular blindness

• A lesion involving the optic nerve (pre-chiasmatic lesion) results in complete loss of vision in the affected eye (ipsilateral monocular blindness) because all visual information from that eye is interrupted before any fibers cross at the optic chiasm.
• The optic nerve contains fibers from both the nasal and temporal retina of the same eye. Damage to the nerve therefore abolishes all visual input from that eye, while vision in the opposite eye remains normal.

Why not the other options?

• B. Bitemporal hemianopia: Results from a lesion of the optic chiasm, where crossing nasal retinal fibers are compressed (classically by a pituitary adenoma).
• C. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia: Occurs due to lesions posterior to the optic chiasm (optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiations, or occipital cortex).
• D. Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"): Caused by a lesion of the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) affecting the inferior retinal fibers that carry the superior visual field.

High-yield visual pathway lesions

| Site of lesion | Visual field defect

| -------------- | -------------------

| Optic nerve | Ipsilateral monocular blindness

| Optic chiasm | Bitemporal hemianopia

| Optic tract / Occipital cortex | Contralateral homonymous hemianopia

| Temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) | Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("Pie in the sky")

| Parietal lobe (Superior optic radiations) | Contralateral inferior quadrantanopia ("Pie on the floor")

Exam pearl:

• Before the chiasm → One eye affected.
• At the chiasm → Temporal visual fields lost.
• After the chiasm → Homonymous visual field defects.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient with a history of smoking and diagnosed hypertension presents to the outpatient department for a routine health evaluation. As part of cardiovascular risk assessment, a device is used to evaluate vascular health and arterial status. The device is shown below. Which of the following statements regarding its functions and capabilities is NOT correct?
options: Based on infrared emitted from RBC's
Check thickness of artery and vein
questions.explanation: The device shown is a Doppler ultrasound machine, which is a cornerstone for evaluating vascular health. The statement that it is "based on infrared emitted from RBC's" (Option A) is NOT accurate. Doppler technology is based on the Doppler shift principle, where high-frequency ultrasound waves (sound, not light/infrared) reflect off moving red blood cells to determine the velocity and direction of blood flow. The other statements are accurate: the device checks blood flow (Option B) to identify stenosis or occlusion; it can localize calcified plaques (Option C) which appear as bright echogenic areas with shadowing; and it can check the thickness of the vessel walls (Option D), such as measuring the carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) as a marker of atherosclerosis. Doppler ultrasound is a non-invasive, safe, and highly effective tool for assessing cardiovascular risk in hypertensive patients and smokers. Understanding the fundamental physics of ultrasound versus infrared is essential for clinical practice

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man presents with a sudden onset of severe headache, dizziness, breathlessness, and blurring of vision while trekking on a mountain at an altitude of 5000 meters. He is unable to climb any further. Which of the following indicates the development of high-altitude cerebral edema?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Altered mental status

Altered mental status is a clinical finding indicative of the development of high-altitude cerebral edema.

At high altitudes, the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere is low. When people ascend to high altitudes hypoxia causes systemic arteriolar dilatation. Consequently, the capillary pressure rises with increased transudation of fluid into the brain tissue and lungs. This results in cerebral edema and pulmonary edema respectively.

Pathophysiology: Vasogenic edema occurs due to the leaking of proteins and water through the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Causes of increased BBB permeability include:

* Mechanical factors: loss of autoregulation and increased capillary pressure due to increased sympathetic activity (option D).

* Increased chemical mediators of permeability: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) (option C), nitric oxide, and cytokines (option A).

Patients with cerebral edema usually present with:

* Headache

* Worsening mental status and reduced alertness.

* Papilledema leading to a blurring of vision

* Breathlessness (due to hypoxia)

* Nausea and vomiting.

Treatment involves administration of oxygen, descent to a lower altitude, and administration of acetazolamide. Acetazolamide counteracts hypoxia by stimulating respiration and also reduces the formation of cerebrospinal fluid, thereby reducing intracranial tension. Glucocorticoids are administered as well.

Portable hyperbaric chambers are increasingly being used in the treatment of high-altitude illnesses when rapid descent is not possible. These chambers are available in armed forces hospitals in high-altitude areas.

Pearl PF1916: Acclimatization to high altitude
questions.learning: Altered mental status Altered mental status is a clinical finding indicative of the development of high-altitude cerebral edema. At high altitudes, the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere is low.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common bacteria found as part of the normal flora of the conjunctiva?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Staphylococcus epidermidis

Staphylococcus epidermidis is present as a normal flora of conjunctiva.

The normal flora of the conjunctiva consists of a variety of microorganisms that exist harmlessly and help maintain ocular health by preventing the colonization of pathogenic organisms. The most commonly found bacteria in the conjunctiva include:

Staphylococcus epidermidis (most common), staphylococcus aureus, corynebacterium species, streptococcus viridans, propionibacterium acnes, etc.

Staphylococcus epidermidis is a novobiocin-sensitive, coagulase-negative, non-pigmented, non-hemolytic cocci. It also doesn't ferment mannitol.

It is present on normal skin flora and mucous membranes and has the following virulence factors:

* Biofilms

* Adhesive proteins

* Teichoic acids

* Lipases and DNAses

Among the Coagulase negative staph species, Staph epidermidis is the most common cause of:

* Healthcare-associated bloodstream infections

* Early prosthetic valve endocarditis

* Peritonitis in dialysis patients

* Infections of orthopedic prosthesis

* CSF shunt infections

S. epidermidis is more resistant than Staph aureus to methicillin and the treatment of choice is Vancomycin.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents to the outpatient department with ear pain and hearing loss following trauma to the right ear. Otoscopic examination shows blood clots in the external auditory canal along with irregular perforations of the tympanic membrane. What should be the next step in management?
options: Aspirate the clot and perform audiometric tests
Maintain dry ear with systemic analegesics
questions.explanation: Following acute traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane, the best management is conservative. The primary goal is to maintain a dry ear to prevent secondary infection, which allows the vast majority of these perforations to heal spontaneously within 6–12 weeks. Systemic analgesics can be used to manage pain. Aspirating clots or performing extensive tests (Option A) should be avoided in the acute stage to minimize irritation. Syringing (Option B) is absolutely contraindicated in the presence of a perforation as it can introduce bacteria and water into the middle ear, causing otitis media. Routine antibiotic ear drops (Option D) are generally avoided unless active infection is present, as some drops (like Gentamycin) can be ototoxic if they reach the inner ear through the perforation. Patients should be counseled to avoid blowing their nose forcefully and to keep water out of the ear during bathing. If the perforation fails to heal after 3 months, surgical repair (myringoplasty) may then be considered

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An enzyme is incubated with a substrate in the presence and absence of uncompetitive inhibitor and Lineweaver-Burk plots are obtained as shown. Which of the following graphs represents uncompetitive inhibition?
options: [Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. [image not included in this edition]

Uncompetitive inhibition occurs when the inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex, forming an inactive ESI complex. This decreases both the maximum velocity (Vmax) and the Michaelis constant (Km) by the same proportion. As a result, on a Lineweaver–Burk plot, the inhibited and uninhibited lines are parallel because the slope (Km/Vmax) remains unchanged.

• In uncompetitive inhibition:

• Vmax decreases → Y-intercept (1/Vmax) increases
• Km decreases → X-intercept (-1/Km) shifts further to the left
• Slope (Km/Vmax) remains unchanged

• Therefore, the Lineweaver–Burk plot shows parallel lines, as seen in Option B

Why not the other options?

• A. Competitive inhibition: Vmax is unchanged, Km increases; lines intersect on the Y-axis.
• B. Mixed inhibition: Both Km and Vmax change, but not proportionally; lines intersect left of the Y-axis.
• D. Noncompetitive inhibition (pure): Vmax decreases while Km remains unchanged; lines intersect on the X-axis.
questions.learning: [image not included in this edition] Uncompetitive inhibition occurs when the inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex, forming an inactive ESI complex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked area in the image given (arrow pointing to the space between the uterus and rectum).
questions.explanation: The marked area in the pelvic image is the Pouch of Douglas, also known as the rectouterine pouch. It is the lowest and most dependent point of the peritoneal cavity in a standing female, located between the posterior wall of the uterus and the anterior wall of the rectum. Morrison’s pouch (Option A) is the hepatorenal space in the upper abdomen, which is the most dependent part when lying supine. The vesicouterine pouch (Option B) is located anteriorly between the uterus and the bladder, situated higher in the pelvic cavity. The ischioanal fossa (Option D) is a fat-filled space located on either side of the anal canal, below the pelvic diaphragm. The Pouch of Douglas is a clinically significant site for the accumulation of fluids like blood, pus, or ascites

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is represented by the given form of replication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Influenza virus

The given image shows generation of mRNA from negative sense RNA within the nucleus. This occurs during the replication of influenza virus.

Orthomyxoviruses (influenza virus) contain segmented (8 segments) negative sense ssRNA that is replicated in the nucleus. Stages of viral replication include the following:

1. Attachment, penetration, uncoating: The virus attaches to cell-surface sialic acid via hemagglutinin. It is then internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis. There is fusion of the viral envelope and cell membrane, resulting in uncoating or release of nucleocapsid into the host cell cytoplasm.
2. Transcription and translation:  mRNAs are produced from nucleocapsids via a virus-encoded polymerase. This process occurs in the nucleus. The mRNAs thus produced are translated into viral proteins in the cytoplasm.
3. Viral RNA replication: The viral genome is replicated by the same virus-encoded polymerase involved in transcription. The negative sense RNA is converted to its positive sense form. The positive sense copies serve as templates for replication of the viral genome.
4. Maturation: The virus matures by budding from the surface of the cell.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 48-year-old female underwent total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The surgical specimen revealed solid ovarian tumour and histology revealed thecoma-fibroma. Which one of the following is the most appropriate statement regarding this condition?
options: It is always associated with gross ascites
It is derived from germ cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial hyperplasia is often associated

Thecoma-fibroma tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary. Thecomas are estrogen-producing tumors, whereas fibromas are usually hormonally inactive. The estrogen secretion by thecoma can stimulate the endometrium, leading to endometrial hyperplasia, Abnormal uterine bleeding and, occasionally, endometrial carcinoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  20% of such tumours are bilateral: Fibromas and thecomas are usually unilateral (>90%). Bilaterality is uncommon.
• C. It is always associated with gross ascites:

• Ascites is not always present.
• Ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion = Meigs syndrome, which occurs only in a minority of patients.

• D. It is derived from germ cells: Thecoma-fibroma tumors arise from the sex cord-stromal cells, not germ cells.
questions.learning: Endometrial hyperplasia is often associated — Thecoma-fibroma tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary. Thecomas are estrogen-producing tumors, whereas fibromas are usually hormonally inactive.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following curves represents gamma-globin chain production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Orange curve

In the given image, the Orange curve represents the gamma-globin chain production. Gamma globin chain is produced in the fetal period and drops to undetectable levels 6 months postpartum which is the pattern represented by the Orange curve.

Hemoglobin in blood has different variants throughout life, in different proportions. The type of hemoglobin essentially depends on the combination of globin chains. Adult hemoglobin is made of 2 alpha and 2 beta chains, whereas fetal hemoglobin is made of 2 alpha and 2 gamma-globin chains. Other combinations of chains can be found in embryonic hemoglobin.

Here,

• Gamma chain - Orange curve
• Alpha chain - Red curve
• Beta chain - Green curve
• Epsilon chain - Black curve
• Delta chain - Blue curve

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Determine the smell resulting from the alteration depicted in the accompanying picture.
questions.explanation: The image shows a mummified body, characterized by dry, shrunken, leathery skin and preservation of body contours. Mummification occurs in hot, dry environments where rapid dehydration prevents bacterial growth and putrefaction. In this process, the body loses moisture quickly, leading to inhibition of decomposition by bacteria. Since putrefaction is minimal or absent, the typical foul-smelling gases and compounds (like hydrogen sulfide and ammonia) are not produced. As a result, mummified bodies are usually odorless or have minimal smell, unlike decomposing bodies. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Pungent: Seen in chemical exposure or early decomposition, not mummification (C) Putrid: Characteristic of putrefaction, not mummified remains (D) Offensive: General term, but not specific; mummified bodies lack foul odor
questions.learning: The image shows a mummified body, characterized by dry, shrunken, leathery skin and preservation of body contours. Mummification occurs in hot, dry environments where rapid dehydration prevents bacterial growth and putrefaction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient came to ED with complaints of weakness, paresthesia, and breathing difficulty. Relevant investigations were done. The ECG obtained is suggestive of :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypokalemia

The symptoms of weakness, paresthesia, and dyspnea along with the given ECG showing depression of the ST segment, a decrease in the amplitude of the T wave (flattening or inversion), and an increase in the amplitude of U waves (at the end of the T wave) are characteristic of hypokalemia.

In the given ECG, leads V1-V6 exhibit T wave inversion. U waves are well appreciated in leads V2-V5.

Hypokalemia leads to dynamic ECG changes. The image given shows the sequence of changes observed:

Hypokalemia is defined as plasma K+ concentration of <3.5meq/L. It can also cause premature atrial and ventricular beats, sinus bradycardia, paroxysmal atrial or junctional tachycardia, atrioventricular block, and ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.

Other options:

Option B: Hyperkalemia causes tall peaked T waves with a shortened QT interval. There is a progressive lengthening of the PR interval and QRS duration with an increase in potassium levels, eventually leading to the disappearance of the P wave; and widening of the QRS complex to a sine wave pattern.

Option C: Hypocalcemia causes prolongation of the QT interval. There is a lengthening of the ST segment, while the T wave (which correlates with the time for repolarization) remains unaltered.

Option D: Hypercalcemia causes shortening of the QT interval and a decrease in the ST segment duration.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In the case of anterior ethmoidal neuralgia, where is the anterior ethmoidal nerve most commonly compressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Middle meatus

The middle meatus is the most common site of compression of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, causing neuralgia.

Anterior ethmoidal neuralgia, also known as Sluder's neuralgia is caused when the anterior ethmoidal nerve, a branch of the nasociliary nerve (which is itself a branch of the ophthalmic nerve, CN V1), is compressed. The most common site of compression is at the middle meatus, where the nerve may be impinged by anatomical variations, inflammation, or other pathologies affecting the paranasal sinuses.

The anterior ethmoidal nerve enters the nasal cavity by descending through the cribriform plate near the crista galli. Once in the nasal cavity, the nerve descends along the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. It runs above the superior border of the middle meatus and provides sensory innervation to the mucosa of the anterior part of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity

The patient typically presents with severe, sharp, and stabbing pain localized to the forehead and the root of the nose, often radiating to the periocular region. The pain is usually unilateral but can occasionally be bilateral. Associated symptoms may include tenderness over the affected area and occasionally nasal congestion or discharge if there is concurrent sinusitis.

Computed Tomography (CT) or Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the paranasal sinuses can be employed to identify anatomical variations, mucosal thickening, or other potential sources of nerve compression.

Management involves analgesics (such as NSAIDs or acetaminophen), and in more severe cases, neuropathic pain medications like gabapentin or pregabalin can be used to alleviate pain.
Nasal corticosteroids or saline nasal irrigation may be prescribed to reduce inflammation and relieve associated nasal symptoms.
Surgical intervention is considered in cases where conservative treatments are ineffective and anatomical abnormalities are identified.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient develops secondary amenorrhea for 9 months following a dilatation and curettage (D&C). Both the progesterone challenge test and the estrogen + progesterone challenge test are negative. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asherman syndrome

Asherman Syndrome occurs due to scar formation inside the uterine cavity, most commonly after D&C procedures. These adhesions obliterate the endometrial cavity, preventing menstruation.

Progesterone Challenge Test

Purpose: Detect estrogenized endometrium.

| Result | Meaning

| ------ | -------

| Withdrawal bleeding present | Estrogen present

| No bleeding | Either low estrogen OR outflow tract problem

Estrogen + Progesterone Test

This test differentiates ovarian failure from uterine causes.

| Result | Interpretation

| ------ | --------------

| Bleeding occurs | Estrogen deficiency

| No bleeding | Endometrial damage or outflow obstruction

Since both tests are negative, it indicates:Endometrial damage → Asherman syndrome.

| Cause | Example

| ----- | -------

| Post D&C | Most common cause

| Postpartum curettage | Retained products

| Uterine infection | Tuberculosis

| Endometrial surgery | Myomectomy

Best investigation: Hysteroscopy

It directly visualizes intrauterine adhesions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with signs of hypothyroidism, including cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and a delayed ankle jerk reflex. Laboratory results show a TSH of 15 IU/L with low T3 and T4 levels. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Order a thyroid radionuclide uptake and scan
questions.explanation: The patient presents with classic clinical signs of hypothyroidism and definitive biochemical confirmation: an elevated TSH (15 IU/L, where normal is typically ) and low T3/T4 levels . This profile is diagnostic of primary overt hypothyroidism. The standard of care and most appropriate next step is to begin treatment with levothyroxine (LT4) (Option A) to restore a euthyroid state. Measuring TBG (Option B) is unnecessary as it only assesses binding capacity rather than thyroid function. A radionuclide scan (Option C) and ultrasonography (Option D) are used to evaluate thyroid anatomy, nodules, or hyperthyroidism, but they have no role in the initial management of confirmed primary hypothyroidism. Treatment aims to normalize TSH levels and resolve symptoms. Therefore, because the diagnosis is already biochemically and clinically established, pharmacological replacement is the definitive next action. Regular TSH monitoring is then used to titrate the LT4 dose
questions.learning: The patient presents with classic clinical signs of hypothyroidism and definitive biochemical confirmation: an elevated TSH (15 IU/L, where normal is typically ) and low T3/T4 levels .

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A newly married female patient, 21 weeks pregnant, underwent a fetal USG which showed myelomeningocele of the fetus. The doctor proposed medical termination of pregnancy (MTP). Which of the following is mandatory in this case? a. Patient's consent b. Patient's partner's consent c. Opinion of 1 doctor d. Opinion of 2 doctors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. a and d

Only the patient/mother's consent is required for MTP; her partner's consent is not required. Consent of parent/guardian is needed if the age of the patient is <18 years or if the patient is mentally ill.

2 doctors' opinion is required as the patient's gestational age is >20 weeks.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint be lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act with 2021 amendments

Indications:

* Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother

* Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure

* Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest

* Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives

Rules:

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Confidentiality:

A register for recording the details of MTP must be kept for at least 5 years. The patient's name must not be entered, only the reference number is used. Unlawful disclosure of patient's details is punishable with 1-year imprisonment ± fine.
questions.learning: a and d Only the patient/mother's consent is required for MTP; her partner's consent is not required. Consent of parent/guardian is needed if the age of the patient is 20 weeks.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with fever and a rash spreading from the face, behind cheeks, and buccal mucosa to other body parts. On examination, Koplik's spot is present. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Measles

The likely diagnosis is measles based on the clinical symptoms and the presence of Koplik spots.

Koplik spots are discrete red lesions with central bluish-white spots seen on the buccal mucosa at the level of premolars.

The measles virus has an incubation period of 8-12 days, after which the prodrome phase begins with mild fever, conjunctivitis, upper respiratory tract infection, and pathognomic Koplik spots. This follows the appearance of maculopapular rash after 4th day of fever, which begins at the face and spreads to the torso and extremities. Lymphadenopathy may be present. Treatment is supportive. The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media.

The image below shows Koplik spots.

Other options:

Option B: Rubella presents with low-grade fever, centrifugal macular rash, and prominent lymphadenopathy (suboccipital, postauricular, and anterior cervical lymph nodes). Forchheimer spots (tiny rose-colored lesions on the soft palate) may be present.

The image below shows Forchheimer spots.

Option C: Varicella presents with fever, malaise, and anorexia, followed by a pruritic maculopapular rash, which forms vesicles with a characteristic "cropping" distribution (simultaneous presence of lesions in various stages of evolution).

Option D: Mumps presents with fever, headache, parotitis, and ipsilateral auricular pain. A morbilliform rash may occur.
questions.learning: Measles — The likely diagnosis is measles based on the clinical symptoms and the presence of Koplik spots. Koplik spots are discrete red lesions with central bluish-white spots seen on the buccal mucosa at the level of premolars.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Among the tumors listed, which one is most sensitive to radiation therapy?
questions.explanation: Tumors vary significantly in their responsiveness to ionizing radiation. Ewing's sarcoma is highly radiosensitive (Option A), making radiotherapy a core component of its multi-modal management alongside chemotherapy and surgery. In contrast, Osteosarcoma (Option C) is generally radioresistant, meaning radiation has a limited role and surgery is the primary curative treatment. Melanoma (Option B) and Renal cell carcinoma (Option D) are also notoriously radioresistant malignancies that require targeted therapies, immunotherapy, or extensive surgical excision. Understanding the radiosensitivity of different tumors is essential for planning appropriate oncological protocols. Ewing's sarcoma cells are sensitive to DNA damage caused by radiation, leading to effective tumor shrinkage. Therefore, Ewing's sarcoma is recognized as the most radiation-sensitive tumor among the choices provided. This sensitivity is a critical diagnostic and therapeutic consideration in pediatric oncology
questions.learning: Tumors vary significantly in their responsiveness to ionizing radiation. Ewing's sarcoma is highly radiosensitive (Option A), making radiotherapy a core component of its multi-modal management alongside chemotherapy and surgery.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nonsense mutation

A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as a nonsense mutation.

A codon is a sequence of three bases present on the mRNA (messenger RNA), and it codes for amino acids. Out of the 64 codons possible, only 61 code for the 20 amino acids. Three codons, UAA, UAG, and UGA  do not code for any of the 20 amino acids. These are known as nonsense/punctator/termination/stop codons and function as translation termination signals. The UGA codon is traditionally considered a stop codon, but it codes for selenocysteine (21st amino acid).

The tRNA (transfer RNA) contains the anticodon which recognizes specific codons present on the mRNA. The sequence of the anticodon is complementary to the codon. The pairing between the codon and anticodon can wobble at the third base. For example, GGU, GGC, and GGA all pair with the anticodon CCI. The wobble phenomenon along with degeneracy reduces the effect of mutations.

A mutation involving a single nucleotide base is known as a point mutation. A nonsense mutation is a type of point mutation where a codon previously coding for an amino acid is changed to a stop codon. This results in premature termination of translation and the formation of a truncated protein. mRNA containing premature stops are removed by the nonsense-mediated degradation pathway.

Other options:

Option A: A missense mutation is a type of point mutation where the new codon, formed by the changed base, codes for a different amino acid.

Option C: Stop mutation is a term that can be used interchangeably with nonsense mutation. Here, nonsense mutation is the best answer.

Option D: Silent mutations are point mutations where the new codon formed still codes for the same amino acid as the codon before the mutation.
questions.learning: Nonsense mutation — A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as a nonsense mutation. A codon is a sequence of three bases present on the mRNA (messenger RNA), and it codes for amino acids.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with anemia and hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral blood smear examination reveals teardrop-shaped red cells, nucleated erythrocytes, and giant platelets. Based on the accompanying bone marrow biopsy findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of anemia, massive hepatosplenomegaly, and the presence of "teardrop" red blood cells (dacrocytes) and a leukoerythroblastic blood picture (nucleated RBCs and immature myeloid cells) is diagnostic of Primary Myelofibrosis (PMF). The bone marrow biopsy is the confirmatory test, showing extensive replacement of normal marrow by collagen fibrosis, often referred to as a "dry tap" during aspiration. This fibrosis is driven by the release of growth factors like TGF-beta from abnormal megakaryocytes. Polycythemia vera (Option A) and Essential thrombocythemia (Option B) can eventually progress to a similar "spent phase" of myelofibrosis, but the primary pathology described here is PMF. Chronic myeloid leukemia (Option D) typically presents with a very high WBC count and the Philadelphia chromosome rather than primary marrow fibrosis. Teardrop cells are characteristic of marrow being squeezed through fibrous tissue
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of anemia, massive hepatosplenomegaly, and the presence of "teardrop" red blood cells (dacrocytes) and a leukoerythroblastic blood picture (nucleated RBCs and immature myeloid cells) is diagnostic of Primary Myelofibrosis (PMF).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the level of prevention when a person receives penicillin injections for the treatment of rheumatic heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary

Receiving penicillin injections for the treatment of rheumatic heart disease is Secondary prevention.

Secondary prevention includes early disease detection, and its target is healthy-appearing individuals with subclinical forms of the disease. This is defined as the action which halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications.

Levels of Prevention :

1. Primordial prevention:

* Involves the prevention of the emergence or development of risk factors in countries or population groups in which they have not yet appeared.

* Examples include adult health problems like obesity and hypertension, which have an early onset due to lifestyles like smoking, eating patterns and physical exercise, which are discouraged from early childhood

* The main intervention in primordial prevention is through individual and mass education.

2. Primary prevention:

* These are defined as "action taken prior to the onset of disease, which removes the possibility that a disease will ever occur''

* It signifies intervention in the pre-pathogenesis phase of a disease or health problem

* Primary prevention is accomplished by measures promoting general health and well-being, and the quality of life of people by specific protective measures.

* They include two strategies:

* Population (mass) strategy: Where the target group is the whole population

* High-risk strategy: Where the target group is limited to the people who are most at risk of developing a particular disease

* Examples: immunity, sanitation, and protection of food.

3. Secondary prevention :

* This is defined as "action which halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications.".

* The specific interventions are early diagnoses like screening tests and adequate treatment.

* The main aim of secondary prevention is to arrest the disease process.

* Secondary prevention is largely the domain of clinical medicine and health programs initiated by governments.

* It is an imperfect tool in the control of the transmission of disease. It is often more expensive and less effective than primary prevention.

4. Tertiary prevention :

* Measures to reduce the duration of mental illness and family and community stresses to prevent further breakdown and disruption.

* Disability limitation belongs to tertiary prevention.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A female patient is on first-line pharmacological therapy for bipolar disorder for 6 months. She is fasting for a few days due to religious reasons and presented with seizures, coarse tremors, confusion, and weakness of limbs. Which of the following investigations should be done to help diagnose her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum lithium level

The clinical features given in the question are most likely suggestive of lithium toxicity, and hence serum lithium levels should be measured to confirm it.

Lithium is a mood stabilizer with a very narrow therapeutic index and is the first line of management in bipolar disorder.

The kidney handles both lithium and Na+ in the same way via ENac channel. Thus during fasting/dehydration, along with Na+ reabsorption in renal tubules, there will be an increase in the reabsorption of lithium leading to lithium toxicity.

Lithium has a very narrow therapeutic index of 0.8-1.2 mEq/L. The severity of lithium toxicity is often divided into the following three grades:

Grade

Sr. lithium concentration (in mEq/L)

Symptoms

Mild symptoms
1.5-2.5
nausea, vomiting, tremor, and fatigue

Moderate intoxication
2.5-3.5
confusion, agitation, delirium, tachycardia, and hypertonia

Severe intoxication
>3.5
coma, seizures, hyperthermia, and hypotension

A fine tremor is common in patients taking lithium at therapeutic doses. Therapeutic lithium tremor is generally symmetric, limited to the arms, and nonprogressive. The tremor from lithium toxicity is coarser and more disabling, may also affect the legs, and occurs with other symptoms of toxicity. Other adverse effects include mental confusion, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and edema.

As lithium is readily dialyzed, lithium overdose or toxicity is treated with hemodialysis.

*Note - Serum Na+ levels are significant with respect to lithium toxicity, where as serum potassium levels becomes significant in digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.
questions.learning: Serum lithium level — The clinical features given in the question are most likely suggestive of lithium toxicity, and hence serum lithium levels should be measured to confirm it.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, nocturnal cough, breathlessness, and wheezing for 4 weeks. Absolute eosinophil count >5000/μL. Chest X-ray shows a miliary pattern. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia

The clinical features along with elevated absolute eosinophil count and miliary pattern in chest x-ray are suggestive of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) is a hyperresponsive pulmonary syndrome that occurs in response to trapped microfilariae within the lung parenchyma. It is a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.

Clinical features:

The patient has a history of residence in a filaria endemic area and usually presents with nocturnal paroxysmal wheeze and cough. Other manifestations include weight loss, low-grade fever, and lymphadenopathy. Hepatosplenomegaly may be seen due to the trapping of microfilariae in the reticuloendothelial system.

Investigations:

• Eosinophilia > 3000/μL, leucocytosis
• X-ray chest: Mottled opacities or military lesions in the middle and lower lung fields, increased bronchovascular markings
• PFT: Restrictive changes in most cases and obstructive defects in half
• Elevated levels of IgE and Antifilarial antibody titers
• Microfilaria are sequestrated in the lungs and hence not found in blood

Treatment: Diethylcarbamazine(DEC) at a daily dosage of 4-6 mg/kg for 14 days.

Differntial Diagnosis:

• Bronchial asthma
• Loffler syndrome
• Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
• Churg strauss syndrome
•

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia

•

Hypereosinophilic syndromes

Other options:

Option A:  The classical symptoms of bronchial asthma are wheezing, dyspnea, and cough which is worse at night and keeps the patient awake in the early morning hours. Chest auscultation reveals rhonchi throughout the chest. The chest x-ray is usually normal but hyperinflation may be seen in severe patients.

Option B: Miliary TB occurs due to the hematogenous spread of tubercle bacilli. Clinical features are nonspecific and depend on the site of involvement. Common manifestations include fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, and weight loss. Blood investigations may reveal anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, leukemoid reactions, and polycythemia. Chest x-ray shows a military reticulonodular pattern in some cases.

Option D: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis, is an inflammatory response to various inhaled antigens. The clinical presentation can be acute, subacute, and chronic. History of exposure to the offending antigen is present. Chest x-ray findings are nonspecific and can show ground-glass opacities or ill-defined micronodular opacities.
questions.learning: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia — The clinical features along with elevated absolute eosinophil count and miliary pattern in chest x-ray are suggestive of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which filter is used in a colposcope?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Green

The filter used in a colposcope is green.

A colposcope is used to perform colposcopy where the cervix is visualized at a distance of around 20 cm with the patient in the lithotomy position.

This instrument provides binocular vision with a magnification of 6x-15x. A green filter is used to study vascular patterns as the vessels appear black. Abnormal areas can be identified by their peculiar vascular pattern such as mosaic, reticular, and punctate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for a patient with a 10 cm renal cell carcinoma located in the lower pole of the kidney, with no regional lymph node involvement?
questions.explanation: For a large Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) measuring 10 cm (classified as stage T2a), the gold standard treatment is a Radical Nephrectomy . This procedure involves the complete removal of the kidney, the surrounding Gerota’s fascia, and the adrenal gland (if indicated). While partial nephrectomy (Option B) is preferred for small masses ( cm), it is generally unsuitable and technically difficult for a large 10 cm tumor, even if it is located at the lower pole. RCC is notoriously resistant to both conventional radiotherapy (Option C) and systemic chemotherapy (Option D); therefore, surgery remains the only curative modality. Modern management for large tumors may utilize a laparoscopic or robotic-assisted radical approach to minimize patient morbidity. Given the size of the lesion and the localized nature (negative nodes), radical surgical excision provides the best long-term oncological control and survival benefit for this patient

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is meant by using a split-thickness skin graft for wound closure on the thigh?
options: Epidermis and variable part of the dermis
questions.explanation: A split-thickness skin graft (STSG) is a surgical graft that includes the entire epidermis and a variable portion of the underlying dermis. It is "split" because it leaves the deep dermal layers and skin appendages (like sweat glands and hair follicles) at the donor site, allowing the donor area to heal spontaneously. Option A describes a Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG), which includes the entire dermis. Option C is incorrect, as a graft consisting of only epidermis would not survive or provide adequate coverage. Option D refers to a composite graft or skin-flap, as grafts never include fat because they require a vascular bed to take. STSGs are preferred for covering large areas, such as the thigh, because they have a higher "take" rate compared to thicker grafts. Therefore, the inclusion of the epidermis and a partial thickness of the dermis is the definitive anatomical description of an STSG

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the tachycardia depicted in the given ECG.
questions.explanation: The ECG shows classic features of Atrial Flutter — characteristic sawtooth/flutter waves (F waves) visible at a rate of approximately 300 bpm with regular ventricular response, most prominent in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Key ECG Features visible: 1. Classic sawtooth pattern of flutter waves 2. Regular atrial activity at ~300 bpm 3. Consistent 2:1 or 4:1 AV conduction ratio 4. Narrow QRS complexes 5. No isoelectric baseline between atrial deflections Why other options are wrong: (A) Atrial fibrillation is incorrect because AF shows irregularly irregular rhythm with chaotic, disorganized fibrillatory waves and no identifiable P waves — completely unlike the regular sawtooth pattern seen here. (C) Ventricular tachycardia is incorrect because VT shows wide, bizarre QRS complexes at 100–250 bpm with no discernible P waves. The QRS complexes here are narrow, ruling out ventricular origin. (D) Ventricular fibrillation is incorrect because VF shows completely chaotic, irregular, disorganized electrical activity with no identifiable waveforms — incompatible with the organized regular pattern visible in this ECG

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 48-year-old man presenting with scrotal swelling, elevated LDH levels, normal AFP levels on tumor marker evaluation, and a characteristic histopathological finding following orchidectomy?
questions.explanation: The histological image and clinical data provided are characteristic of a seminoma, the most common type of germ cell tumor in adults. The pathognomonic histological features seen are large, uniform, polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm (due to glycogen) and "fried-egg" nuclei, organized in nests separated by thin fibrous septa containing lymphocytic infiltrates. Clinically, seminomas often cause elevated Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) but are typically negative for Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP); a high AFP would instead suggest a yolk sac tumor (Option A) or a mixed germ cell tumor. Teratomas (Option B) would show tissues from multiple germ layers (hair, teeth, etc.). Embryonal carcinoma (Option D) features pleomorphic cells in glandular or papillary patterns with more aggressive necrosis. Given the uniform cell population, clear cytoplasm, and the characteristic lymphocytic septa, seminoma is the definitive diagnosis for this middle-aged patient

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which anatomical structure is indicated at the site marked within the anatomical snuff box?.
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuff box is a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist. Its lateral (anterior) boundary is formed by the tendons of the Abductor pollicis longus and the Extensor pollicis brevis. The medial (posterior) boundary is formed by the tendon of the Extensor pollicis longus. The image points to the lateral boundary, making Extensor pollicis brevis the correct identification. Adductor pollicis (Option A) is a deep muscle of the hand and not a boundary of this space. Flexor pollicis longus (Option C) is located on the volar aspect of the wrist. While the Cephalic vein (Option D) and the superficial branch of the radial nerve cross over the snuff box, they are not the tendon structure highlighted. The floor of the snuff box contains the radial artery and the scaphoid bone, making it a critical site for palpating the pulse and assessing scaphoid fractures
questions.learning: The anatomical snuff box is a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist. Its lateral (anterior) boundary is formed by the tendons of the Abductor pollicis longus and the Extensor pollicis brevis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Name the parasite whose microfilaria have a sheath with no nuclei at the tail end.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wuchereria bancrofti

A sheathed microfilaria with a pointed tail free of nuclei is suggestive of Wuchereria bancrofti.

Wuchereria bancrofti causes lymphatic filariasis and most cases are seen in India.

Clinical features include massive eosinophilia, hepatosplenomegaly, pulmonary manifestations like dry nocturnal cough, asthmatic wheezing, and dyspnea. It can also cause arthritis, glomerulonephritis, thrombophlebitis, etc. The classical features seen in lymphatic filariasis are usually absent.

Elephantiasis refers to the painful swelling of the legs and genital organs seen in late-stage disease.

Image showing elephantiasis-

Investigations:

Demonstration of the microfilaria in peripheral blood, chylous urine, hydrocele fluid, etc is done.  The specimen of choice is peripheral blood. Night blood samples between 10 pm and 4 am are preferred. This is because the microfilaria shows nocturnal periodicity.

DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with a dilated, tortuous vein in the leg. He reports a history of trauma to the same area 10 years ago. On examination, a pulsatile vein is also noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of a dilated, tortuous vein that is pulsatile following remote trauma is highly characteristic of an acquired Arteriovenous (A-V) Fistula. Penetrating or blunt trauma can create an abnormal communication between an adjacent artery and vein. Over time, high-pressure arterial blood enters the low-pressure venous system, causing the vein to dilate (venous hypertension) and exhibit palpable pulsations or a "thrill." Standard varicose veins (Option A) are common but are not pulsatile; they result from valvular incompetence rather than arterial shunting. Angiofibromas (Option B) are highly vascular benign tumors, usually found in the nasopharynx of adolescent males, not the leg. Hemangiomas (Option C) are congenital vascular malformations or tumors that typically present in childhood and do not usually develop pulsations later in life due to trauma. Therefore, the combination of a traumatic history and pulsatile venous dilation confirms an A-V fistula as the most probable etiology
questions.learning: The presentation of a dilated, tortuous vein that is pulsatile following remote trauma is highly characteristic of an acquired Arteriovenous (A-V) Fistula.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The thermic effect is highest in ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proteins

The thermic effect is highest in proteins.

Specific dynamic allowance (previously called the thermic effect of food): This refers to the increased heat production or increased metabolic rate following the intake of food (diet-induced thermogenesis).

The values of SDA are

• 30% for proteins: This means that out of every 100 grams of proteins consumed, the energy available for doing useful work is 30% less than the calculated value - i.e 30% of the energy content in protein is used in its own metabolism.
• 15% for lipids, and
• 5% for carbohydrates.

Importance: It is a common experience that during hot weather following the consumption of a protein-rich meal, one feels hot and humid for a while. On the other hand, in cold weather, the same would provide a comfortable feeling.

The energy generated by the metabolism of the macronutrients is used for three energy-requiring processes that occur in the body:

• Resting metabolic rate
• Thermic effect of food (formerly termed specific dynamic action)
• Physical activity
questions.learning: Proteins — The thermic effect is highest in proteins. Specific dynamic allowance (previously called the thermic effect of food): This refers to the increased heat production or increased metabolic rate following the intake of food (diet-induced thermogenesis).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is considered harmful to a newborn baby in the immediate postnatal period?
options: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab
Giving a bath immediately after birth
Placing the baby on the mother's chest
questions.explanation: Bathing a newborn immediately after birth is considered harmful as it can cause rapid heat loss, leading to life-threatening hypothermia. Immediate bathing also removes the vernix caseosa, a naturally occurring coating that provides essential antimicrobial protection and moisturizing properties to the neonatal skin. Furthermore, it interrupts critical early bonding and delays the initiation of breastfeeding, which should ideally occur within the first hour of life. World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines mandate delaying the first bath for at least 24 hours, or a minimum of 6 hours if cultural factors intervene. Cleaning the eyes with sterile swabs (Option A) is a safe practice to prevent neonatal ophthalmia. Placing the infant on the mother’s chest (Option D) is a recommended practice to encourage warmth and early feeding. Thus, immediate bathing is the only harmful practice among the choices
questions.learning: Bathing a newborn immediately after birth is considered harmful as it can cause rapid heat loss, leading to life-threatening hypothermia. Immediate bathing also removes the vernix caseosa, a naturally occurring coating that provides essential antimicrobial…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: On palpation at the site marked by the red arrow on the image a bony ridge is felt. What is the vertebral level of the marked arrow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. T4-T5 intervertebral disc

A body ridge felt when palpated a few centimeters from the suprasternal notch represents the angle of Louis/sternal angle. Recent data place the sternal angle between the T4 vertebra and the upper half of the T5 vertebra in the majority of adults.

The mediastinum is divided into superior and inferior by a line joining the sternal angle to the T4-T5 intervertebral disc.

The sternal plane is traditionally reported to pass through the intervertebral disc between the T4-T5 vertebrae posteriorly and the manubriosternal joint (sternal angle or angle of Louis) at the level of the second costal cartilage anteriorly. It can be used as an anatomical landmark for structures of the mediastinum.

Pearl PF0473: Angle of Louis

The angle of Loius (sternal angle) is formed by the manubriosternal joint at the level of 2nd costal cartilage anteriorly.

A plane joining the angle of Louis to the intervertebral disc between T4 and T5, called the sternal plane marks the following anatomical landmarks:

* Separates superior mediastinum form inferior mediastinum.

* Marks the position superior limit of pericardium.

* Bifurcation of pulmonary trunk

* Bifurcation of trachea (newer studies shows its lower)

* Origin of arch of aorta.

* Site where superior venacava pierces the pericardium.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia most commonly presents as _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Female pseudohermaphroditism

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) most commonly presents as female pseudohermaphroditism as the most common enzyme deficiency is 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

A female pseudohermaphrodite is a genotypically normal female (46, XX), whose external genitalia resembles a male's.

The image below shows ambiguous genitalia in a female with CAH:

The mechanism underlying the endocrine defects in 21-hydroxylase deficiency is depicted in the image below:

Babies with 21-hydroxylase deficiency typically present around 10-14 days of age with the subset of symptoms due to aldosterone deficiency, cortisol deficiency and androgen excess.

Aldosterone deficiency leads to salt-wasting crises marked by hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and metabolic acidosis.

Cortisol deficiency causes manifestations like hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation, weight loss, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, and shock.

Androgen excess in 21-hydroxylase deficiency results in virilization of females, leading to female pseudohermaphroditism, and precocious puberty in males. Virilization is usually apparent at birth in females and within 2 to 3 years of life in males.

Without treatment, shock, cardiac arrhythmias, and death may occur within days or weeks.

Other options:

Option A: Male pseudohermaphroditism is seen in CAH due to 17α-hydroxylase deficiency resulting in incomplete virilization. 17α-hydroxylase deficiency is 2nd most common enzyme affected in CAH.

Option C: True hermaphroditism is presently referred to as an ovotesticular disorder of sex development(DSD). Here, both ovarian and testicular tissue is present. It is not due to CAH.

Option D: 46 XY intersex (now called 46 XY DSD) has under virilization of genitalia. Adrenal causes include lipoid adrenal hyperplasia, 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency,  17-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency, and not 21 hydroxylase deficiency.
questions.learning: Female pseudohermaphroditism Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) most commonly presents as female pseudohermaphroditism as the most common enzyme deficiency is 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

She also mentions difficulty in making certain facial expressions due to skin tightness. ANA staining pattern of the patient is shown in the image below.

Correct answer: A. Centromeric

• Raynaud phenomenon
• Tight, shiny skin (sclerodactyly)

Anti-RNA polymerase III → renal crisis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents with labour pain and on per vaginal examination her cervix is 7 cm dilated and fully effaced.What stage of labour is she in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phase of maximum slope

This woman, with 7 cm dilation and fully effaced cervix, is in the active phase of labor specifically the phase of maximum slope, where cervical dilatation occurs most rapidly.

Based on Friedman’s curve, the first stage of labor is divided into two phases; the latent and the active phase, which were further subcategorized only for the purpose of partograph-based monitoring.

The latent phase of labour is defined as the period between the onset of true labour pain and the point when the cervical dilatation becomes 3–4 cm.

The active phase has got three components:

* Acceleration phase with cervical dilatation of 3–4 cm.

* The phase of maximum slope of 4–9 cm dilatation.

* The phase of deceleration of 9–10 cm dilatation.

Note: Newer guidelines have demonstrated that in active labor cervical dilatation typically progresses at 5–6 cm. As per WHO 2020, active labour begins at ≥5 cm and as per ACOG 2019 ≥6 cm.
questions.learning: Phase of maximum slope — This woman, with 7 cm dilation and fully effaced cervix, is in the active phase of labor specifically the phase of maximum slope, where cervical dilatation occurs most rapidly.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are poor prognostic factors in endometrial adenocarcinoma? I. Estrogen and progesterone receptor positivity II. HER-2/neu gene expression III. Histologic types papillary serous or clear cell carcinoma IV. Aneuploid tumours Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

Endometrial adenocarcinoma is the most common gynecological malignancy in developed countries. Prognosis depends on several clinicopathological factors, including stage, grade, histological subtype, depth of myometrial invasion, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), receptor status, and molecular markers. Poor prognostic factors are associated with aggressive tumor behavior, increased recurrence, and reduced survival. The following are poor prognostic factors:

• II. HER-2/neu gene expression: Overexpression of HER-2/neu is associated with high-grade tumors, aggressive disease, and poor prognosis, particularly in uterine serous carcinoma.
• III. Histologic types papillary serous or clear cell carcinoma: These are Type II endometrial carcinomas, which are high-grade, aggressive tumors with early extrauterine spread and poor prognosis.
• IV. Aneuploid tumors: DNA aneuploidy is associated with higher tumor grade, increased recurrence, and worse survival.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. Estrogen and progesterone receptor positivity: ER and PR positivity are favorable prognostic factors because they indicate:

• Better differentiation
• Better response to hormonal therapy
• Improved survival

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: During prolonged starvation, which hormone is predominantly secreted to help maintain blood glucose levels?
questions.explanation: During starvation, glucagon is the primary hormone secreted to maintain blood glucose levels. It functions by stimulating glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) and gluconeogenesis (glucose synthesis) in the liver, while also increasing lipolysis in adipose tissue to provide alternative fuel sources. Insulin (Option B) levels decrease during starvation to limit glucose uptake by peripheral tissues and conserve it for the brain. Amylase (Option C) is a digestive enzyme, not a metabolic hormone. Somatostatin (Option D) inhibits both insulin and glucagon but does not directly drive the glucose elevation needed during a fast. As starvation progresses past the first 24 hours, glucagon remains essential for driving hepatic gluconeogenesis as glycogen stores are depleted. Cortisol and growth hormone also eventually increase to support these long-term metabolic adaptations

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 27-year-old man sustains a neck injury from an iron nail after falling while climbing stairs. Subsequently, he has difficulty shrugging his shoulders and turning his head, indicating damage to a structure responsible for these actions. Which anatomical structure is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The patient's inability to shrug his shoulders and turn his head points directly to a lesion of the spinal accessory nerve (Cranial Nerve XI). This nerve provides motor innervation to two major muscles in the neck and shoulder: the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid. The trapezius is responsible for shoulder shrugging and scapular elevation, while the sternocleidomastoid allows for head rotation to the opposite side. While the sternocleidomastoid muscle (Option C) itself is involved in the movement, the mechanism of injury (a penetrating nail in the neck) is more likely to damage the nerve supplying it. The deltoid muscle (Option B), supplied by the axillary nerve, is involved in shoulder abduction, not shrugging. The long thoracic nerve (Option D) innervates the serratus anterior; its injury causes "winging of the scapula" but does not impair head rotation or shrugging. Consequently, the spinal accessory nerve is the most likely injured structure

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old apparently healthy man who was carrying laxatives and enema apparatus developed abdominal pain at the airport and an X-ray was done which appears as shown below. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Body packer syndrome

The given image shows multiple cylindrical capsules in the stomach and intestine consistent with a diagnosis of body packer syndrome.

Body packers are individuals who swallow illegal costly drugs like heroin, cocaine with the purpose of smuggling. Usually, the drugs are carefully wrapped in latex or plastic and swallowed, to be excreted later on with the help of laxatives. Drugs are usually of similar radio-opacity as fecal material and may be difficult to detect on X-rays. CT scan may be done to aid in diagnosis.

Body stuffer syndrome refers to the act of ingesting or inserting drugs into the rectum or vagina when a person fears being caught, typically to hide evidence of possession. Drug toxicity may be seen due to systemic absorption

Other options:

Bezoar formation is generally seen in mentally disturbed individuals due to the consumption of indigestible substances

Pica is eating things which are non-edible like chalk, mud, etc seen in patients of Iron deficiency anemia

Fecolith may not be seen in stomach like this and may not be perfectly shaped
questions.learning: Body packer syndrome — The given image shows multiple cylindrical capsules in the stomach and intestine consistent with a diagnosis of body packer syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the following clinical finding seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior cranial fossa fracture

The image shows bilateral periorbital ecchymoses, which is called the panda sign, and it is seen in anterior cranial fossa fractures. It is also known as panda eyes/raccoon eyes.

Anterior cranial fossa fracture occurs due to direct impact. It is a contrecoup injury that occurs when there is a direct blow to the chin (in boxing). The impact is transmitted to the maxilla and base of the skull and results in a contrecoup fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. It presents with CSF rhinorrhea and periorbital hematoma or raccoon eyes and the image is shown below.

The pooling of blood surrounding the eyes is most commonly associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. This finding is typically not present during the initial evaluation.  It is delayed by 1 to 3 days. If bilateral, this finding is highly predictive of a basilar skull fracture.
questions.learning: Anterior cranial fossa fracture — The image shows bilateral periorbital ecchymoses, which is called the panda sign, and it is seen in anterior cranial fossa fractures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arises from 6th pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ductus arteriosus

Ductus arteriosus arises from the 6th pharngeal arch.

Pharyngeal arches appear in the 4th or 5th week of development and contribute to the formation of the head and neck region. They are formed as a series of 6 thickenings in the cranial most part of the foregut (the future pharynx). They are craniocaudally numbered from I to VI. The 5th pharyngeal arch disappears, so only 5 arches remain.

* The first pharyngeal arch is also known as the mandibular arch.

* The second pharyngeal arch is also known as the hyoid arch.

* The 3rd, 4th, and 6th pharyngeal arches have no special names.

Other options:

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the main role of Phase 1 in xenobiotic metabolism?
options: To make the compound more permeable across membranes
To extract functional proteins through oxidase/reductase reactions
To introduce or expose functional groups for further metabolism
To directly conjugate the compound and facilitate excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. To introduce or expose functional groups for further metabolism

Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) introduce or expose polar functional groups on xenobiotics. These reactions are mainly mediated by CYP450 enzymes. The purpose is to prepare the molecule for Phase II conjugation. Thus, Phase I increases chemical reactivity for further metabolism.

| Reaction | Example

| -------- | -------

| Oxidation | CYP450 mediated

| Reduction | Nitro → amine

| Hydrolysis | Ester breakdown

| Feature | Phase I | Phase II

| ------- | ------- | --------

| Function | Functionalization | Conjugation

| Reaction | Oxidation, reduction | Glucuronidation, sulfation

| Enzymes | CYP450 | Transferases

| Result | Slightly polar | Highly water-soluble
questions.learning: To introduce or expose functional groups for further metabolism Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) introduce or expose polar functional groups on xenobiotics.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child with B/L sensorineural hearing loss was given hearing aids, which have not been beneficial. Which of the following is the next treatment option for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cochlear implant

The next treatment option for this child is a cochlear implant.

A cochlear implant is an electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from hearing aid.

The principle of the surgery is to place the electrode array within the Scala Tympani Of Cochlea. Intact 8th nerve and the higher auditory pathway is a prerequisite for surgery. The facial recess (posterior tympanotomy) approach is the preferred surgical approach. Auditory brainstem implant is placed in the lateral recess of 4th ventricle

Pearl PF1581: Cochlear implant

A cochlear implant replaces the organ of Corti i.e. when hair cells of the organ of Corti are severely damaged these implants bypass it and directly stimulate the auditory nerve.

Indication: Bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss i.e. > 70 dB.

Components:

Preoperative investigation: Complete audiological evaluation and HRCT and MRI (to detect the structure of cochlea, cochlear nerve and CNS abnormalities).

Surgical approach: Two surgical techniques to approach the cochlea for implantation are the facial recess approach (via facial recess) and the pericanal technique (via EAC).

Postoperatively: Activation of the device after 3-4 weeks and evaluation is by HRCT (MRI is contraindicated).

Contraindications:

* Absence of cochlea (Michel aplasia)

* Deafness due to absent cochlear nerve, lesions of cochlear nerve or lesions of the central auditory pathway
questions.learning: Cochlear implant — The next treatment option for this child is a cochlear implant. A cochlear implant is an electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from hearing aid.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, which disease is being controlled by targeting the insect shown in the image as its vector?
questions.explanation: The insect shown in the image is a Culex mosquito, which can be identified by its brownish body, short palps, and resting position parallel to the skin surface. Under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, control measures targeting Culex mosquitoes are primarily aimed at preventing Japanese encephalitis (JE), a viral disease caused by a flavivirus. The principal vector is Culex tritaeniorhynchus, which breeds in rice fields and stagnant water and transmits the infection from animal reservoirs like pigs and birds to humans. Other options are incorrect: (A) Chikungunya is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus), not Culex. (B) Malayan filariasis can be transmitted by Culex species, but the primary disease targeted under NVBDCP with this vector image is Japanese encephalitis. (C) Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is transmitted by sandflies (Phlebotomus), not mosquitoes. Thus, the mosquito shown is most closely associated with Japanese encephalitis control
questions.learning: The insect shown in the image is a Culex mosquito, which can be identified by its brownish body, short palps, and resting position parallel to the skin surface.

questions.text: A 36-year-old PLHIV presents with occasional fever, productive cough, and haemoptysis for 3 months. The chest X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tuberculosis

A 36-year-old PLHIV (Person Living with HIV) with:

• Chronic symptoms (3 months)
• Fever
• Productive cough
• Hemoptysis

This classic triad strongly points toward Pulmonary tuberculosis.

Inhalation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Alveolar macrophage infection

Granuloma formation

Hemoptysis + chronic cough

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the right knee. Radiograph shows the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patellar fracture

The radiograph shows the displaced patellar fracture.

A patellar fracture can either occur via a direct injury to the knee or because of a violent contraction of the quadriceps.

The fracture may be undisplaced either because of the pre-patellar expansion of the quadriceps tendon which holds the fragments together or because of the patellar retinaculae on the sides.

Patellar fracture results in the disruption of the extensor apparatus (not the flexor apparatus).

Due to the disruption of the extensor apparatus, the patient will not be able to lift his leg with the knee in full extension; it remains in a position short of full extension (extensor lag). Clinically, it can be tested using the Active Straight leg raising (SLR) test, which the patient will not be able to perform.

The extensor apparatus of the knee includes the Quadriceps femoris muscle with its tendon, the patella bone and, the ligamentum patellae with its insertion into the tibial tuberosity.

An un-displaced fracture of the patella is treated with a plaster cast extending from the groin to just above the malleoli, with the knee in full extension. This is called as a cylinder cast and is usually left in place for a period of at least 3 weeks.

A two part fracture (Displaced transverse fracture) of the patella must be reduced, and the fragments are fixed with tension band wiring using K wires and the extensor retinaculae is repaired

Other treatment options which are available for patellar fracture are:

* Undisplaced patellar fractures with minimal joint incongruity and intact extensor retinaculum can be treated by cylinder cast.

* Displaced patellar fractures are usually treated by tension band wiring.

* Severely comminuted fractures where the reduction of the fragments is difficult are treated by patellectomy.

Pearl PF1177: Tension band wiring

A tension band wire is a form of internal fixation used to convert distraction forces into compression forces, promoting bone healing.

It is used in:

* Fracture patella

* Fracture olecranon

* Fracture lateral malleolus

* Fracture greater trochanter
questions.learning: Patellar fracture — The radiograph shows the displaced patellar fracture. A patellar fracture can either occur via a direct injury to the knee or because of a violent contraction of the quadriceps.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the anatomical term for the vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?
questions.explanation: The human body is divided by standard anatomical planes to describe the orientation and location of structures. The coronal plane (Option A), also known as the frontal plane, is a vertical plane that passes through the body from side to side, effectively separating it into anterior (front) and posterior (back) sections. This plane is perpendicular to both the median and transverse planes. The transverse or axial plane (Options B and C) is a horizontal plane that divides the body into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) portions. The median or midsagittal plane (Option D) is a vertical plane that passes directly through the midline, dividing the body into equal right and left halves. Understanding these planes is fundamental for clinical examinations, surgical planning, and interpreting radiological imaging like CT and MRI. Therefore, based on the definition of dividing the body into front and back sections, the coronal plane is the correct term
