questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the diagnostic test for carcinoid tumors?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine neoplasms that can secrete excessive amounts of serotonin. The most definitive diagnostic screen for carcinoid syndrome is measuring 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels. 5-HIAA is the primary end-metabolite of serotonin. For accurate results, patients must avoid serotonin-rich foods like bananas, walnuts, and pineapples before the test. 24-hour urinary catecholamines (Option A) are used to diagnose pheochromocytoma. Serum calcitonin (Option B) is a marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma. Serum chromogranin A (Option C) is a useful general marker for neuroendocrine tumors but is less specific for the carcinoid syndrome than urinary 5-HIAA. Carcinoid syndrome typically presents with flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing, often occurring only after the tumor has metastasized to the liver. Imaging studies like OctreoScan or Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT are used to localize the primary tumor and assess the extent of metastasis
questions.learning: Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine neoplasms that can secrete excessive amounts of serotonin. The most definitive diagnostic screen for carcinoid syndrome is measuring 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with symptoms of delayed adaptation to vision in dark places, gritty sensation in the eyes, dry eyes, and softening of the cornea. What is the likely deficiency in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoic acid

The clinical picture of delayed adaptation to vision in dark places, gritty sensation in the eyes, dry eyes, and softening of the cornea is suggestive of vitamin A deficiency in the patient. Hence retinoic acid (the active form of vitamin A) is likely to be deficient.

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that can occur as carotenoids (most common - beta carotene from plant sources) or retinoids (from animal sources).

3 forms of retinoids are:

• Retinal is required mainly for normal vision (present in the visual pigment rhodopsin).
• Retinol is important for the normal functioning of the reproductive system.
• Retinoic acid has a role in the regulation of gene expression and tissue differentiation.

Ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency include loss of sensitivity to green light (earliest to appear), nyctalopia (night blindness), xerophthalmia.

Xerophthalmia includes conjunctival xerosis (dryness) with Bitot’s spots (white patches of keratinized epithelium appearing on the sclera), corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia (softening of the cornea) that leads to corneal scarring and ultimately, blindness.

Other manifestations: General impairment of immunity, keratinization of skin (phrynoderma/toad skin).

Treatment: The WHO recommended schedule for all patients above the age of 1 year (except women of reproductive age): 200,000 IU of vitamin A orally or 100,000 IU by intramuscular injection should be given immediately on diagnosis (day 0) and repeated the following day (day 1) and 14 days later.
Dietary sources of vitamin A are liver, fish, eggs, dark green, and deeply colored fruits and vegetables.

Bitot's spots

The below image shows phrynoderma with multiple keratotic papules

Other options:

Option B: Ocular manifestations of riboflavin deficiency (vitamin B2) are photophobia, burning sensation, and vascularization of the cornea. Other features include cheilosis, magenta-colored tongue, glossitis, and seborrheic dermatitis.

Corneal vascularization. Seen in riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency.

Option C: Niacin deficiency (vitamin B3) leads to pellagra. Dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia are its common features.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency

Option D: Features of pantothenic acid deficiency (vitamin B5) are burning foot syndrome ( "nutritional melalgia"), dermatitis, enteritis, alopecia, ataxia.
questions.learning: Retinoic acid — The clinical picture of delayed adaptation to vision in dark places, gritty sensation in the eyes, dry eyes, and softening of the cornea is suggestive of vitamin A deficiency in the patient.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which metallic poisoning causes proximal convoluted tubule damage with proteinuria and muscle pain ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arsenic

Arsenic poisoning causes PCT damage with proteinuria and muscle pain.

Nephropathy is caused by most of the heavy metals. However, muscle pain is seen with arsenic poisoning.

Salient features of Arsenic poisoning:

Acute poisoning: Resembles cholera; garlicky odor

Chronic poisoning: Following features are seen:

• Raindrop pigmentation seen on temples, eyelids and neck
• Aldrich-Mee’s lines (transverse white striae on the fingernails)
• Hyperkeratosis of palms and soles
• Painful paraesthesia of hands and feet
• Red velvety appearance of stomach
• Blackfoot disease - a gangrenous condition affecting the extremities

Tests to detect Arsenic poisoning:

• Marsh test and Reinsch test

Treatment:

Freshly prepared hydrated ferric oxide.

BAL(British Anti Lewisite)

Penicillamine(If BAL not available)

Note: Mercury does not cause muscle pain though it commonly causes PCT damage.

Mee’s lines- Transverse white striae of the fingernails

Hyperkeratosis of palms and soles

Rain drop pigmentation
questions.learning: Arsenic Arsenic poisoning causes PCT damage with proteinuria and muscle pain. Nephropathy is caused by most of the heavy metals.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly male patient presented with severe pain in ear and otorrhoea. Investigations revealed that his HbA1C is 10%. The likely diagnosis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant otitis externa

Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea indicates malignant otitis externa.

It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa:

* Pseudomonas infection in the elderly diabetics and those on immunosuppressive drugs.

* Excruciating pain, profuse discharge & granulations on the floor of EAC.

* Facial paralysis is common.

* Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection.

* Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen causing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

* Technetium 99 bone scan reveals bone infection, but the test remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to monitor the disease. Gallium-67 is more useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the patient

The treatment of malignant otitis external would include control of diabetes, ear toileting to remove the discharge, debris or granulation tissue, antibiotic therapy against Pseudomonas with fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins, beta-lactam antibiotics with/without aminoglycosides.

If the patient is not responsive, culture and sensitivity of ear discharge should be done.
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea indicates malignant otitis externa. It is termed malignant, though being an infection due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which element plays a key role in the activation of the complement system via the alternative pathway?
questions.explanation: The alternative complement pathway is a key component of innate immunity and is unique because it is antibody-independent. It is continuously active at a low level through a process known as “C3 tick-over.” In this pathway, C3 undergoes spontaneous hydrolysis, generating C3b, which can bind directly to the surfaces of pathogens. This binding initiates the formation of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), which cleaves additional C3 molecules and creates a powerful amplification loop of complement activation. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. C1 (Option A), C4 (Option D), and C2 (Option B) are components of the classical and lectin pathways, not the alternative pathway. In those pathways, they form the C3 convertase C4b2a after antibody or lectin binding. 2. Because C3 is the central component where all complement pathways converge, deficiency of C3 leads to severe, recurrent pyogenic infections due to impaired opsonization and complement activation. Thus, C3 is the crucial element involved in activation of the complement through the alternative pathway
questions.learning: The alternative complement pathway is a key component of innate immunity and is unique because it is antibody-independent. It is continuously active at a low level through a process known as “C3 tick-over.” In this pathway, C3 undergoes spontaneous…

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl has intense cravings for food. She eats large amounts of food, which is followed by self-induced vomiting. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulimia nervosa

The probable diagnosis in the given scenario of a 16-year-old girl with intense food cravings followed by self-induced vomiting is bulimia nervosa.

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder, often seen in young women. It is characterized by binge-eating episodes, followed by inappropriate, compensatory measures to stop weight gain, like self-induced vomiting, laxative abuse, diuretics, enema, and emetic abuse. These binge-eating episodes occur at least once a week and are present for at least 3 months. The patient fears gaining weight and has a relentless drive to be thin.

The weight is normal in most patients with bulimia nervosa. However, few patients may either be overweight or underweight. There is a risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

Treatment modalities are cognitive behavioral therapy, psychotherapy, and antidepressants such as fluoxetine.

Other options:

Option A: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder that is often seen between the ages of 10 and 30. Typical features are self-induced starvation, voluntary and unhealthy reduction in weight, intense drive for thinness, and fear of becoming obese. These symptoms are usually present for at least a period of 3 months. Associated features can include depression, anxiety, amenorrhea in females, hypothermia, and bradycardia.

Option C: Atypical depression is a type of depression characterized by mood reactivity, which is brightening of the mood in response to positive events; significant weight gain or increase in appetite; hypersomnia; leaden paralysis; and/or interpersonal rejection sensitivity, resulting in significant social or occupational impairment.

Option D: Binge-eating disorder is the most common eating disorder. It is characterized by rapid intake of abnormally large quantities of food over a short period of time, even when not hungry. There are feelings of guilt about the eating episodes, but these patients do not compensate in any way following the episodes of binge.
questions.learning: Bulimia nervosa — The probable diagnosis in the given scenario of a 16-year-old girl with intense food cravings followed by self-induced vomiting is bulimia nervosa.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Ritodrine, which prevents premature labour, causes all of the following maternal complications, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoglycaemia

Ritodrine when administered predisposes to fetal hypoglycaemia and maternal hyperglycaemia.

Preterm labour and delivery (labour starts before the 37th completed week, counting from the first day of the last menstrual period) can be delayed by drugs such as ritodrine, in order to improve the perinatal outcome. A short-term delay of 48 hours allows the use of corticosteroids that can reduce perinatal mortality and serious morbidity significantly.

Complications of ritodrine are as follows :

* Maternal:

* Headache

* Palpitation

* Tachycardia

* Pulmonary oedema

* Hypotension

* Cardiac failure

* Hyperglycaemia

* Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)

* Hyperinsulinemia

* Lactic acidemia

* Hypokalaemia

* Potential death

2. Fetal:

* Hypoglycaemia

* Intraventricular haemorrhage

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman experiences unilateral, pulsating headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia, with relief in a dark room. Which medication is appropriate for preventing and reducing the frequency of future headache episodes?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral pulsating headache, nausea, and photophobia—are diagnostic of migraine. The question asks for a medication to reduce the frequency of future episodes, which indicates prophylactic therapy rather than acute treatment. Propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker, is one of the first-line agents approved for migraine prophylaxis. It works by modulating thalamocortical excitability and vascular tone. Alprazolam (Option B) and Diazepam (Option C) are benzodiazepines used for anxiety and have no role in preventing migraines. Fluoxetine (Option D) is an SSRI used for depression; while some antidepressants like Amitriptyline are used for migraine, Fluoxetine is not a standard prophylactic choice. Prophylaxis is generally indicated if a patient has more than two to three disabling attacks per month. Patients must be counseled that Propranolol is a preventive measure and will not provide relief during an acute attack. Thus, Propranolol is the most appropriate prophylactic agent listed for this 26-year-old female
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral pulsating headache, nausea, and photophobia—are diagnostic of migraine. The question asks for a medication to reduce the frequency of future episodes, which indicates prophylactic therapy rather than acute treatment.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents with a mass in the neck. Her T4 levels are high with decreased TSH. She undergoes thyroid ablation therapy using I-131. What is the most likely adverse effect associated with I-131 treatment in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypothyroidism

I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for treatment of thyroid cancer. The most likely adverse effect is hypothyroidism.

I131 emits both beta and gamma rays. It is used both for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes for thyroid disorders.

I-131 therapy is commonly used to ablate any remaining thyroid tissue after a total thyroidectomy, particularly in cases of thyroid cancer or hyperthyroidism. The goal is to destroy these remaining cells, and while effective, this process almost invariably leads to hypothyroidism. This is an expected and often desired outcome, as the patient will then be managed with levothyroxine replacement therapy to maintain normal thyroid hormone levels.

Other options:

Options A and C: Thyroid storm is a state of severe hyperthyroidism, I-131 destroys thyroid tissue, making hyperthyroidism or thyroid storm unlikely.

Option D: Osteoporosis is not a known side effect of I-131 therapy.
questions.learning: Hypothyroidism I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for treatment of thyroid cancer.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the correct order of a family cycle?
options: Formation, extension, complete extension, dissolution, contraction, complete contraction
Formation, contraction, extension, complete extension, dissolution, complete contraction
Formation, contraction, complete contraction, extension, complete extension, dissolution
Formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution

The order of the family cycle is formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction and dissolution.

Pearl PF1702: The Family as a Social Organization

* A family is a group of biologically related individuals living together under the same roof and eating from a common kitchen.

* It is the most primary and basic unit of all societies.

* The basic and arbitrary model of a family cycle has six phases:

Phase

Beginning

End

1

Formation

Marriage

Birth of 1st child

2

Extension

Birth of 1st child

Birth of last child

3

Complete extension

Birth of last child

1st child leaves home

4

Contraction

1st child leaves home

Last child leaves parental home

5

Completed contraction

Last child leaves parental home

Death of 1st spouse

6

Dissolution

Death of 1st spouse

Death of survivor

* Types of families:

* A nuclear family or elementary family consists of only the married couple and their offspring while they are dependants.

* The term new family is applied when nuclear families are younger than 10 years and consist of parents and children.

* A joint family or extended family consists of a number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood. All property in joint families is held in common with the family income going into a common pocket. A senior male member is usually the head of the family who makes decisions.

* A three generation family is one where there are representatives from three different generations in one house.

* A communal family is one in which all the members play a part in its management.

* Functions of the family:

* Residence (patrilocal and matrilocal)

* Division of labour

* Reproduction and raising children

* Socialization and social care

* Economic functions

* Problems families are those that lag behind the rest of the community in terms of standard and quality of life of its members.

* Broken families are those in which the parental or family system has been disrupted by separation, divorce or death.
questions.learning: Formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution The order of the family cycle is formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction and dissolution.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which contraceptive device has the longest duration of effectiveness?
questions.explanation: The Copper T 380 A (Option B) is one of the most effective and long-lasting forms of reversible contraception. It is FDA-approved for 10 years of continuous protection, which is the longest duration among the devices listed. Progestasert (Option A) was an early progesterone-releasing IUD that required replacement every year. Mirena (Option C), a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), is approved for 5 to 8 years of use depending on the specific clinical indication and regional guidelines. The Nova T (Option D) is a copper-containing IUD with a typical effective duration of 5 years. Because the CuT 380 A contains a larger amount of copper wire and sleeves (380 ) than other models, it provides the most durable long-term prevention of pregnancy, making it a highly cost-effective option for women seeking long-term birth control
questions.learning: The Copper T 380 — A (Option B) is one of the most effective and long-lasting forms of reversible contraception. It is FDA-approved for 10 years of continuous protection, which is the longest duration among the devices listed.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with lung adenocarcinoma comes for her chemotherapy treatment. She has had multiple complaints of nausea and vomiting during her previous treatment visits. Which of the following is used to prevent chemotherapy-induced emesis and vomiting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Palonosetron

Palonosetron is used in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

Palonosetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist that blocks serotonin in vagal terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ). It has a higher receptor affinity as compared to the first-generation 5HT3 antagonists making it more potent. It is also useful in delayed emesis associated with chemotherapy due to its long half-life.

During chemotherapy, there is cell lysis and 5HT(serotonin) is released from the gut mucosa. The released serotonin acts on the 5HT3 receptors and activates the vagal afferents in the gut that carry the emetogenic impulses to the nucleus tractus solitarius and chemoreceptor trigger zone. The selective blockade of 5HT3 receptors reduces the emetogenic impulses.

It is used in combination with netupitant in acute and delayed nausea and vomiting. Netupitant is an NK1 receptor antagonist. It augments the effects of palonosetron. This combination is particularly anti-emetogenic when given along with dexamethasone.

Other options:

Option A: Metoclopramide is a 5HT4 agonist and D2 blocker and is used as an antiemetic agent.

Option B: Ropinirole is an antiparkinsonian drug that is a dopamine agonist and is also the drug of choice for restless leg syndrome.

Option C: Domperidone is not used in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
questions.learning: Palonosetron Palonosetron is used in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Palonosetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist that blocks serotonin in vagal terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding bempedoic acid:
options: It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase
It inhibits the de novo synthesis of cholesterol in hepatocytes
It can be used concomitantly with statins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase

Bempedoic acid works upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol synthesis pathway.

This enzyme: ATP-Citrate Lyase (ACL)

converts citrate → acetyl-CoA, which is required for cholesterol synthesis.

Bempedoic acid inhibits ATP citrate lyase, a key enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Bempedoic acid blocks cholesterol synthesis earlier than statins, Less muscle toxicity compared to statins

It is a dicarboxylic acid that reduces de novo cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes.

Statin + Bempedoic acid → synergistic LDL reduction

It can be safely used in combination with statins for additive LDL reduction.

adverse effects:

• Hyperuricemia

• Gout

• Tendon rupture (rare)

The inhibition of ATP citrate lyase is not non-competitive, making option A false.
questions.learning: It is a non-competitive Inhibitor ATP citrate lyase Bempedoic acid works upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol synthesis pathway. This enzyme: ATP-Citrate Lyase (ACL) converts citrate → acetyl-CoA, which is required for cholesterol synthesis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: While performing surgery for acute appendicitis on a 2 year old child the following structure was found 2 feet proximal to ileocaecal junction and it was 2 inches long. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meckel's diverticulum

The given clinical viignette and image is suggestive of Meckel's diverticulum which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel.

The most common true diverticulum is Meckel's diverticulum, which occurs in the ileum.

A true diverticulum is a blind outpouching of the alimentary tract that communicates with the lumen and includes all three layers of the bowel wall. Meckel diverticulum occurs as a result of the failed involution of the vitelline duct, which connects the lumen of the developing gut to the yolk sac.

Meckel’s Diverticulum:

* Meckel’s diverticulum is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5 to 7 of gestation.

* The rule of 2s (Mnemonic for Meckel’s diverticulum) :

* 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic)

* 2% incidence

* located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve

* approximately 2 inches in length

* Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age

* Most common presentation is painless, massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years.

* A Meckel's can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.

* The bleeding Meckel's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect gastric mucosa.

* Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel’s diverticulum. A simple V-shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach.

Pearl PF0287: Rule of two’s in Meckel's diverticulum

* 2% prevalence

* 2:1 male predominance

* Location 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve in adults

* 2 inches in length

* Half of those who are symptomatic are under 2 years of age.

Pearl PF0326: Zenker’s Diverticulum

* Hypopharyngeal diverticulum

* False diverticulum

* Pulsion diverticulum

* Acquired diverticulum, seen in the elderly (>60 years)

* Herniation is through the Killian’s triangle (a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor) in the posterior pharyngeal wall

* Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

* Investigation of choice: Barium swallow (Lateral X rays)

* Treatment

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure

Zenker’s diverticulum
questions.learning: Meckel's diverticulum — The given clinical viignette and image is suggestive of Meckel's diverticulum which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of heartburn and regurgitation of food for the past few years. Endoscopy and biopsy results reveal red, velvety mucosa admixed with white mucosa, along with the presence of goblet cells. Which of the following epithelial transformations will be observed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Squamous to intestinal columnar epithelium

This patient's clinical features and biopsy findings are suggestive of Barrett's oesophagus, which is characterised by epithelial transformation from squamous to intestinal columnar epithelium above the gastro-oesophageal junction.

Microscopically, it is seen as the replacement of the squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells. The greatest concern in Barrett's oesophagus is that it confers an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma. Barrett's oesophagus is a complication of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and it is estimated to occur in about 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD.

Symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, and sometimes dysphagia. Obese white men over the age of 60 years represent the highest-risk group. On endoscopy, Barrett's is recognised as areas of red, velvety mucosa extending proximally from the gastro-oesophageal junction. Such areas alternate with normal pale squamous esophageal mucosa. Diagnostic confirmation is by endoscopic biopsy. A biopsy reveals intestinal metaplasia characterised by the presence of goblet cells. Goblet cells are seen as cells with pale mucous vacuoles that stain blue.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly woman presents with a chronic history of pain in the small joints of hands with stiffness of joints in the early hours of the day. The image of the patient’s hands is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatoid Arthritis

The above image shows flexion at the PIP joint and extension in the DIP joints which is known as boutonniere deformity which is seen in rheumatoid arthritis(RA).

If the patient gives a history of pain/stiffness in the joints in the early hours of the day which usually decreases as the day progresses suggesting inflammatory arthritis and if it presents with predominant involvement of smaller joints, it is most likely a case of RA(option A).

It occurs due to the accumulation of inflammatory mediators which on increased joint mobility are flushed out due to increased blood supply.

Pain and stiffness in osteoarthritis (Option B) usually increase as the day progresses due to an increase in the activity of the joint. They typically present with nodules around the distal interphalangeal joint (Heberden nodes) and proximal interphalangeal joint (Bouchard nodes).
questions.learning: Rheumatoid Arthritis — The above image shows flexion at the PIP joint and extension in the DIP joints which is known as boutonniere deformity which is seen in rheumatoid arthritis(RA).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Labour induction is not done in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Induction of labor (artificial initiation of contractions) is contraindicated in Central (Type IV) Placenta Previa. In this condition, the placenta completely covers the internal os of the cervix. Attempting a vaginal delivery (via induction) would lead to massive, life-threatening maternal hemorrhage and fetal distress as the cervix dilates. All such cases must be delivered via a planned or emergency cesarean section. Gestational hypertension (Option B), Premature Rupture of Membranes (PROM) (Option C), and certain cases of stable Abruptio placenta (Option D) are actually common indications for induction to ensure the safety of the mother and fetus. Other contraindications for induction include prior classical C-section scars and active genital herpes. Proper selection of patients for induction is critical in obstetric practice to avoid high-risk vaginal delivery attempts where the placental position or structural anomalies make it unsafe
questions.learning: Induction of labor (artificial initiation of contractions) is contraindicated in Central (Type IV) Placenta Previa. In this condition, the placenta completely covers the internal os of the cervix.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During neurological examination, the clinician observes concentric rings with multiple colors around the periphery of the patient’s iris. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of "concentric rings" around the outer edge of the iris in a 30-year-old woman with an unsteady gait and labile moods is diagnostic of Kayser-Fleischer (K-F) rings. These rings are golden-brown or greenish deposits of copper in the Descemet membrane of the cornea, which occur in Wilson's disease—a disorder of impaired biliary copper excretion. The patient's neurological symptoms result from copper accumulation in the basal ganglia. Neurofibromatosis 1 (Option C) is associated with Lisch nodules, which are small, raised pigment spots on the iris. Neurofibromatosis 2 (Option A) and cataracts (Option D) do not produce these specific corneal rings. The K-F ring is a pathognomonic clinical finding that requires confirmation via slit-lamp examination. Early diagnosis of Wilson's disease is critical as it is treatable with copper-chelating agents. Therefore, the combination of specific ocular and neurological signs confirms the diagnosis
questions.learning: The presence of "concentric rings" around the outer edge of the iris in a 30-year-old woman with an unsteady gait and labile moods is diagnostic of Kayser-Fleischer (K-F) rings.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which anticancer drug is used in the treatment of both Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST) and Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)?
questions.explanation: Imatinib is a breakthrough targeted therapy that works as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It was specifically designed to inhibit the BCR-ABL fusion protein found in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), which is created by the "Philadelphia chromosome" translocation. Additionally, Imatinib is the standard treatment for Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST) because it inhibits the c-KIT and PDGF receptor tyrosine kinases that drive these tumors. This drug revolutionized the treatment of CML, turning what was once a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition. Methotrexate (Option B) is an antimetabolite used for many cancers and autoimmune diseases. Doxorubicin (Option C) is an anthracycline that works by DNA intercalation. Cisplatin (Option D) is a platinum-based alkylating agent. Imatinib's success paved the way for the development of many other targeted "small molecule" inhibitors, which focus on specific genetic mutations in cancer cells while sparing normal tissue, significantly reducing side effects compared to traditional chemotherapy
questions.learning: Imatinib is a breakthrough targeted therapy that works as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It was specifically designed to inhibit the BCR-ABL fusion protein found in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), which is created by the "Philadelphia chromosome" translocation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the medicine OPD with acute vomiting shortly after consuming fried rice. Based on this clinical presentation and food history, which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The association between consuming "fried rice" and subsequent rapid-onset vomiting is a classic clinical clue for food poisoning caused by Bacillus cereus. B. cereus is a spore-forming bacterium often found in rice. If rice is cooked and then left at room temperature, the spores can germinate and produce a heat-stable emetic toxin. Reheating (frying) the rice does not inactivate this toxin, leading to vomiting within 1 to 6 hours of ingestion. Clostridium perfringens (Option A) and the diarrheal form of B. cereus typically present with diarrhea and a longer incubation period. Staphylococcus aureus (Option C) also causes rapid-onset vomiting but is usually linked to dairy products or meats. Bacillus anthracis (Option D) causes anthrax and is not a common cause of standard food poisoning. Therefore, Bacillus cereus is the most likely pathogen given the specific rice-based history
questions.learning: The association between consuming "fried rice" and subsequent rapid-onset vomiting is a classic clinical clue for food poisoning caused by Bacillus cereus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Acid Citrate Dextrose (ACD), used to store blood, preserves the RBCs for a period of 21 days. The storage period when adding phosphate alone and when adding adenine and phosphate together to ACD would respectively be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 21 days and 35 days

The storage period when adding phosphate alone to ACD would be 21 days and when adding adenine and phosphate together would be 35 days.

When adding phosphate to ACD, Citrate Phosphate Dextrose (CPD) is formed – It has a storage period of 21 days. There is no change in the shelf life as phosphate only increases the 2,3 DPG levels of the stored blood.

When adding both phosphate and adenine to ACD, Citrate Phosphate Dextrose Adenine (CPDA-1) is formed. It has a storage period of 35 days. It increases the shelf life by improving ATP synthesis of RBCs.

Using additive solutions containing saline, adenine, and glucose, with or without mannitol (SAGM) decreases RBC hemolysis, thus increasing the storage period to 42 days.
questions.learning: 21 days and 35 days The storage period when adding phosphate alone to ACD would be 21 days and when adding adenine and phosphate together would be 35 days.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following investigations provides the most accurate prognostic information with respect to predicting risks of perioperative cardiac complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dobutamine stress echocardiography

Among the given investigations, dobutamine stress echocardiography provides the most accurate prognostic information with respect to predicting risks of perioperative cardiac complications.

Preoperative cardiac stress testing can help identify the presence and severity of preexisting CAD. The prognostic performance of these tests is better assessed based on positive and negative likelihood ratios. Among all the given options, dobutamine stress echocardiography has the maximum positive likelihood ratio and hence provides the most accurate prognostic information.

Even though coronary angiography is considered the gold standard, it may not absolutely risk-stratify patients because many perioperative cardiac events may be related to noncritical coronary lesions.
questions.learning: Dobutamine stress echocardiography Among the given investigations, dobutamine stress echocardiography provides the most accurate prognostic information with respect to predicting risks of perioperative cardiac complications.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with golden-brown ring over iris on examination. What next is done to diagnose the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum ceruloplasmin

A golden-brown ring at the corneal periphery (Kayser–Fleischer ring) is characteristic of Wilson’s disease due to copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane.

Next best diagnostic step: Serum ceruloplasmin ↓ (initial screening test)

Supporting investigations:

• ↑ 24-hour urinary copper excretion
• ↑ hepatic copper (gold standard confirmation)
• Slit-lamp exam for KF ring

Why not others:

• Serum iron: Hemochromatosis
• Alpha-1 antitrypsin: AAT deficiency (liver/lung disease)
• Alpha-fetoprotein: Hepatocellular carcinoma marker
questions.learning: Serum ceruloplasmin — A golden-brown ring at the corneal periphery (Kayser–Fleischer ring) is characteristic of Wilson’s disease due to copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1-month-old infant presents with immediate crying after breastfeeding, along with diarrhea and vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The infant presents with immediate crying after breast feeding, along with diarrhea and vomiting, which suggests a problem related to milk digestion. Lactose intolerance occurs due to deficiency of lactase, the enzyme required to break down lactose into glucose and galactose. Pathophysiology : Undigested lactose remains in the intestine, leading to: 1. Osmotic diarrhea (draws water into lumen) 2. Gas production by bacterial fermentation → bloating, discomfort, crying 3. Symptoms appear immediately after feeding Why other options are incorrect: (B) Duodenal atresia: Presents with bilious vomiting soon after birth, not feeding-related crying and diarrhea (C) Galactosemia: Causes feeding intolerance with jaundice, hepatomegaly, not immediate crying after feeds (D) Pyloric stenosis: Presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting, usually without diarrhea Immediate symptoms after milk intake with diarrhea strongly indicate lactose intolerance
questions.learning: The infant presents with immediate crying after breast feeding, along with diarrhea and vomiting, which suggests a problem related to milk digestion. Lactose intolerance occurs due to deficiency of lactase, the enzyme required to break down lactose into…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with an intentional tremor, has difficulty performing the heel-to-shin test, and repeatedly misses the target on the finger- to-nose test. Based on these findings, what is the likely site of the lesion?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of intentional tremor (tremor that worsens as the target is approached), dysmetria (repeatedly missing the finger-nose test), and ataxia (demonstrated by the failed heel-to-shin test) is the classic triad of cerebellar dysfunction. The cerebellum is the brain's primary center for coordinating smooth, precise movements and maintaining balance. Lesions in the basal ganglia present differently: the Caudate (Option B) and Globus Pallidus (Option C) are involved in Parkinson's disease, showing resting tremors and bradykinesia. The Subthalamic nucleus (Option D) is associated with hemiballismus (violent, flinging movements). Intentional tremor is specifically a "kinetic" tremor characteristic of cerebellar strokes, tumors, or multiple sclerosis. Clinical evaluation of coordination is the cornerstone of the neurological exam for localizing the lesion to the posterior fossa. Management involves addressing the underlying cause and physical therapy for rehabilitation
questions.learning: The clinical combination of intentional tremor (tremor that worsens as the target is approached), dysmetria (repeatedly missing the finger-nose test), and ataxia (demonstrated by the failed heel-to-shin test) is the classic triad of cerebellar dysfunction.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is the first-line drug used to control seizures in a child presenting with febrile seizures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Midazolam

The first-line drug to control the seizures in febrile seizures is a benzodiazepine like midazolam or lorazepam.

Febrile seizures occur in children of the age of 6-60 months with a high-grade fever of 38°C (100.4 F) or higher without underlying CNS infections, metabolic abnormality, or prior afebrile seizures.

Risk factors:

Major:

* Age less than 1 year

* Duration of fever less than 24 hr

* Fever range: 38-39°C (100.4-102.2°F)

Minor:

* Family history of epilepsy

* Daycare

* Male gender

* Complex febrile seizure

* Family history of febrile seizures

* Lower serum sodium at the time of presentation

Types of febrile seizures:

Simple febrile seizures
Complex (atypical) febrile seizures

Occurs within 24 hours of the onset of fever
Can occur at any time during a fever

Generalized seizures
Focal seizures

Duration is <15 min
Prolonged (>15 min)

No recurrence within 24 hrs of seizures
Recurrent within 24 hours

Chances of going into epilepsy 1%
Chances of going into epilepsy 6%

Investigations:

* Lumbar puncture should be performed in the first episode of seizures with fever, for all infants <6 months age (to exclude meningitis).

* EEG and neuroimaging are advised for children with atypical febrile seizures.

Acute treatment of febrile seizures includes lorazepam and midazolam for seizures lasting more than 5 minutes. Rectal diazepam is prescribed to use at home as rescue medication if febrile seizures last more than 5 minutes. The use of antipyretics can decrease the discomfort of the child but does not reduce the risk of having a recurrent febrile seizure.

Prophylaxis:

* Intermittent prophylaxis includes oral clobazam for 3 days during the fever episode, if the febrile seizures recur at the rate of ≥3 seizures in 6 months, or ≥4 in 1 year.

* Continuous prophylaxis with sodium valproate and phenobarbitone can be used for failed intermittent prophylaxis and in recurrent atypical febrile seizures.

Note:

* Intermittent oral nitrazepam, clobazam, and clonazepam have also been used. Such therapies help reduce, but do not eliminate, the risks of recurrence of febrile seizures.

* Future epilepsy does not change with or without antiepileptic therapy.

* Iron deficiency is associated with an increased risk of febrile seizures, and thus screening and treating it would be appropriate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Laboratory investigations of a patient being evaluated for jaundice show elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels. Levels of the remaining liver enzymes are normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obstructive jaundice

The given laboratory reports showing elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin points to a likely diagnosis of obstructive jaundice.

Obstructive jaundice arises due to an obstruction in the biliary outflow due to choledocholithiasis, cholelithiasis, biliary strictures, etc. The patient presents with jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, pruritus, dark urine, and light-colored stools. The symptoms can be intermittent in cases of periampullary carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma.

Elevated conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) are characteristic of the condition. An associated rise in gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) levels confirms the hepatic origin of ALP.

An ultrasound is done initially in suspected cases of obstructive jaundice. A CT or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is recommended next. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is considered the gold standard for choledocholithiasis.

Jaundice arises due to the deposition of bilirubin in the body tissues. Bilirubin is a breakdown product of heme that circulates in the blood in the unconjugated/ indirect form. In the hepatocytes, it is conjugated with glucuronic acid to form conjugated/ direct bilirubin. Direct and indirect bilirubin can be assessed using Van den Bergh reaction.

Jaundice is broadly classified into:

• Pre-hepatic jaundice
• Hepatic jaundice
• Posthepatic jaundice

Other options:

Options B and D: Hemolytic jaundice is one of the common causes of prehepatic jaundice. These include sickle cell anemia, spherocytosis, and thalassemia. Inherited enzyme disorders, such as Gilbert's syndrome, and Crigler-Najjar types I and II, are other causes. In these cases, there is an isolated elevation of unconjugated bilirubin.

Option C: Hepatic jaundice shows an elevation of aspartate transaminase (AST) and alaline transaminase (ALT) out of proportion to ALP. An increased bilirubin level is also seen. Common causes include viral hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. An AST/ALT ratio ≥ 2 is highly suggestive of alcoholic hepatitis.
questions.learning: Obstructive jaundice — The given laboratory reports showing elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin points to a likely diagnosis of obstructive jaundice.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A girl develops eye pain after returning from a picnic and reports poor hygiene while handling her contact lenses. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation: Improper contact lens hygiene, particularly combined with exposure to contaminated water (picnic/outdoor setting), is a primary risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis. This free-living protozoan can invade the cornea, causing severe pain out of proportion to clinical signs, redness, and photophobia. A classic advanced sign is a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate. Plasmodium (Option B) causes malaria and does not affect the eye in this manner. While Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) is a common bacterial cause of contact lens keratitis, the clinical context of outdoor water exposure often points toward protozoal causes in exams. Herpes simplex (Option D) causes dendritic ulcers and is not specifically linked to contact lens hygiene. Therefore, Acanthamoeba is the most likely cause
questions.learning: Improper contact lens hygiene, particularly combined with exposure to contaminated water (picnic/outdoor setting), is a primary risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 56-year-old female with a history of myocardial infarction 2 years back now came with complaints of a cough and breathlessness on walking for a short distance. On examination, there was dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds on the right side. Chest X-ray showed moderate pleural effusion. Thoracocentesis was performed under ultrasound guidance and the lab investigations are given below. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis in this patient? Pleural fluid findings: * Appearance: turbid * pH: 7.1 * Protein: 3.2 g/dL * Lactate dehydrogenase: 80 U/L (normal serum LDH - 50-150 U/L) * Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio : 0.34 * Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH : 0.3 * Glucose: 54 mg/dL * WBC count: 4000 cells/μL with > 50% lymphocytes * Adenosine deaminase: 30 U/L * AFB smear microscopy: negative * Gram staining and microscopy: no organisms, no pus cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congestive heart failure

This patient's clinical presentation and laboratory findings are suggestive of congestive heart failure in which the effusion is transudative in nature.

In this patient,

* Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio : 0.34 (<0.5)

* Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH : 0.3 (<0.6)

* Pleural fluid LDH is < 2/3rd the upper limit of normal serum LDH (normal serum LDH - 50-150 U/L)

In this patient, according to Light's criteria, the pleural effusion is transudative.

Examples of transudative pleural effusions are effusions due to congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrosis. Exudative pleural effusions are caused by malignancies, bacterial infections, rheumatoid pleuritis, and pulmonary embolism

Other options:

Option A: In parapneumonic pleural effusion too, the effusion is exudative with pH < 7.2 and glucose < 60 mg/dL. However, the WBC count is usually >10,000 cells/μL with a predominance of neutrophils. Appearance is generally cloudy.

Option B: Pleural effusion associated with malignant pleural effusion is exudative in nature.

Option D: Although tubercular pleural effusion is also exudative with a predominance of lymphocytes, adenosine deaminase levels < 40 U/L as in this patient rules out tubercular effusion.

Pearl PF0570: Types of pleural effusion

Transudative Pleural effusion

* Congestive heart failure

* Cirrhosis

* Nephrotic syndrome

* Peritoneal dialysis

* Superior vena cava obstruction

* Myxedema

* Urinothorax

Exudative Pleural effusion

* Neoplastic disease: metastatic disease and mesothelioma

* Infectious disease

* Pulmonary embolization

* GI: Esophageal perforation, pancreatic disease, intraabdominal abscess etc.,

* Collagen vascular disease: SLE, rheumatoid pleuritis, Wegener's, Churg Strauss syndrome etc.,

* Post coronary bypass surgery

* Asbestos exposure

* Sarcoidosis

* Drug-induced pleural disease: nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine, amiodarone etc.,

* Radiation therapy

* Hemothorax

* Chylothorax

Cardiac failure (usually produce bilateral effusion; if unilateral predominantly right sided)

Cirrhosis of liver (hepatic hydrothorax)

Amebic liver abscess

Acute pancreatitis

Aortic dissection

Esophageal rupture

Dressler’s syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presented with an episode of acute onset dizziness and loss of consciousness which lasted for a few seconds followed by a regain of full consciousness. There were no similar episodes in the past. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this scenario?
options: ECG to rule out atrial fibrillation
If ECG is normal, CT scan should be done
Vestibular neuritis is a possible condition that can cause these symptoms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ECG to rule out atrial fibrillation

The clinical scenario of transient loss of consciousness in this patient is suggestive of syncope. Hence, an ECG must be done to rule out cardiac causes for syncope like - arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, sinus node dysfunction, supra ventricular tachycardias) or a structural cardiac abnormality.

A CT would only be required if a seizure or transient ischemic attack (TIA) is suspected. However, in this case - the episode only lasted for a few seconds, the patient has no history of similar episodes in the past and there are no lasting neurological deficits after the episode. Therefore, option B is incorrect.

Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness caused by global cerebral hypoperfusion. It can be due to multiple causes, but is broadly divided into - neurally mediated syncope, orthostatic hypotension and cardiac syncope.

The initial workup for a case of syncope includes:

1. Detailed history of the episode and past history of similar episodes
2. Physical examination mainly to check BP in standing and supine positions to
3. rule out orthostatic hypotension.
4. A resting ECG to look for cardiac arrhythmia
5. Option B: If the ECG is normal, no further tests are needed. If the ECG is suggestive of cardiac arrhythmia, then further tests including continuous ECG monitoring and electrophysiological studies may be done.

Option C: Tilt-table testing is done in patients with recurrent syncopal attacks who are suspected to have vasovagal syncope. Psychiatric evaluation is done in patients with recurrent unexplained syncopal attacks.

Option D: Vestibular neuritis is associated with vertigo, where the patients typically complain of dizziness and a sense of spinning of the head.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Fatty acid transport through mitochondrial membrane is via?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carnitine

Long-chain fatty acids cannot directly cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their transport into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation requires the carnitine shuttle system.

Mechanism (Carnitine shuttle):

1.      Fatty acids are activated to fatty acyl-CoA in the cytosol.

2.      Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine (outer mitochondrial membrane).

3.      Acyl-carnitine is transported across the inner membrane via a translocase.

4.      CPT-II reconverts acyl-carnitine to acyl-CoA inside the mitochondria for β-oxidation.

Defects in the carnitine shuttle (e.g., CPT deficiency) lead to impaired fatty acid oxidation → hypoketotic hypoglycemia and muscle weakness.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Acyl carrier protein: Involved in fatty acid synthesis, not transport.
• Cholesterol transporter: Not related to fatty acid mitochondrial entry.
• LCAT (Lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase): Involved in cholesterol metabolism (HDL function).
questions.learning: Carnitine Long-chain fatty acids cannot directly cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their transport into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation requires the carnitine shuttle system.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A woman who had undergone total knee replacement surgery comes with complaints of knee pain with the loosening of implants. The following histopathological slide was obtained which showed foreign body giant cells along with the appearance highlighted in the image below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metallosis

The given clinical scenario and image with the said foreign body giant cell point towards a diagnosis of metallosis.

Metallosis is an uncommon complication following total joint replacements of high wear joints like hip and knees. The metal from the prosthesis infiltrates the bone and soft tissue surrounding it. It presents with pain or squeaking on weight bearing or loosening of implant. Sometimes it may be asymptomatic with imaging findings (cloud sign or bubble sign). Aspiration reveals dark fluid consisting of metallic debris.
questions.learning: Metallosis — The given clinical scenario and image with the said foreign body giant cell point towards a diagnosis of metallosis. Metallosis is an uncommon complication following total joint replacements of high wear joints like hip and knees.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the WHO classification of astrocytoma, which specific grade is glioblastoma categorized as?
questions.explanation: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification of tumors of the central nervous system, astrocytomas are graded from I to IV based on their degree of malignancy and histological features. Glioblastoma (previously known as glioblastoma multiforme) is the most aggressive and lethal form, and it is definitively categorized as Grade IV. Grade I refers to benign, localized tumors like pilocytic astrocytoma. Grade II (Option B) are low-grade diffuse astrocytomas. Grade III (Option C) are anaplastic astrocytomas, which are malignant but less aggressive than glioblastoma. Grade IV tumors like glioblastoma are characterized by high mitotic activity, nuclear atypia, and pathognomonic features such as microvascular proliferation and/or necrosis. These tumors are highly invasive and have a very poor prognosis despite aggressive therapy. Therefore, Grade IV is the standard classification for glioblastoma in both academic and clinical settings
questions.learning: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification of tumors of the central nervous system, astrocytomas are graded from I to IV based on their degree of malignancy and histological features.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In a patient with CSOM, labyrinthine fistula most commonly involves
questions.explanation: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM), particularly the atticoantral type associated with cholesteatoma, can cause erosion of the bony labyrinth. The lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal (SCC) is the most common site for a labyrinthine fistula because it lies in the medial wall of the aditus and antrum, making it highly susceptible to pressure and osteolytic enzymes from a growing cholesteatoma. Option A (Superior SCC) and Option C (Posterior SCC) are involved much less frequently. Option D (Utricle) is deeper and better protected. Patients with a fistula often present with "fistula sign," where changes in ear canal pressure induce vertigo and nystagmus. Vertigo may also occur when cleaning the ear or with loud sounds (Tullio phenomenon). The presence of a fistula is a surgical priority during mastoidectomy. The surgeon must carefully remove the disease while preserving the underlying endosteum to prevent total sensorineural hearing loss (dead ear)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with unilateral throbbing headache accompanied by photophobia, nausea, and vomiting, with symptomatic relief following the use of sumatriptan. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of unilateral, throbbing pain with sensory sensitivities like photophobia and gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea/vomiting is the classic presentation of a migraine headache. The patient’s specific response to sumatriptan further confirms this diagnosis. Sumatriptan is a selective 5-HT receptor agonist that acts as a vasoconstrictor to reverse the cerebral vasodilation that occurs during the headache phase. Tension headaches (Option B) are typically bilateral, feel like a "band" of pressure, and lack systemic symptoms. Cluster headaches (Option C) feature severe peri-orbital pain with autonomic signs like eye watering and nasal congestion. Sinus headaches (Option D) are associated with facial pressure and nasal discharge, not photophobia. Migraines can occur with or without an aura—neurologic disturbances like scintillating scotomas that often precede the pain
questions.learning: The combination of unilateral, throbbing pain with sensory sensitivities like photophobia and gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea/vomiting is the classic presentation of a migraine headache.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is planned for laparoscopic surgery under general anesthesia as a day care procedure. Which of the following factors would make him unsuitable for day care surgery?
options: Home is 45 minutes away from the hospital
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
The patient has had general anesthesia in the past without complications
questions.explanation: The presence of a responsible adult attendant at home for the first 24 hours is a non-negotiable safety requirement for day care (ambulatory) surgery under general anesthesia. Post-anesthesia patients may have impaired judgment and a risk of falls or adverse reactions to pain medication. Living 45 minutes away (Option A) is generally acceptable as it allows for timely return if complications arise. A 1-hour surgery (Option B) is well within the typical limits for day care procedures. A previous history of uncomplicated anesthesia (Option D) is a positive indicator of suitability rather than a contraindication. Without a caregiver to monitor the patient, they cannot be safely discharged on the day of surgery
questions.learning: The presence of a responsible adult attendant at home for the first 24 hours is a non-negotiable safety requirement for day care (ambulatory) surgery under general anesthesia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following can be prevented by transfusing irradiated RBCs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Graft versus host disease

Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevent the incidence of graft versus host disease (GVHD) associated with the transfusion.

GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients and the transferred cells recognize the alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation but may occur following transplantation of solid organs too.

GVHD maybe of two types: acute and chronic.

Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalized rash), liver( in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But the affected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes.

Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensive skin damage, with destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemic sclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will be involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also be recurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to the grafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result in autoantibodies production.

Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation, before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence of GVHD. But irradiation also has its side effects such as recurrence of tumor in leukemic patients, increased incidence of graft failures and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents for emergency contraception within a few hours of unprotected sexual intercourse and prefers a single-dose option rather than multiple pills. What would be the most appropriate recommendation in this case?
questions.explanation: For emergency contraception (EC) following unprotected intercourse, Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is the most appropriate single-pill regimen. This progestin-only pill is highly effective when taken within 72 hours and fulfills the patient's preference for a single dose. It also avoids the high risk of nausea and vomiting associated with estrogen-containing pills. Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg (Option A) requires two doses taken 12 hours apart, which is less convenient. The combination regimen (Option B), known as the Yuzpe regimen, is less effective and has more side effects. Desogestrel 3 mg (Option D) is a daily contraceptive and is not a standard drug for emergency use. While the copper IUD is the most effective EC method, among oral options, the 1.5 mg single-dose levonorgestrel is the clinical standard

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with severe headache and neck stiffness but no other neurological deficits. An urgent CT scan is performed, showing the findings below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The patient presents with a sudden severe headache (thunderclap headache) and neck stiffness, which are classic clinical features of SAH caused by irritation of the meninges. On the non-contrast CT scan, the arrow indicates a hyperdense area in the basal cisterns, representing acute blood in the subarachnoid space. This appearance is characteristic and often described as a “star-shaped” pattern around the circle of Willis. Option (A) subdural hemorrhage is incorrect because it appears as a crescent-shaped collection along the cerebral convexity, not within the basal cisterns. Option (B) pituitary apoplexy typically presents with hemorrhage in the sellar/suprasellar region and may show visual disturbances rather than diffuse basal cistern hyperdensity. Option (D) pituitary carcinoma is extremely rare and presents as a mass lesion, not an acute hemorrhagic pattern on CT. Thus, the clinical presentation combined with CT findings confirms subarachnoid hemorrhage
questions.learning: The most likely diagnosis is subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The patient presents with a sudden severe headache (thunderclap headache) and neck stiffness, which are classic clinical features of SAH caused by irritation of the meninges.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to occur during a normal pregnancy? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elevated systolic blood pressure

Normal pregnancy is associated with major cardiovascular adaptations to meet increased maternal and fetal metabolic demands. Physiologic cardiovascular changes in pregnancy:

• Increased heart rate
• Increased cardiac output
• Increased blood volume
• Decreased systemic vascular resistance

Because systemic vascular resistance falls due to progesterone-mediated vasodilation and placental circulation, blood pressure usually:

• Decreases slightly during mid-pregnancy
• Returns toward baseline near term

Therefore, elevated systolic blood pressure is not a normal finding in pregnancy and may suggest hypertensive disorders such as gestational hypertension or preeclampsia.
questions.learning: Elevated systolic blood pressure Normal pregnancy is associated with major cardiovascular adaptations to meet increased maternal and fetal metabolic demands.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with a long history of dyspnea, chronic cough with sputum, and wheezing died of respiratory failure following a bout of lobar pneumonia. She was not a smoker or an alcoholic. The lung at autopsy is shown in the image below. Which of the following is most likely to cause the pathological changes shown?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency

The above gross specimen shows emphysematous damage involving enlargement of the entire acinus suggestive of panacinar emphysema. It is caused due to alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency.

In panacinar (panlobular) emphysema, the acini are uniformly enlarged from the level of the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli. It occurs commonly in the lower zones and in the anterior margins of the lung and is most severe at the bases.

The image below shows panacinar emphysema.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is brought by a lady police sub-inspector with an alleged history of sexual violence 2 days back. She was accompanied by her mother. The registered medical practitioner should do which of the following as the next step?
options: Documentation of injuries and examination findings
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Take a detailed history

The registered medical practitioner should take a detailed history as the next step.

The registered medical practitioner must take a detailed history and then take informed consent for examination. In case of refusal, an informed refusal is to be documented after explaining to them the consequences of choice. As part of the examination, they should collect specimens, preserve clothing, and document injuries and examination findings. Medical treatment and testing for pregnancy have to be done for all victims of sexual assault free of cost and police should be informed as per section 357-C of CrPc.

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 considers all individuals (both male and female) below the age of 18 years as children and protects them from sexual abuse. It defines various forms of sexual offenses which include:

• Sexual harassment: A person is said to commit sexual harassment upon a child when such person with sexual intent,

• Carries out any act with sexual connotations
• makes a child exhibit his/her body
• shows any object to a child in any form/media for pornographic purposes.

• Sexual assault

• Any act with sexual intent that involves physical contact without penetration.

• Aggravated sexual assault

• Similar to sexual assault along with the criteria explained under the term "aggravated".

• Penetrative sexual assault

• An act with sexual intent that involves physical penetration.

• Aggravated penetrative sexual assault

• Similar to penetrative sexual assault along with the criteria explained under the term "aggravated".

• Pornography

The term aggravated is used for those assaults done:

• by a person in a position of trust or authority such as police officer, security forces, relative, doctor.
• in the course of communal violence.
• on mentally & physically disabled.
• gang sexual assault.
• using deadly weapons.
• causing grievous hurt

The Act prescribes stringent punishment graded as per the gravity of the offense, with a maximum term of rigorous imprisonment for life and fine. Section 21(1) of the POCSO Act, 2012 requires mandatory reporting of cases of child sexual abuse to law enforcement authorities and applies to everyone including parents, doctors, and school personnel. Failure to report a suspicion of child abuse is an offense under the Act.
questions.learning: Take a detailed history — The registered medical practitioner should take a detailed history as the next step. The registered medical practitioner must take a detailed history and then take informed consent for examination.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which criteria is not included in the definition of severe NPDR?
questions.explanation: The international clinical grading for Severe Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) follows the "4-2-1 rule". A patient is classified as having severe NPDR if they meet any one of the following criteria: 1. More than 20 intraretinal hemorrhages in each of the four quadrants (Option B). 2. Definite venous beading in two or more quadrants (Option D). 3. Prominent Intra-Retinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMA) in one or more quadrants. Microaneurysms (Option A) are the earliest sign of NPDR and are present in all stages, but their specific count in all quadrants is not the primary diagnostic threshold for "severe" compared to the 4-2-1 rule. Venous looping (Option C) is a common vascular change in diabetes, but it is not one of the specific criteria used in the 4-2-1 rule to define the "severe" stage. Recognizing severe NPDR is critical because these patients have a very high risk of progressing to Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) within one year. Close monitoring and timely pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) can prevent severe vision loss in these high-risk individuals

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding radiation enteritis and proctocolitis: 1. Diarrhoea in the acute phase should be treated with codeine or loperamide. 2. Surgery is the treatment of choice and involves resection of the injured intestine. 3. Sucralfate enemas and hyperbaric oxygen are effective treatments. 4. Small bowel strictures and rectovaginal fistulae may develop as chronic complications. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3 and 4

Radiation enteritis and radiation proctocolitis are complications of abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy. They may present as acute (during or within 3 months of radiotherapy) or chronic (months to years later). Treatment is primarily conservative, while surgery is reserved only for severe complications.

• 1. Diarrhoea in the acute phase should be treated with codeine or loperamide ✓: Acute radiation enteritis is managed symptomatically with antidiarrheal agents (loperamide or codeine), hydration, and nutritional support.
• 2. Surgery is the treatment of choice and involves resection of the injured intestine ✗: Surgery is not the treatment of choice because irradiated bowel heals poorly and surgery has high morbidity. It is reserved only for complications such as obstruction, perforation, fistula, or refractory bleeding.
• 3. Sucralfate enemas and hyperbaric oxygen are effective treatments ✓: Sucralfate enemas are effective for chronic radiation proctitis, while hyperbaric oxygen therapy promotes healing in refractory cases.
• 4. Small bowel strictures and rectovaginal fistulae may develop as chronic complications ✓: Chronic radiation injury can cause fibrosis leading to strictures, fistulae, obstruction, and chronic bleeding.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Radiation enteritis and radiation proctocolitis are complications of abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy. They may present as acute (during or within 3 months of radiotherapy) or chronic (months to years later).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with the following injury that he sustained on being tackled by an opponent during the course of a football match. As the Casualty medical officer, you would enter the wound description in the case sheet as ____________________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laceration

The given image shows a laceration.

A laceration is a tear or a split in the skin, mucous membrane, muscle, or any internal organ, with a depth spanning more than the covering epithelium of the skin or an organ, and is produced by blunt force.

Features of laceration:

• Margins are irregular with pieces of tissue attached in between called tissue tags or bridges
• Bruising is seen around the margin
• Deeper tissues are unevenly divided with tissue tags
• Hair bulbs are crushed
• Depth of the wound contains abundant foreign material such as dust particles, paint material of the vehicle involved, etc
• In skin lacerations, usually one of the margins overhangs the other, which could help in assessing the direction of the force
• A laceration, on healing, produces a permanent scar.

Classification of a laceration:

• Split laceration (incised - like laceration)

• This occurs when the skin is crushed between two hard objects
• For example, during a fall, the scalp gets crushed between the skull from inside and hard ground outside. This results in a wound, which usually mimics an incised one unless examined closely.

• Stretch laceration

• As the name implies, it occurs due to the over-stretching of the skin, beyond its elasticity.
• This typically occurs in the setting of a fractured femur, where the fracture fragment may stretch and pierce the skin to project out

• Avulsed laceration

• An avulsion is a lesion where the skin only separates by tearing from the underlying tissues or peels off and overhangs the wound
• This is common in road traffic accidents.
questions.learning: Laceration — The given image shows a laceration. A laceration is a tear or a split in the skin, mucous membrane, muscle, or any internal organ, with a depth spanning more than the covering epithelium of the skin or an organ, and is produced by blunt force.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident with acute respiratory distress and distended neck veins. Imaging shows a large collection of air on the left side of the chest. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of trauma, respiratory distress, dilated neck veins (elevated JVP), and an X-ray showing a large volume of air in the hemithorax is pathognomonic for a Tension Pneumothorax. This is a life-threatening emergency where air under pressure compresses the heart and the opposite lung. The most appropriate immediate management is needle decompression. According to modern ATLS guidelines, this is performed by inserting a wide-bore needle into the 5th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line (or the 2nd space mid-clavicular line). This converts the tension pneumothorax into a simple one, stabilizing the patient until a chest tube can be placed. Intubation (Option B) and tracheostomy (Option C) address airway obstruction, not pleural air. Pericardiocentesis (Option D) is for cardiac tamponade. Therefore, immediate decompression is the life-saving next step
questions.learning: The clinical combination of trauma, respiratory distress, dilated neck veins (elevated JVP), and an X-ray showing a large volume of air in the hemithorax is pathognomonic for a Tension Pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During general anesthesia, which peripheral nerve is most commonly stimulated with a nerve stimulator to monitor the depth of neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is the standard site for peripheral nerve stimulation during anesthesia to monitor neuromuscular blockade (NMB). It is preferred because it is superficial at the wrist and provides a clear, measurable motor response in the adductor pollicis muscle. This response accurately reflects the depth of muscle relaxation and helps determine the timing for reversal or extubation. The radial nerve (Option A) is deeper and less reliable for this purpose. The median nerve (Option C) is typically used for somatosensory monitoring rather than NMB. While the tibial nerve (Option D) can be monitored, it is technically more difficult and less standardized than the ulnar approach. Thus, the ulnar nerve remains the gold standard
